aperture-duty-cycle.toml:
# Aperture duty-cycle demonstrator (ground segment & operations).
#
# How a contact plan divides a pool of steerable apertures between navigation
# (ranging / tracking) and communications (data), and what each session loses when
# more sessions are active than there are apertures.
#
# THE ARBITRATION POLICY IS AN INPUT. A duty figure is only meaningful relative to
# a stated rule for who wins the aperture, so the policy is declared here, echoed
# back in the report with its full definition, and named in the one-line summary.
#   navigation-priority       (default) navigation preempts communications
#   communications-priority             communications preempts navigation
#   first-come-first-served             non-preemptive; the holder keeps the aperture
#
# Re-run with `apertures = 1` to see the one-aperture time-share: on this plan
# navigation is served in full either way and the whole contention loss lands on
# the communications sessions.
#
# HONEST SCOPE: MODELLED scheduling arithmetic over the supplied windows. No slew /
# retune / changeover time is charged when an aperture changes service or session;
# no data volume, buffer state, energy budget or link closure enters the decision;
# and the contact windows are inputs -- their geometry is whatever produced them
# (the `passes` scenario emits the same aos_s / los_s vocabulary). Not a
# ground-segment scheduling product.
# Run:  kshana scenarios/aperture-duty-cycle.toml
kind = "aperture-duty-cycle"

apertures = 2
arbitration = "navigation-priority"

# The reporting horizon defaults to the plan envelope (earliest aos_s -> latest
# los_s), which is what sets the duty denominator (apertures * horizon_s). Override
# it to score the plan over a fixed operational day instead:
#   horizon_start_s = 0.0
#   horizon_end_s = 86400.0

# The contact plan. ILLUSTRATIVE: three navigation sessions and three
# communications sessions over a 9 000 s envelope, each navigation session
# overlapping a communications one.
[[contacts]]
name = "nav-1"
service = "navigation"
aos_s = 0.0
los_s = 600.0

[[contacts]]
name = "comms-1"
service = "communications"
aos_s = 300.0
los_s = 1500.0

[[contacts]]
name = "nav-2"
service = "navigation"
aos_s = 3600.0
los_s = 4500.0

[[contacts]]
name = "comms-2"
service = "communications"
aos_s = 4200.0
los_s = 6000.0

[[contacts]]
name = "nav-3"
service = "navigation"
aos_s = 7200.0
los_s = 7800.0

[[contacts]]
name = "comms-3"
service = "communications"
aos_s = 7200.0
los_s = 9000.0
araim-gps-galileo.toml:
# Dual-constellation ARAIM availability: GPS + Galileo evaluated with the advanced
# ARAIM engine, including the constellation-wide fault hypothesis (`araim_dual`).
#
# Unlike `integrity-raim.toml` (single-constellation solution-separation RAIM), this
# runs `araim_dual_raim` at every epoch over a combined GPS + Galileo geometry: the
# fault-free, single-satellite, AND per-constellation fault hypotheses all feed one
# MHSS integrity-risk budget (P_HMI). The primary constellation is fault group 0 and
# each `[[constellations]]` entry the next group.
#
# Constellation-fault-robust integrity (staying safe even if an entire constellation
# fails) is the demanding mode: under the constellation-fault hypothesis the residual
# constellation must carry the fix alone, so it always costs availability relative to
# pooling. How much depends on the sky. On the real 2026-06-07 GPS + Galileo catalogue,
# evaluated at one common epoch, it still reaches 0.990 at a 12 m VAL against 1.000
# pooled (tests/araim_dual_real_data.rs) — two full constellations can carry it; a
# depleted one is where a third constellation or SBAS augmentation earns its place.
# The numerically exact EU ARAIM TN Table A-3 reproduction is an external follow-on
# (docs/ARAIM_REFERENCE.md).
kind = "integrity"

mask_deg = 5.0
sigma_uere_m = 0.75   # ISM σ_URA (dual-frequency, m)
p_fa = 1.0e-5         # false-alarm / continuity budget
p_md = 1.0e-3
al_h_m = 40.0         # horizontal alert limit (APV-I)
al_v_m = 50.0         # vertical alert limit (APV-I)
araim_dual = true     # advanced dual-/multi-constellation ARAIM
p_hmi = 1.0e-7        # per-axis integrity-risk budget

[time]
step_s = 300.0
duration_s = 43200.0  # 12 h

[user]
altitude_km = 0.4
inclination_deg = 45.0
raan_deg = 10.0
u0_deg = 0.0

[constellation]       # GPS-like Walker 24/6/1
altitude_km = 20200.0
inclination_deg = 55.0
planes = 6
sats_per_plane = 4
phasing_f = 1.0

[[constellations]]    # Galileo-like Walker 24/3/1
altitude_km = 23222.0
inclination_deg = 56.0
planes = 3
sats_per_plane = 8
phasing_f = 1.0
araim-reference-check.toml:
# The engine's ARAIM protection levels against the WG-C subgroup's OWN worked examples.
#
# This is an EXTERNAL check, not a self-test: two published certification reference vectors
# are committed as fixtures, each carrying its retrieval URL, retrieval date, source-file
# SHA-256 and page number, and the engine's numbers are run against them at the tolerance
# (TOL_PL = 5e-2 m) those documents themselves state.
#
#   * Reference Airborne Algorithm Description Document v3.1 (2019), Appendix D — internally
#     self-consistent, and the acceptance vector.
#   * Milestone 3 Report (2016), Annex A section A.IX — the statement the research
#     bibliographies cite.
#
# Every published input (the 10-satellite 2-constellation geometry matrix, the C_int and
# C_acc variance diagonals, b_nom, P_sat, P_const and the LPV-200 constant set) and every
# published output (VPL, HPL, EMT, sigma_v_acc, K_fa_3, and each constellation-fault mode's
# sigma_3, sigma_ss_3 and b_3) is reported beside the engine's own number and their absolute
# difference. A transcribed figure is labelled `published` so it can never be mistaken for a
# computed one.
#
# The protection-level equation is NOT re-solved here. The reference's mode list is handed
# to the engine's existing raim::araim_protection_level / araim_integrity_risk, so the
# bisection and the Gaussian-tail algebra under test are the engine's own; only the geometry,
# the sub-solutions, the detection thresholds and the published budget split are built for it.
#
# RESULT against the 2019 vector: VPL 18.2926 m vs 18.3 m published, HPL 13.4063 m vs
# 13.45 m, EMT 7.2997 m vs 7.2998 m, sigma_v_acc 1.3694 m vs 1.3694 m, and all six published
# intermediates to within half a unit in their last printed decimal.
#
# The 2016 vector carries two internal defects the report STATES rather than hides — a sign
# typo in row 3 of G, and a K_fa_3 evaluated at 57 fault modes while the document states
# N_fault_max = 1 (12 modes). Its geometry intermediates reproduce exactly; its protection
# levels are reported as measured discrepancies and excluded from the acceptance figure.
# The tolerance is never widened to absorb them.
#
# SCOPE: only N_fault_max = 1 (single-satellite and single-constellation fault modes) is
# implemented, and a case whose priors require simultaneous multi-event fault subsets is
# REFUSED rather than silently truncated. Fault detection, exclusion, the chi-square
# consistency check and the double-counting re-allocation step are out of scope. This
# reproduces a published reference algorithm's worked example — it is not a certification,
# an airworthiness artefact, or an approval.
#
# Omit `vector` to run both; set it to select one.

kind = "araim-reference-check"
attitude-budget.toml:
# 3-DOF attitude & pointing error budget demonstrator (pre-hardware AOCS/GNC).
#
# The worst-case gravity-gradient disturbance torque ((3/2)(mu/R^3)*dI) and a
# root-sum-square pointing-error budget over named 1-sigma contributors, with the
# dominant term -- a scalar pointing figure of merit to bracket before committing
# to a control design.
#
# HONEST SCOPE: MODELLED scalar error budget -- a pre-hardware complement to
# Basilisk/42, NOT a control-loop / 6-DoF / flexible-mode simulation. The
# gravity-gradient term is reported as a torque (mapping it to pointing needs a
# control stiffness the caller owns); the budget is the quadrature sum of the
# supplied 1-sigma contributors.
# Run:  kshana scenarios/attitude-budget.toml
kind = "attitude-budget"

altitude_km = 600.0
i_max_kg_m2 = 100.0
i_min_kg_m2 = 60.0

[[contributors]]

[[contributors]]
name = "reaction_wheel_jitter"
sigma_arcsec = 8.0
[[contributors]]
name = "thermal_distortion"
sigma_arcsec = 4.0
[[contributors]]
name = "alignment"
sigma_arcsec = 3.0
automotive-urban-canyon.toml:
# Road vehicle through an urban canyon: GNSS/INS dead-reckoning across an underpass and
# a roadside jammer, against a lane-level budget.
#
# The mission question a driver-assistance or automated-driving team asks: a car's
# Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) receiver loses the sky under an overpass and
# then again near a roadside jammer (a low-power in-vehicle "privacy" jammer on a
# neighbouring vehicle is the common case). How long does the fused GNSS/inertial
# navigation system (INS) solution stay inside half a lane? The 1.5 m threshold is half
# a 3.5 m lane less a margin, a budget chosen here, not a standard's figure.
#
# The pack is `gnss-ins`: a three-axis strapdown navigator disciplined by a 15-state
# error-state extended Kalman filter (EKF), then coasting through the outages. The
# GNSS timeline: open sky for 60 s, a 15 s underpass, 45 s of open sky, then 60 s
# near the jammer.
#
# The pack has two fixed slots named `imu_quantum` and `imu_classical`. Here
# `imu_quantum` carries the BETTER unit, a tactical-grade comparator, and
# `imu_classical` carries an automotive MEMS (micro-electro-mechanical system) unit.
# Nothing quantum is modelled in this file. Both use the representative class
# coefficients from the engine's grade table (Groves 2013, Table 4.1 band; the same
# figures as `imu_grade` in `ins-trn-coast`), NOT a datasheet for any part:
#   - tactical: accelerometer bias 300 ug = 2.94e-3 m/s^2, gyro bias 1 deg/h =
#     4.848e-6 rad/s;
#   - industrial (automotive MEMS sits in this band): accelerometer bias 3000 ug =
#     2.94e-2 m/s^2, gyro bias 20 deg/h = 9.696e-5 rad/s, accelerometer scale factor
#     2000 ppm.
#
# Honest scope (inherited from the `gnss-ins` pack): loosely coupled, the pack's single
# deterministic driving profile (a forward-acceleration and yaw square wave), not a
# recorded drive; no odometer or wheel-speed aiding (the engine has none), no
# multipath model, and constant biases, which the filter can learn while GNSS is up,
# so the coast is a best case for these classes. MODELLED: every figure is modelled.
kind = "gnss-ins"
seed = 7
threshold_m = 1.5
fix_interval_s = 1.0
sigma_pos_m = 1.0
sigma_vel_mps = 0.05
lat_deg = 48.137
lon_deg = 11.575
alt_m = 520.0

[time]
step_s = 0.1
duration_s = 180.0

[gnss]
windows = [
  { t0 = 0.0,   t1 = 60.0,  state = "nominal" },
  { t0 = 60.0,  t1 = 75.0,  state = "denied" },
  { t0 = 75.0,  t1 = 120.0, state = "nominal" },
  { t0 = 120.0, t1 = 180.0, state = "denied" },
]

[imu_quantum]
id = "tactical-imu"
provenance = "Tactical-grade class (Groves 2013 Table 4.1 band, engine grade table): accel bias 300 ug = 2.94e-3 m/s^2, gyro bias 1 deg/h = 4.848e-6 rad/s; signs chosen"
accel_bias = [2.94e-3, -2.94e-3, 0.0]
gyro_bias = [0.0, 0.0, 4.848e-6]

[imu_quantum.filter_prior]
sigma_accel_bias = 2.94e-3
sigma_gyro_bias = 4.848e-6

[imu_classical]
id = "automotive-mems"
provenance = "Industrial-grade class, where automotive MEMS units sit (Groves 2013 Table 4.1 band, engine grade table): accel bias 3000 ug = 2.94e-2 m/s^2, gyro bias 20 deg/h = 9.696e-5 rad/s; signs chosen"
accel_bias = [2.94e-2, -2.94e-2, 0.0]
gyro_bias = [9.696e-5, -9.696e-5, 9.696e-5]

[imu_classical.filter_prior]
sigma_accel_bias = 2.94e-2
sigma_gyro_bias = 9.696e-5

# The class's accelerometer scale-factor error (2000 ppm) layered on the constant bias.
[imu_classical.error_model]
scale_accel_ppm = [2000.0, 2000.0, 2000.0]
campaign-jam-spoof-holdover-integrity.to:
# A chained mission: nominal, jamming, spoofing, GNSS loss with clock holdover and
# inertial coasting, an integrity alarm, and recovery, on one shared timeline.
#
# Every phase runs ordinary scenarios of existing kinds, each dispatched exactly as
# `kshana <file>.toml` would run it. The campaign reads their outputs into channels
# on one mission timeline (a 10 s grid, zero-order hold) and draws them as synced
# panels: clock time error against its guard, the carrier-to-noise density ratio
# (C/N0) against the tracking floor, the vertical protection level against the
# alert limit, the inertial position error, and the alarm flags.
#
# State is handed on between phases in two ways here:
# - `end_at`: the spoofing phase ends when the clock-aided spoofing monitor of the
#   `spoof` run detects the ramp (its `classical.detect_time_s`), not at a fixed time.
# - `carry`: the holdover and integrity-alarm phases continue the clock time error
#   from where the previous phase left it, so the offset the spoofer pulled in before
#   detection is where the free-running clock starts. Recovery re-synchronises to
#   GNSS, so it carries nothing.
#
# The receiver is the jamming example's (52 N, 4 E) under a GPS-like 24-satellite
# Walker shell; the jammer is 1 km away and its power sets the phase: off, -30 dBW
# (links degraded but still tracking), 10 dBW (every satellite lost). The clock is a
# chip-scale atomic clock (Microchip SA.45s datasheet sigma_y(1 s) = 3e-10), the
# inertial unit the gnss-ins example's tactical class, and the integrity monitor the
# integrity example's snapshot receiver autonomous integrity monitoring (RAIM) with
# the approach-with-vertical-guidance (APV-I) alert limits, run on that example's
# own user track (a 0.4 km-altitude circular track, not the jamming receiver's
# fixed site). The integrity alarm is produced by a 25 deg elevation mask, standing
# in for the partial sky a receiver has while reacquiring; recovery returns to 5 deg.
#
# MODELLED: the chaining is a modelling choice (additive carry, zero-order hold), and
# each phase is as good as the kind that ran it.
kind = "campaign"
title = "Jamming, spoofing, holdover and integrity: a chained mission"
seed = 20260928

[timeline]
step_s = 10.0

# ---------------------------------------------------------------- nominal
[[phases]]
name = "nominal"
duration_s = 600.0

[[phases.runs]]
[phases.runs.scenario]
seed = 42
threshold_ns = 50.0
[phases.runs.scenario.time]
step_s = 10.0
duration_s = 600.0
[phases.runs.scenario.gnss]
windows = [{ t0 = 0.0, t1 = 600.0, state = "nominal" }]
[phases.runs.scenario.clock_quantum]
id = "optical-sr-lattice"
provenance = "Strontium optical lattice clock, space-oriented goal sigma_y(1s)=1e-15 (arXiv:1503.08457); not flown."
y0 = 5.0e-17
q_wf = 1.0e-30
q_rw = 0.0
[phases.runs.scenario.clock_classical]
id = "csac-sa45s"
provenance = "Microchip SA65 / SA.45s CSAC datasheet sigma_y(1s)=3e-10; q_wf=sigma_y(1s)^2."
y0 = 5.0e-10
q_wf = 9.0e-20

campaign-monte-carlo-clock-holdover.toml:
# A seeded Monte Carlo ensemble through a campaign, on a case with a closed form.
#
# A chip-scale atomic clock (Microchip SA.45s datasheet sigma_y(1 s) = 3e-10, so a
# white-frequency-noise intensity q_wf = 9e-20 s^2/s and nothing else stochastic) is
# disciplined to GNSS for 600 s and then coasts to 3600 s. The holdover predictor
# removes the deterministic frequency offset exactly, so the time error at the end
# of the run is the accumulated white-frequency noise since the last synchronisation
# at 590 s: Gaussian, mean zero, variance q_wf * tau with tau = 3010 s, a standard
# deviation of sqrt(9e-20 * 3010) s = 16.46 ns (NIST Technical Note 1337, the random
# walk of phase under white frequency noise).
#
# Realisation k runs the scenario with `seed = 42 + k`, so the ensemble reproduces
# exactly. The campaign reports, per metric, the mean, the standard deviation, the
# 5th, 50th and 95th percentiles and a fixed-seed bootstrap 95% confidence interval
# on the mean. The test suite checks that the mean falls inside that interval around
# zero and that the spread matches 16.46 ns.
#
# MODELLED: the clock is a datasheet-level model, not a measurement of any unit.
kind = "campaign"
title = "Monte Carlo: free-running clock error against its closed form"
seed = 20260928

[monte_carlo]
runs = 200
seed_key = "seed"
metrics = [
  { name = "final_error", path = "classical.series[-1].error_ns" },
  { name = "timing_rms", path = "classical.fom.timing_rms_ns" },
]

[monte_carlo.scenario]
seed = 42
threshold_ns = 20.0
[monte_carlo.scenario.time]
step_s = 10.0
duration_s = 3600.0
[monte_carlo.scenario.gnss]
windows = [
  { t0 = 0.0, t1 = 600.0, state = "nominal" },
  { t0 = 600.0, t1 = 3600.0, state = "denied" },
]
[monte_carlo.scenario.clock_quantum]
id = "optical-sr-lattice"
provenance = "Strontium optical lattice clock, space-oriented goal sigma_y(1s)=1e-15 (arXiv:1503.08457); not flown."
y0 = 5.0e-17
q_wf = 1.0e-30
q_rw = 0.0
[monte_carlo.scenario.clock_classical]
id = "csac-sa45s"
provenance = "Microchip SA65 / SA.45s CSAC datasheet sigma_y(1s)=3e-10; q_wf=sigma_y(1s)^2."

campaign-spectrum-holdover-integrity.tom:
# A chained mission driven by the L-band spectrum: a chirp jammer takes GPS L1 C/A and
# Galileo E1, the clock holds over, and a continuous-wave (CW) tone left on the L1
# carrier keeps C/A down while E1 recovers, so the receiver falls back to Galileo and
# its integrity monitor runs on a Galileo-only sky.
#
# Every phase runs ordinary scenarios of existing kinds, each dispatched exactly as
# `kshana <file>.toml` would run it. The carrier-to-noise density ratio (C/N0) of each
# band comes from the `spectrum` kind: the jammer's spectral separation coefficient
# against that band's own modulation, through (C/N0)_eff = [1/(C/N0) + sum (J/S) kappa]^-1
# (see docs/SPECTRUM.md). The campaign reads the L1 C/A and E1 rows of the spectrum
# timeline into two channels on one mission timeline (a 1 s grid, zero-order hold).
#
# State is handed on between phases in two ways here:
# - `end_at`: the onset phase ends when the spectrum run first loses L1 C/A
#   (`timeline.bands[0].first_loss_t_s`, 10 s here), not at a fixed time; the clock's
#   holdover starts at that instant.
# - `carry`: the holdover phase continues the clock time error from the end of the
#   onset phase. The fallback phase re-synchronises the clock to Galileo, so it
#   carries nothing.
#
# The jammers are the ones in scenarios/l-band-waterfall-jamming.toml: a 16 MHz chirp
# privacy device at -13 dBW EIRP, 100 m away, and a CW tone on 1575.42 MHz at -20 dBW
# EIRP, 1 km away, both through the jamming kind's free-space path loss. The clock is
# a chip-scale atomic clock (Microchip SA.45s datasheet sigma_y(1 s) = 3e-10). The
# integrity monitor is the integrity example's snapshot receiver autonomous integrity
# monitoring (RAIM) with the approach-with-vertical-guidance (APV-I) alert limits, on
# a GPS-like 24-satellite Walker shell during onset and on a Galileo-like Walker
# 24/3/1 (29 599.8 km semi-major axis, 56 deg; Galileo OS SDD 1.1) during fallback.
#
# MODELLED: the chaining is a modelling choice (additive carry, zero-order hold), and
# each phase is as good as the kind that ran it. E1 recovering under the CW tone rests
# on the spectrum kind's continuous-spectrum treatment (a CW tone on the MBOC carrier
# null couples nothing); a real tone would couple through the code's spectral lines.
kind = "campaign"
title = "L-band jamming from the spectrum, clock holdover and a Galileo-only fallback"
seed = 20260928

[timeline]
step_s = 1.0

# loss of L1 C/A that the spectrum run computes.

duration_s = 60.0
end_at = "timeline.bands[0].first_loss_t_s"
end_at_run = 1

cislunar-arc-recovery.toml:
# Independent-estimator test of the cislunar arc-length observability threshold (R6, paper B).
#
# Paper B's threshold is a RANK read on an observability matrix assembled from the ANALYTIC
# range Jacobian rows and the ANALYTIC variational state-transition matrix, and its
# square-root-information-filter cross-check folds those same rows. The paper says so: that
# is a consistency check between two numerical machines, not corroboration. This scenario is
# the missing arbiter — a batch least-squares estimator that actually RECOVERS the chief's
# initial state from simulated measurements, with the measurement partials taken as CENTRAL
# FINITE DIFFERENCES of the composed forward model.
#
# It calls no analytic Jacobian row, no variational STM, no singular-value or eigen
# decomposition, no rank tolerance and no square-root information filter. That is enforced,
# not promised: a source-text guard in tests/cislunar_arc_recovery_reference.rs fails if any
# of them appears. The dynamics (the same RK4 CR3BP flow), the initial conditions (the same
# differential-corrected constellation), the scalar observable and the epoch grid ARE shared,
# deliberately and by name, in the emitted `independence` block — two analyses of one
# physical problem must agree about the physics to be comparable.
#
# Two criteria, each swept over five decades of its own bound:
#   * NOISE-FREE RECOVERY — every seeded trial's final state error at most recovery_factor
#     times its a-priori displacement. The rank analogue, with no singular-value tolerance
#     anywhere in it.
#   * MONTE-CARLO ESTIMABILITY — measured RMS position error over a seeded noise ensemble
#     below a stated bound. The estimability analogue, measured rather than predicted.
#
# MEASURED on the published planar DRO grid: the estimator recovers the four-state from
# 0.782609 h against the rank criterion's 2.086957 h at rel_tol 1e-6, a ratio of 0.375 — so
# the rank threshold is NOT corroborated as a recoverability boundary. The measured
# estimability boundary lands in the same grid cell as the formal one, 5.739130 h, and the
# measured error curve reproduces the formal 1-sigma over 21 arc lengths to a geometric-mean
# ratio of 0.98.
#
# MODELLED: the constellation design, the epoch grid, the single tracked link, the
# displacement magnitude, the measurement sigma and the two stated bounds.
# Not a certified navigation-performance product.

kind = "cislunar-arc-recovery"
cislunar-observability.toml:
# Planar cislunar constellation observability over a tracking arc (P6).
#
# A small four-spacecraft near-DRO planar constellation near the Moon is tracked by
# inter-satellite ranging. The scenario answers the batch-estimator question: how much of a
# spacecraft's four-state [x, y, xdot, ydot] does the arc actually make observable, and how
# does that grow with arc length? It assembles the observability structure from the crate's
# finite-difference-validated CR3BP variational STM (src/cr3bp.rs) and the analytic
# inter-satellite range / range-rate Jacobians (src/intersat_range.rs), and emits:
#   1. the rank-vs-arc-length table for a single range-only link -- instantaneously rank-1,
#      growing toward the full four-state as the arc lengthens (P6 Table 1);
#   2. the observability-Gramian eigen-spectrum + condition number over the arc; and
#   3. the range-only vs range+range-rate instantaneous-rank comparison (the Doppler design
#      lever) plus range-only-singular / range+rate-defined GDOP reporting.
# (src/cislunar_observability.rs, src/observability_gramian.rs)
#
# Honesty: MODELLED. VALIDATED core -- the observable RANK is a rank-revealing
# singular-value threshold cross-checked against the Gramian eigen-rank; the eigen-spectrum
# obeys the spectral invariants (trace = sum eig, det = prod eig, Frobenius^2 = sum eig^2);
# the variational STM is the finite-difference-validated CR3BP STM; the range / range-rate
# Jacobian rows are finite-difference-validated analytic partials (cross-checked against the
# crate's 3-D range-rate observable); a rank-deficient snapshot is flagged GDOP-undefined
# (fim condition = inf), never a bogus finite value -- the same singular-geometry guard
# pvt::solve_spp applies. MODELLED -- the four near-DRO planar initial conditions (a
# differential-corrected DRO seeder is a follow-on) and the specific rank progression they
# produce. Not a certified navigation-performance product.
kind = "cislunar-observability"

# Every field is optional and shown at its default. Uncomment to override.

combined-altpnt.toml:
# Combined gravity + magnetic + terrain GPS-denied navigator — fused alt-PNT.
#
# The capstone alternative-PNT demo: a vehicle flying with no GNSS takes THREE scalar
# measurements at each waypoint — gravity anomaly (mGal), magnetic-anomaly total intensity
# (nT), and ground elevation (m). For a candidate constant drift offset the joint likelihood
# is the PRODUCT of the three field likelihoods, so the information adds: the joint posterior
# is sharper (a lower CRLB) than any single field. The demo shows a bounded error under 500 m
# over the outage that is never worse than the best single channel — exactly why sensor fusion
# is the path where any one weak field alone would struggle.
#
# Consumed by `kshana::altpnt::terrain::run_combined_altpnt` (and its unit tests), dispatched
# as `kind = "combined-altpnt"`. The gravity field is a low-degree spherical-harmonic trend +
# synthetic mascons; the magnetic channel is the smooth IGRF-14 main field minus its regional
# mean PLUS synthetic crustal-anomaly mascons (the IGRF main field alone is too smooth to
# localise — the real crustal map is a follow-on, see docs/CAPABILITY.md); the terrain channel
# is the self-contained synthetic DEM. Recovery is checked against the INDEPENDENTLY injected
# drift, never any field's own value (non-circular).
#
# NOTE: every top-level scalar key precedes the `[[...]]` array-of-tables blocks — a scalar
# after an array-of-table would be absorbed into that table by TOML.
kind = "combined-altpnt"

# Track + drift + search (shared across the three channels).
start_lat_deg = 12.05
start_lon_deg = 20.05
step_lat_deg = 0.004
step_lon_deg = 0.003
waypoints = 60

drift_lat_deg = 0.5
drift_lon_deg = -0.4

search_half_deg = 0.8
search_step_deg = 0.08
refine_stages = 3
refine_factor = 8.0
noise_seed = 1

# ---- Gravity channel ----
# Each single-channel σ is set so that channel ALONE recovers only to ~600–900 m (well above
# the ~140 m grid floor), making the fusion gain visible: the three-channel product collapses
# to ~250 m (< 500 m), no worse than the best single channel.
nmax = 3
gravity_sigma_mgal = 3.0

# ---- Magnetic channel (IGRF main field + synthetic crustal anomaly mascons, nT) ----
igrf_year = 2025.0
igrf_alt_km = 0.0
magnetic_sigma_nt = 30.0

# ---- Terrain channel (synthetic DEM) ----
dem_seed = 1
terrain_sigma_m = 40.0

# Low-degree anomalous gravity coefficients (the regional trend).
[[coeffs]]
n = 2
m = 0
cbar = 6.0e-6
sbar = 0.0

[[coeffs]]
n = 3
m = 1
cbar = 3.0e-6
sbar = 2.0e-6

# Localized gravity mascons (mGal) the track crosses.
[[mascons]]
lat_deg = 12.18

sigma_deg = 0.05

[[mascons]]

lon_deg = 20.18
amp_mgal = 250.0
sigma_deg = 0.05

[[magnetic_mascons]]
lat_deg = 12.24
lon_deg = 20.20
amp_mgal = -200.0
sigma_deg = 0.045
conflict-resilience.toml:
# Layered-PNT conflict resilience (paper P7).
#
# A contested-environment user fields four RF PNT layers that all ride the same band
# and therefore share the jamming/spoofing denial vector — the fragile, correlated
# case. The scenario reports:
#   * total-loss probability vs threat intensity (Monte-Carlo vs the closed-form
#     independent product it converges to),
#   * the ~7x layered-vs-single-layer resilience ratio under the independence
#     assumption,
#   * how that ~7x collapses toward 1 as the denial correlation rises (a one-factor
#     Gaussian copula) — correlation defeats layering, and
#   * a §4.2 per-vector usable-PNT survival breakdown: for each named threat vector
#     (jamming/spoofing/kinetic/cyber) acting alone, the graceful-degradation curve
#     S_v(x) = 1 - Prod_i (1 - a_i*(1 - clamp(susceptibility_i,v * x, 0, 1))). Jamming
#     is the sharpest vector for this correlated-RF stack.
#
# Every per-layer magnitude is a MODELLED input with provenance; see
# src/conflict_threat_params.rs for the sourced [min, nominal, max] priors and the
# per-vector susceptibility profiles (JammerTest 2024, TEXBAT, EASA SIB 2022-02,
# RTCA DO-229, LunaNet/IOAG). Leaving `layers` out runs the same sourced four-layer
# baseline; it is written out here — including each layer's vector_profile — for
# transparency.

kind = "conflict-resilience"
trials = 4000
seed = 20260709
primary_layer = 0

[intensity]
min = 0.0
max = 1.0
steps = 11

[correlation]
values = [0.0, 0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8, 0.95]

[[layers]]
name = "GNSS L1 C/A (open service)"
availability = 0.99
sigma_m = 4.0
vulnerability = 0.90
vector_weight = 0.58
# Denied at the lowest jammer power of any tracked signal; unauthenticated ⇒ spoofable.
[layers.vector_profile]
jamming = 0.98
spoofing = 0.85
kinetic = 0.12
cyber = 0.18

[[layers]]
name = "GNSS L5 / E5a (wideband)"
availability = 0.97
sigma_m = 3.0
vulnerability = 0.85
vector_weight = 0.60
# Wideband ⇒ more jam-resistant than L1 C/A but still RF-denied.
[layers.vector_profile]
jamming = 0.90
spoofing = 0.80
kinetic = 0.12
cyber = 0.18

[[layers]]
name = "Galileo E1 OS + OSNMA"
availability = 0.98
sigma_m = 4.0
vulnerability = 0.88
vector_weight = 0.59
# OSNMA authentication sharply lowers spoofing susceptibility; shared band keeps jamming high.
[layers.vector_profile]
jamming = 0.92
spoofing = 0.40
kinetic = 0.12
cyber = 0.22

[[layers]]
name = "SBAS / augmentation (WAAS/EGNOS-class)"
availability = 0.96
sigma_m = 3.0
vulnerability = 0.86
vector_weight = 0.60
# Rides the L1/L5 band (jam-fragile) and, as a networked augmentation service, carries a
# larger cyber and ground-segment kinetic surface.
[layers.vector_profile]
jamming = 0.90
spoofing = 0.68
kinetic = 0.28
cyber = 0.55
constellation-multi-gnss-coverage.toml:
# Multi-constellation coverage: the four global navigation satellite systems (GNSS) together,
# as a map of satellites in view, dilution of precision (DOP) and availability over the whole
# Earth for one day.
#
# Each system is a preset built from its operator's published nominal elements:
#   - GPS: the baseline 24-slot constellation, GPS Standard Positioning Service Performance
#     Standard, 5th edition (2020), Tables 3.2-1 and 3.2-3;
#   - Galileo: the Walker 24/3/1 reference constellation at 29 599.801 km semi-major axis and
#     56 deg, Galileo Open Service Service Definition Document issue 1.1, Tables 1 and 23;
#   - BeiDou: 24 medium Earth orbit satellites in a Walker 24/3/1 at 21 528 km and 55 deg,
#     3 geostationary and 3 inclined geosynchronous satellites, BeiDou Open Service
#     Performance Standard 3.0, section 4.1 (the medium-orbit phase and the inclined
#     geosynchronous crossing longitude are modelled, the standard does not state them);
#   - GLONASS: 24 satellites, 3 planes, 19 100 km, 64.8 deg, from the slot formula of the
#     GLONASS Interface Control Document edition 5.1, section 5.2.
#
# The receiver estimates one clock per system (clock = "per-constellation"), so a fix needs
# three position unknowns plus one clock for every system in view. The four systems' slot
# tables come from different reference epochs, so their relative phase is not a snapshot of
# any real date; the statistics over a day are what the run is for.
#
# What the run answers: how many satellites are in view, the position, horizontal, vertical
# and geometric DOP per 10 deg cell, and the share of time the position DOP (PDOP) is at or
# below 6 above a 10 deg mask. MODELLED: two-body orbits, a spherical Earth, geometry only.

kind = "constellation-design"
body = "earth"
duration_s = 86164.0
step_s = 900.0
mask_deg = 10.0
pdop_threshold = 6.0
grid_step_deg = 10.0
clock = "per-constellation"
track_points = 25
max_tracks = 102

[[constellation]]
name = "GPS"
preset = "gps-baseline"

[[constellation]]
name = "Galileo"
preset = "galileo"

[[constellation]]
name = "BeiDou"
preset = "beidou"

[[constellation]]
name = "GLONASS"
preset = "glonass"
earth-gnss-lunar.toml:
# Earth-GNSS reception at lunar distance.
#
# A GNSS constellation is built to serve users under it. A receiver near the Moon is
# roughly fifteen times the orbital radius away, outside that service volume entirely, and
# three facts decide whether it can hear anything at all:
#
#   1. THE EARTH BLOCKS THE BORESIGHT. From 26,560 km the Earth subtends a half-angle of
#      about 13.9 deg. Any ray that reaches the Moon must therefore leave the transmitter
#      at least that far off nadir — the peak of the beam is geometrically unavailable
#      before a single dB is computed.
#   2. WHAT IS LEFT IS THE EDGE OF THE MAIN LOBE AND THE SIDELOBES. The usable rays sit in
#      a thin annulus just outside the limb, where the transmit gain is already falling.
#      This is the regime the LuGRE payload operated in when it tracked GNSS at the Moon
#      in 2025.
#   3. THE PATH LOSS IS ABOUT 208 dB AT L1 — some 25 dB more than a terrestrial user pays.
#      The budget closes only with a high-gain receiving antenna, and it closes narrowly.
#
# The run reports one row per satellite (off-boresight angle, Earth occultation, range,
# path loss, transmit gain at that angle, received power, C/N0) and then aggregates only
# the links that clear the tracking threshold.
#
# READ THE CONDITIONING, NOT JUST THE COUNT
# Every satellite the receiver can hear lies inside a cone a couple of degrees wide, so the
# lines of sight are nearly parallel and the dilution of precision is enormous. That is not
# a defect of the model; it is the defining property of the layer. An Earth-GNSS fix at
# lunar distance is a TIMING-grade observation far more than a position-grade one, and the
# report prints the DOP rather than quietly omitting it.
#
# WHAT IS MODELLED, AND WHY IT IS NOT VALIDATED
# The transmit gain at angle is a uniformly illuminated circular aperture — an Airy
# pattern. A real GPS L1 antenna is a twelve-element helical array whose measured pattern
# has a shaped main lobe, deliberately peaked off-boresight to even out power across the
# Earth disc, and sidelobes that are not Airy at all. Measured patterns are published; they
# are not vendored in this repository, so they are not used here. Orderings and orders of
# magnitude are meaningful. The dB of any single satellite is not.
#
# Also absent, and every one of these makes the budget OPTIMISTIC: no ionospheric or
# tropospheric loss on the limb-grazing rays (which do clip the upper atmosphere at small
# clearance angles), no polarisation mismatch, no pointing loss, no receiver implementation
# loss, and a spherical Earth with no refractive extension of the occultation.
#
# Upgrading this to Validated needs two things the repository does not hold: a measured
# transmit pattern, and LuGRE normal points to check against. Neither is invented here.
#
# The Moon position is an INPUT — a range and an inertial direction — not an ephemeris
# lookup. What is under test is the link and the beam geometry; the engine models the lunar
# ephemeris elsewhere and coupling them would only obscure which part is being checked.

kind = "earth-gnss-lunar"

# The constellation: a 24-satellite Walker at GPS altitude and inclination.
altitude_km = 20180.0
inclination_deg = 55.0
planes = 6
sats_per_plane = 4
phasing_f = 2.0
epoch_s = 0.0

# The receiver, at the mean lunar distance along the inertial x-axis.
receiver_range_m = 384400000.0
receiver_ra_deg = 0.0
receiver_dec_deg = 0.0

# Transmitter: about 27 W into an aperture sized so the boresight gain lands near the
# 13 dBi a GPS L1 antenna is usually quoted at.
tx_power_dbw = 13.4
tx_diameter_m = 0.35
tx_efficiency = 0.6
freq_hz = 1575420000.0

# Receiver: a modest high-gain lunar antenna and a room-temperature system.
rx_gain_dbi = 12.0
system_temp_k = 290.0
tracking_threshold_dbhz = 25.0
eo-coverage.toml:
# Earth-observation payload footprint & coverage demonstrator (SMAD space triangle).
#
# Turns an orbit altitude + sensor field of view into the Earth angular radius,
# swath width, nadir ground sample distance, maximum off-nadir access, circular
# period and equatorial ground-track spacing (with a contiguous-coverage flag).
#
# HONEST SCOPE: MODELLED spherical-Earth geometry only -- no radiometry / MTF /
# atmosphere / pointing-jitter / sun-glint model; ground-track spacing is the
# simple nodal R_e*omega*T (no J2 nodal regression).
# Run:  kshana scenarios/eo-coverage.toml
kind = "eo-coverage"

altitude_km = 700.0
half_fov_deg = 7.5               # nadir half-angle from boresight
ifov_microrad = 14.0             # per-pixel IFOV for the nadir GSD
max_off_nadir_deg = 45.0         # slewable field of regard
ephemeris.toml:
kind = "ephemeris"

# Ephemeris & ground track — "where is the satellite right now".
#
# Propagate the ISS (ZARYA) for one revolution and emit, at every 30 s step: the
# inertial TEME and GCRS (≈ J2000) state (position AND velocity), the Earth-fixed
# ITRF/ECEF position, the WGS-84 sub-satellite point (latitude / longitude /
# altitude — the ground track drawn in the chart), and the topocentric azimuth /
# elevation / range and range-rate (the geometric Doppler) seen from a ground
# station. The frame chain is the one validated to the millimetre against the
# published Vallado vectors; the velocity is validated against the official AIAA
# tcppver vectors.
#
# A TLE's epoch is its own (UTC); the ground track therefore starts at the TLE
# epoch. Swap in any current TLE (e.g. from CelesTrak) to track a live satellite.
tle = """
1 25544U 98067A   20045.18587073  .00000950  00000-0  25302-4 0  9990
2 25544  51.6443 242.0161 0004885 264.6060 207.3845 15.49165514212791
"""
step_s = 30.0
duration_s = 16740.0   # ~three ISS revolutions

# Earth-orientation: dut1_s = UT1 - UTC (0 => the DUT1 ~ 0 approximation, a few-
# arcsecond / few-hundred-metre longitude shift in the ground track); xp_arcsec /
# yp_arcsec are the IERS polar-motion pole coordinates. Leave at 0 for a quick run,
# or supply IERS values.
dut1_s = 0.0
xp_arcsec = 0.0
yp_arcsec = 0.0

# Optional ground station — ESA's European Space Operations Centre, Darmstadt.
# Drives the az / el / range and the range-rate / Doppler columns.
[station]
lat_deg = 49.8707
lon_deg = 8.6217
alt_m = 144.0
europa-surface-pnt.toml:
# Positioning a lander on Europa: the Jovian-moon case.
#
# A lander at 20 deg north, 60 deg east on Europa's surface navigates for one Europan day
# (3.55 Earth days, the synchronous rotation period) with twelve navigation satellites at
# 4 500 km in three planes inclined 55 deg, under a 10 deg elevation mask, and a two-way
# range from Earth whenever the Earth is above the lander's horizon. Europa is tidally
# locked, so from a fixed site Jupiter never moves in the sky, while the Earth, riding
# with Jupiter, rises and sets once per Europan day: the Earth link is available only for
# part of the run, and the report shows what the local constellation must carry alone.
#
# The Europa constants (gravitational parameter, mean radius, International Astronomical
# Union (IAU) pole and prime meridian)
# are the published values cited in src/body.rs; no J2 (second zonal harmonic) is carried
# for Europa, so the relay
# orbits are two-body. The Earth-Europa light time is about 36 minutes one way at this
# epoch, near a Jupiter opposition.
#
# One simplification matters more here than at Mars: the relays orbit inside Europa's Hill
# sphere (about 13 700 km) but Jupiter's pull on them is not modelled, so their orbits are
# idealised. The run shows the geometry and what the Earth link adds (availability rises
# from about half the Europan day to about three quarters), not a flyable design.
#
# MODELLED: the constellation, the noise and the measurement model are modelling choices.
kind = "body-pnt"
body = "Europa"
epoch = "2027-02-19T00:00:00"
duration_s = 306822.0
step_s = 1800.0
seed = 11

[user]
kind = "surface"
lat_deg = 20.0
lon_deg = 60.0

[constellation]
planes = 3
sats_per_plane = 4
altitude_km = 4500.0
inclination_deg = 55.0
sigma_range_m = 1.0
mask_deg = 10.0

[earth_link]
enabled = true
sigma_range_m = 1.0

#
# The filter learns the clock frequency offset and the platform velocity while
# GNSS is available, then coasts through the outage propagating those estimates;
# its joint covariance gives the joint integrity. To keep the filter's process
# noise consistent with truth, the accelerometers here are noise-driven (bias set
# to zero) — augmented-state estimation of constant biases is future work.
# Vendor-neutral; clock and noise parameters are public/cited or illustrative.

gnss-ins.toml:
# Loosely-coupled GNSS/INS: the three-axis strapdown navigator disciplined by a
# 15-state error-state EKF, then coasting through a 60 s GNSS outage. Unlike the
# `inertial` pack (a 1-DOF scalar dead-reckoner with a truth-snap reset at every
# fix), this runs the genuine closed-loop filter: it learns from noisy fixes while
# GNSS is up and coasts on the corrected state during the gap. The reported error
# is the real horizontal residual against truth; each sensor also carries its
# open-loop free-INS RMS so the filter's value is explicit.
#
# Honest framing: loosely-coupled, a single deterministic driving trajectory, a
# flat-Earth tangent-plane INS<->GNSS comparison. The lower-bias (quantum-grade)
# sensor has the better unaided coast. Both biases here are constant and noise-free,
# so the filter learns them while GNSS is up and the fused coast is a best case; a
# bias that keeps drifting is what ends a real one (see small-uas-jammed-nav.toml).
# Revised in 0.27.3: a sign error in the filter's gyro-bias coupling had put a floor
# of tens of metres under the fused outage error; see the CHANGELOG.
kind = "gnss-ins"
seed = 7
threshold_m = 50.0
fix_interval_s = 1.0
sigma_pos_m = 1.0
sigma_vel_mps = 0.05
lat_deg = 45.0
lon_deg = -57.3
alt_m = 50.0

[time]
step_s = 0.1
duration_s = 160.0

[gnss]
windows = [
  { t0 = 0.0,   t1 = 100.0, state = "nominal" },
  { t0 = 100.0, t1 = 160.0, state = "denied" },
]

[imu_quantum]
id = "cold-atom-imu"
provenance = "Quantum-grade inertial unit: low residual accelerometer/gyro bias (cold-atom-class); the better unaided coast"
accel_bias = [0.015, 0.0, 0.0]
gyro_bias = [0.0, 0.0, 5.0e-5]

[imu_classical]
id = "tactical-imu"
provenance = "Tactical-grade MEMS/quartz inertial unit: larger residual bias; the free-running INS diverges much faster"
accel_bias = [0.03, -0.02, 0.0]
gyro_bias = [0.0, 0.0, 1.0e-4]

# Optional: layer the full deterministic IMU error chain on top of the constant
# biases above. Every field defaults to zero, so omitting this block leaves the
# sensor a pure constant-bias source (the run is then identical to before this
# schema existed). The terms drive the three-axis strapdown mechanization through
# the IMU error model (IEEE Std 952-1997 §A.2; Groves 2013 §4.3). Scale-factor is
# in ppm; misalignment in rad (off-diagonal); g-sensitivity in (rad/s)/(m/s²);
# quantization in the sensor's output units; rate-ramp is a linear-in-time drift.
# [imu_classical.error_model]
# scale_gyro_ppm  = [1500.0, 1500.0, 1500.0]
# scale_accel_ppm = [1000.0, 1000.0, 1000.0]
# g_sensitivity   = [5.0e-5, 5.0e-5, 5.0e-5]
# rate_ramp_gyro  = [0.0, 1.0e-6, 0.0]
# quant_gyro      = [1.0e-5, 1.0e-5, 1.0e-5]
gnss-sim-raim.toml:
# Measurement-domain GNSS simulation: pseudoranges with ionospheric and
# tropospheric delays, fed to snapshot RAIM for protection levels.
#
# Unlike the purely-geometric `orbit` pack (visibility + DOP only), this synthesises
# each visible satellite's pseudorange:
#   ρ = geometric range + c·δt_rx − c·δt_sv + I(Klobuchar) + T(Saastamoinen·Niell)
#       + thermal noise + multipath
# and forms the measurement residuals that drive snapshot RAIM (HPL/VPL, fault
# detection). The per-epoch per-satellite measurements are emitted in the JSON
# `gnss_measurements` array for downstream tools.
kind = "gnss-sim"
seed = 7
mask_deg = 5.0
noise_sigma_m = 1.5      # 1σ thermal noise per pseudorange (set 0 for a noise-free run)
multipath_m = 0.5        # peak deterministic multipath, scaled by (1 − sin elevation)
sat_clock_rms_m = 30.0   # peak per-PRN satellite clock offset
uere_m = 3.0             # RAIM 1σ user-equivalent range error
p_fa = 1.0e-5
p_md = 1.0e-3
alert_limit_h_m = 40.0
alert_limit_v_m = 50.0

[time]
step_s = 60.0
duration_s = 3600.0

[receiver]
lat_deg = 40.4
lon_deg = -3.7
alt_m = 660.0
clock_bias_m = 1500.0

# A GPS-like 24-satellite Walker shell propagated through the validated SGP4 core.
[constellation]
altitude_km = 20200.0
inclination_deg = 55.0
planes = 6
sats_per_plane = 4
phasing_f = 1.0

# Klobuchar single-frequency ionosphere (IS-GPS-200 §20.3.3.5.2.5): the eight
# broadcast coefficients and the GPS seconds-of-day at the start of the run.
[iono]
alpha = [3.82e-8, 1.49e-8, -1.79e-7, 0.0]
beta = [1.43e5, 0.0, -3.28e5, 1.13e5]
gps_seconds_of_day = 50400.0

# Saastamoinen zenith troposphere (Davis 1985 / Groves §9.4) with Niell (1996)
# mapping: surface meteorology and the day-of-year.
[tropo]
pressure_hpa = 1013.25
temp_k = 288.15
humidity = 0.5
day_of_year = 180.0
gps-denied-gravity-nav.toml:
# 60-minute GPS-denied gravity-map-matching benchmark (quantum alt-PNT).
#
# The validation-grade form of `gravity-map-nav.toml`: a vehicle flies a ~700 km track for
# a full one-hour GNSS outage, its inertial solution drifting to ≈ 70 km of position error.
# A cold-atom gravimeter samples the gravity anomaly along the track (with its real, seeded
# white-noise floor injected), and a hierarchical coarse-to-fine particle/grid matcher
# recovers the constant INS drift to a few hundred metres — the < 500 m GPS-denied target
# of ESA NAVISP's "Quantum Wayfarer" gravity-aided navigation.
#
# Consumed by `kshana::gravimeter::run_gps_denied_gravity_nav` (and its unit tests). The
# reference field is a low-degree spherical-harmonic trend plus synthetic mascons; Kshana
# does not bundle the full EGM2008 coefficient set, and a Monte-Carlo over map-representation
# error realisations is a documented follow-on (see docs/CAPABILITY.md).

# Dispatched by the scenario engine as `kind = "gravity-map"` (also consumed directly by
# `run_gps_denied_gravity_nav` in the unit tests, which ignore this field).
kind = "gravity-map"

# Maximum spherical-harmonic degree/order of the reference field.
nmax = 3

# Track flown GPS-denied: 90 waypoints, 40 s gravimeter averaging each ⇒ 3600 s = 60 min.
# An oblique leg keeps the scalar gravimeter sequence observable in both north and east.
start_lat_deg = 10.0
start_lon_deg = 20.0
step_lat_deg = 0.06
step_lon_deg = 0.045
waypoints = 90

# True constant INS position drift accumulated over the one-hour outage (≈ 70 km at ~13° lat,
# i.e. far past the 10 km the matched solution must beat).
drift_lat_deg = 0.5
drift_lon_deg = -0.4

# Cold-atom gravimeter: 1e-7 m/s²/√Hz ASD (≈10 µGal/√Hz), 40 s averaging ⇒ σ ≈ 1.6e-3 mGal.
gravimeter_asd = 1.0e-7
averaging_time_s = 40.0

# Map/representation error (mGal): combined with the sensor white noise into the matching σ.
map_sigma_mgal = 2.0

# Hierarchical offset search: ±0.8° at 0.08° to start, then three coarse-to-fine stages each
# shrinking the window and step 8× ⇒ final offset resolution 0.08° / 8² ≈ 140 m.
search_half_deg = 0.8
search_step_deg = 0.08
refine_stages = 3
refine_factor = 8.0
noise_seed = 1

# Low-degree anomalous, fully-normalised coefficients (the always-on regional trend).
[[coeffs]]
n = 2
m = 0
cbar = 6.0e-6
sbar = 0.0

[[coeffs]]
n = 3
m = 1
cbar = 3.0e-6
sbar = 2.0e-6

# Localized Gaussian anomalies (mascons) the track crosses — the distinctive high-degree
# features that make the constant drift observable.
[[mascons]]
lat_deg = 11.0
lon_deg = 20.8
amp_mgal = 45.0
sigma_deg = 0.30

[[mascons]]
lat_deg = 12.4
lon_deg = 21.9
amp_mgal = -38.0
sigma_deg = 0.28

[[mascons]]
lat_deg = 13.8
lon_deg = 23.0
amp_mgal = 50.0
sigma_deg = 0.32
gravity-map-nav.toml:
# Quantum gravity-map-matching navigation scenario (GPS-denied alt-PNT).
#
# Targets ESA NAVISP "Quantum Wayfarer" / QT-CCI gravity-map-matching vocabulary: a
# vehicle with an inertial unit and a cold-atom-interferometer gravimeter navigates with
# no GNSS by matching the gravity-anomaly signature it flies through against a stored
# reference field. The reference field is a low-degree spherical-harmonic anomaly plus
# synthetic mascons — Kshana does not bundle the full EGM2008 coefficient set (see
# docs/CAPABILITY.md).
#
# This is a runnable scenario kind: the CLI dispatches `kind = "gravity-map"` to
# `kshana::gravimeter::run_gps_denied_gravity_nav` (the validation-grade noisy/refined
# form) and emits JSON + an SVG drift chart (free-inertial vs gravity-matched error).
# The same config also backs `run_gravity_map_benchmark` (the noise-free geometric-
# observability benchmark) and its unit test, which read this file directly.
kind = "gravity-map"

# Maximum spherical-harmonic degree/order of the reference field.
nmax = 3

# Track flown GPS-denied: an oblique leg so the scalar gravimeter sequence is observable
# in both north and east (a single anomaly measurement only constrains a level set).
start_lat_deg = 12.0
start_lon_deg = 24.0
step_lat_deg = 0.18
step_lon_deg = 0.13
waypoints = 12

# True constant INS position drift accumulated over the outage (≈ 80 km at ~13° lat).
drift_lat_deg = 0.55
drift_lon_deg = -0.45

# Cold-atom gravimeter: 1e-7 m/s²/√Hz ASD (≈10 µGal/√Hz), 100 s averaging ⇒ σ ≈ 1e-3 mGal.
gravimeter_asd = 1.0e-7
averaging_time_s = 100.0

# Map/representation error (mGal): reference-field inaccuracy + grid quantisation, combined
# with the sensor white noise into the effective matching σ. Dominates a quantum gravimeter.
map_sigma_mgal = 2.0

# Offset search grid (degrees): ±1.0° at 0.05° resolution around the no-drift prior.
search_half_deg = 1.0
search_step_deg = 0.05

# Low-degree anomalous, fully-normalised coefficients (the regional trend).
[[coeffs]]
n = 2
m = 0
cbar = 4.0e-6
sbar = 0.0

[[coeffs]]
n = 3
m = 1
cbar = 2.0e-6
sbar = 1.0e-6

# Localized Gaussian anomalies (mascons) the track crosses — the stand-in for the
# high-degree EGM features that make gravity-map matching observable.
[[mascons]]
lat_deg = 13.0
lon_deg = 25.0
amp_mgal = 32.0
sigma_deg = 0.45

[[mascons]]
lat_deg = 12.6
lon_deg = 24.6
amp_mgal = -26.0
sigma_deg = 0.35
hybrid-optical-rf.toml:
# Heterogeneous optical + RF PNT joint availability / precision / integrity (P5).
#
# Composes the Phase-7 pieces into one end-to-end analysis:
#   * L26 optical link budget  -> photon-limited two-way ranging CRLB + diffraction footprint
#   * L22 cross-modality RAIM   -> position AND timing protection level (loose RF x tight optical)
#   * L24 optical availability  -> N-station clear-sky diversity (independent + correlated union)
#   * L23 optical<->RF handoff  -> proven bit-continuous (no-jump) mean + NEES chi-square gate
#   * L25 joint FoM             -> P(available AND precision-grade AND integrity-assured)
#
# MODELLED. Validated closed forms: ranging CRLB (sigma_tau/sqrt(N)), diffraction footprint
# (lambda/D * range), chi-square protection-level quantile, union combinatorics, handoff
# mean-continuity + NEES gate, and the joint independent product. The loss allocations,
# sigma magnitudes, cloud-climatology inputs, correlations and P_HMI budget are Modelled
# representative inputs. Every field below is optional and shown at its default.
kind = "hybrid-optical-rf"

# --- L26 optical (1550 nm) two-way link budget ---
wavelength_nm      = 1550.0     # telecom C-band, eye-safe, low atmospheric loss
tx_power_w         = 1.0e-3     # 1 mW mean optical power (photon-starved lunar regime)
tx_aperture_m      = 0.85       # -> ~0.7 km diffraction footprint at lunar range (lambda/D)
rx_aperture_m      = 0.85
range_km           = 384000.0   # mean Earth-Moon distance
pulse_rms_ps       = 50.0       # signal-pulse RMS temporal width
integration_s      = 1.0
atmospheric_loss_db = 3.0       # Modelled 1550 nm clear-sky allocation
pointing_loss_db    = 3.0       # Modelled terminal pointing/jitter allocation
optics_efficiency   = 0.5       # Modelled
detector_efficiency = 0.7       # Modelled
two_way             = true      # round-trip ranging: range = c*dt/2, double-pass geometry

# --- RF (loose) reference solution ---
rf_pos_sigma_m      = 1.0       # horizontal 1-sigma
rf_vertical_sigma_m = 1.5       # vertical 1-sigma (vertical dilution)
rf_clock_sigma_s    = 3.0e-9    # 3 ns clock 1-sigma

# --- L22 cross-modality RAIM ---
p_fa              = 1.0e-5
p_md              = 1.0e-3
alert_limit_h_m   = 10.0
alert_limit_v_m   = 15.0
alert_limit_t_s   = 20.0e-9

# --- precision grade (the high-grade service the FoM scores) ---
grade_pos_m  = 0.1              # 10 cm position grade
grade_time_s = 1.0e-9           # 1 ns timing grade

# --- L24 optical ground-network availability ---
n_optical_sites  = 5
site_correlation = 0.15         # representative modest spatial (weather) correlation

# --- L25 joint FoM + L23 handoff ---
fom_correlation   = 0.5         # positive co-occurrence of the three P5 conditions
handoff_inflation = 0.2         # modality-transition covariance inflation at the switch
p_hmi             = 1.0e-7      # integrity-risk budget

# --- G15 bias / ramp fault injection against the cross-modality monitor ---
# The minimum detectable bias and the detection-power curve are ANALYTIC (non-central
# chi-square inversion), so they need no inputs of their own. These two only set the ramp
# rate the reported time-to-detect is a rate conversion of. Both MODELLED.
fault_ramp_rate_pos_m_s   = 0.05      # position-axis bias growth (m/s)
fault_ramp_rate_clock_s_s = 1.0e-11   # clock-axis bias growth (s/s)

# --- G17 post-handover coast: process noise and the alert-limit crossing ---
# Random walk on the existing 4-state (east, north, up, clock) handoff filter. The alert
# limits are the ones already declared above; only the process noise and the coverage
# factor are new. Both PSDs are MODELLED representative inputs and the crossing times
# scale directly with them.
process_noise_pos_psd_m2_s   = 1.0e-3   # 1 m (1-sigma) of unmodelled growth per 1000 s, per axis
process_noise_clock_psd_s2_s = 1.0e-22  # white-FM phase random walk at sigma_y(1 s) = 1e-11
# coast_coverage_k                      # default Phi^-1(1 - P_HMI/2) = 5.327; uncomment to override

# --- G16 RF link leg: availability, and the like-for-like ranging comparison ---
# The RF side of a hybrid service needs its own link, and this is it. Both the RF
# availability block (A_rf = I_closure * I_track over the Eb/N0 margin and the tracking
# threshold) and the RF leg of the optical-versus-RF ranging ratio are evaluated from
# exactly these values, at the range_km and integration_s already declared above, so the
# two modalities can never be compared at different operating points.
rf_band                     = "x"       # s | x | ka -> the CCSDS-401 / DSN-810-005 band centre
rf_eirp_dbw                 = 26.0      # MODELLED: the lunar augmented-forward-signal EIRP
rf_g_over_t_db              = 53.0      # MODELLED: DSN 34 m beam-waveguide X-band figure of merit
rf_other_losses_db          = 3.0       # MODELLED: lumped pointing/polarisation/atmosphere/implementation
rf_data_rate_bps            = 1.0e6     # sets Eb/N0 and the closure margin; does not touch C/N0
rf_required_eb_n0_db        = 4.5
rf_chip_rate_hz             = 1.023e6   # GPS C/A reference chip rate
rf_correlator_spacing_chips = 0.5       # standard half-chip early-late correlator
rf_tracking_threshold_dbhz  = 25.0      # MODELLED receiver loss-of-lock threshold
rf_degraded_margin_db       = 6.0       # MODELLED: DEGRADED band above that threshold
# rf_dll_bandwidth_hz                   # DERIVED as 1/(2*integration_s) = 0.5 Hz, the loop
#                                       # noise bandwidth whose equivalent averaging time is
#                                       # exactly the optical accumulation time. Overriding it
#                                       # so the two disagree REFUSES the ranging ratio rather
#                                       # than quoting one at two operating points.

hybrid-ukf.toml:
# 17-state hybrid quantum + classical tightly-coupled GNSS/INS UKF (MODELLED).
#
# Surfaces the 17-state error-state unscented Kalman filter (src/fusion/tightly_coupled17.rs)
# as a runnable scenario. The state is:
#
#   x = [ p(3) | v(3) | psi(3) | b_a(3) | b_g(3) | b  d ]
#        position velocity attitude  accel-bias gyro-bias  clock(phase,freq)
#
#   * 15 INS error states (position, velocity, attitude misalignment, accel + gyro bias)
#     propagated through the strapdown mechanization driven by the IMU — the CLASSICAL
#     short-term inertial solution.
#   * the accel-bias triad b_a is the CAI-DERIVED inertial bias correction: the cold-atom
#     interferometer below sets the velocity-random-walk floor q_va, so the long-term coast
#     drift is the QUANTUM-sensor-limited one — the quantum long-term half of the hybrid.
#   * the two-state clock [b, d] (phase + frequency, in range units) is driven by the
#     q-parameter clock engine (clock_state::q_from_allan) from the Allan profile below.
#
# The platform is GNSS-aided for a 100 s lead-in (the filter learns the biases, velocity and
# clock), then coasts through a 120 s GNSS outage on the CAI IMU + clock alone.
#
# FIGURE OF MERIT — filter self-consistency (NEES + innovation-whiteness), the only thing a
# simulation can honestly assert about an estimator. Over a Monte-Carlo ensemble whose truth
# is generated from exactly the noise the filter assumes, the pooled NIS (whiteness) and NEES
# means must land inside their 95% chi-squared bands. This is a SELF-CONSISTENCY statement,
# NOT a real-world accuracy guarantee.
#
# HONESTY: everything here is MODELLED / SIMULATION. The CAI and clock inputs are bracketed,
# literature-representative values, not measured hardware; the CAI hardware and its Key-Person
# stay partner-owned. No TRL>3, no flight heritage, no external validation.
kind = "hybrid-ukf"
seed = 1771

# Residual accelerometer bias the CAI-derived correction state estimates (m/s^2), body x-axis.
# A cold-atom-grade post-calibration residual (illustrative, bracketed).
residual_accel_bias_m_s2 = 1.0e-4

# Constant-velocity surface trajectory (+y, m/s).
speed_m_s = 100.0

# GNSS measurement noise (1-sigma): ~1 m code pseudorange, ~5 cm/s Doppler (Groves 2013 §9.3).
sigma_pr_m = 1.0
sigma_rr_mps = 0.05

# Monte-Carlo seeds the consistency oracle pools over, and the filter mistuning multipliers.
# 24 seeds give run-based chi-squared NEES bands (8*24 DOF) tight enough to discriminate a
# matched from a mistuned filter while keeping the run cheap. Set q_factor / r_factor away
# from 1.0 to mistune the filter and watch the consistency gate reject it (q_factor scales the
# assumed process noise, r_factor the assumed measurement noise).
consistency_seeds = 24
q_factor = 1.0
r_factor = 1.0

[time]
step_s = 0.5
duration_s = 220.0

[gnss]
windows = [
  { t0 = 0.0,   t1 = 100.0, state = "nominal" },
  { t0 = 100.0, t1 = 220.0, state = "denied" },
]

# Inertial sensor. The [accel.cai] block makes this the QUANTUM cold-atom interferometer: its
# velocity-random-walk floor q_va is derived from the interferometer physics (k_eff = 4*pi/lambda,
# projection noise 1/(C*sqrt(N)), cycle time), NOT from the supplied q_va. Remove the [accel.cai]
# block to fall back to a classical datasheet sensor at the supplied q_va.
[accel]
id = "cold-atom-interferometer"
provenance = "Cold-atom (Rb-87 D2) interferometric accelerometer; bracketed parameters in the GAIN/MAIUS literature range (Freier et al. arXiv:1512.05660; Becker et al. Nature 2018). Modelled, partner-owned hardware."
bias = 0.0
q_va = 1.0e-9          # fallback classical value (overridden by the [accel.cai] physics below)

[accel.cai]
wavelength_m = 780.241209e-9   # Rb-87 D2 line (RB87_D2_WAVELENGTH_M)
pulse_sep_t = 0.02              # interrogation pulse separation T (s)
atom_number = 1.0e6            # detected atoms per shot N
contrast = 0.5                # initial fringe contrast C0
cycle_time_s = 0.5            # measurement cycle time T_c (s)

# Onboard clock Allan profile, fed to the q-parameter clock engine. A space-oriented optical /
# ultra-stable oscillator class: white-FM sigma_y(1 s) ~ 1e-13, random-walk-FM two decades below.
[clock]
id = "ultrastable-optical"
provenance = "Ultra-stable/optical onboard oscillator class, white-FM sigma_y(1 s) ~ 1e-13 (Riley NIST SP 1065; bracketing the achievable, not a flight unit). Modelled."
white_fm_adev_1s = 1.0e-13
rw_fm_level = 1.0e-15

ins-trn-coast.toml:
# INS/TRN coasting error model — position error against coast duration, and the coast
# durations at which it crosses 10 m and 50 m.
#
# The question this answers: when a GNSS (or aperture-duty-cycled) study says "assume a
# dead-reckoning drift of 0.001–0.050 m/s", where does that number come from? It comes
# from the IMU, and this scenario computes it instead of sweeping it. Five growth terms —
# accelerometer bias (t^2), gyro-bias tilt through gravity (t^3), velocity random walk
# (t^1.5), angle random walk (t^2.5) and scale factor times the travelled distance — are
# combined under a stated rule, and the threshold crossings are located by bisection on
# the combined model. Every crossing carries the per-contribution breakdown that says
# which error source put it there.
#
# Consumed by `kshana::inertial::coast` and dispatched as `kind = "ins-trn-coast"`. The
# growth laws are cross-checked against the engine's own stochastic dead-reckoner
# (`inertial::AccelModel`, Monte-Carlo) and its IMU error model
# (`inertial::imu_errors::ImuErrorModel`, double-integrated); the IMU class coefficients
# are representative Groves-Table-4.1-band figures, NOT a datasheet for any part.
kind = "ins-trn-coast"

# Representative IMU class: navigation, tactical, industrial or consumer. Any individual
# coefficient below can be overridden, which relabels the reported grade as `custom`.
imu_grade = "navigation"

# Airborne cruise. The scale-factor error mis-scales the TRAVELLED DISTANCE, so the speed
# is part of the error model, not decoration: at 250 m/s a 100 ppm scale factor is a
# 0.025 m/s floor on the mean drift rate that no coast duration falls below.
speed_m_s = 250.0
ref_accel_m_s2 = 0.0

# How the five contributions combine into one number. A MODELLING CHOICE, stated: `rss`
# reads each coefficient as a 1-sigma spec, `linear-sum` is the coherent worst case, and
# `det-sum-stoch-rss` adds the systematic terms while root-sum-squaring the independently
# driven random walks. All three are reported in `combination_sensitivity` either way.
combination = "rss"

# The crossings to report (m). These are inputs: the 10 m / 50 m pair is the default, not
# a constant compiled into the model.
crossing_thresholds_m = [10.0, 50.0]

# The drift-rate band a duty-cycle study sweeps (m/s), checked against per grade.
drift_band_lo_m_per_s = 0.001
drift_band_hi_m_per_s = 0.050

# Terrain-referenced aiding. TRN in this engine (`altpnt::terrain`, `altpnt::sequential`)
# recovers a POSITION offset by matching measured ground elevation against a stored DEM,
# so it bounds the coast with a fix rather than slowing the growth between fixes.
# `position-only` is what a bare position fix does — velocity error and tilt keep
# integrating across it; `full-reset` re-zeroes the whole error state, as
# `AccelModel::reset` does for a GNSS re-alignment.
trn_fix_mode = "position-only"
trn_fix_interval_s = 120.0
# The matching sigma of the shipped terrain-nav configuration: hypot(altimeter 8 m,
# DEM 15 m). NOT the achieved batch-matcher residual on that scenario's track.
trn_fix_residual_m = 17.0
mission_duration_s = 1200.0
integrity-raim.toml:
# GNSS integrity (RAIM) availability over a GPS-like constellation.
#
# At each epoch the visible satellites are propagated, the snapshot-RAIM
# horizontal/vertical protection levels are computed from the geometry and the
# user-equivalent range error, and availability is judged against the APV-I
# alert limits (HAL 40 m, VAL 50 m). The output is an HPL/VPL availability map:
# per-epoch protection levels and the fraction of epochs that meet the limits.
#
# The ranging error here (1 m, 1-sigma) is representative of a modern
# dual-frequency, carrier-smoothed receiver — single-frequency RAIM (~5-6 m) does
# not meet the vertical APV-I limit on a single constellation, which is why
# vertical guidance uses SBAS / dual-frequency / ARAIM. The constellation is a
# synthetic 24-satellite Walker-delta pattern (6 planes of 4), illustrative of
# GPS geometry; swap in a `tle` block for a real one.
#
# The result also carries a vertical Stanford(-ESA) integrity diagram: at each
# protected epoch a seeded no-fault range-error draw is mapped through the
# geometry to an actual vertical error and classified against the VPL and the
# vertical alert limit (Available / System-Unavailable / Misleading / Hazardously
# Misleading). `seed` makes that error realization reproducible.
kind = "integrity"

seed = 7
mask_deg = 5.0
sigma_uere_m = 1.0   # 1-sigma user-equivalent range error (dual-frequency, smoothed)
p_fa = 1.0e-5        # allowed false-alarm probability
p_md = 1.0e-3        # allowed missed-detection probability
al_h_m = 40.0        # horizontal alert limit (APV-I)
al_v_m = 50.0        # vertical alert limit (APV-I)

jamming-demo.toml:
# RF jamming: a ground-based broadband jammer denying GNSS to a nearby receiver.
#
# The chain (Kaplan & Hegarty, Understanding GPS/GNSS, 3rd ed. §9.4): the jammer's
# received power (transmit power + gains − free-space path loss) sets the
# jammer-to-signal ratio J/S at the receiver; the despreading processing gain
# (C/A chip rate) and the spectral-separation factor Q convert that into an
# effective C/N0 per satellite; a satellite loses lock when its effective C/N0
# falls below the tracking threshold (25 dB-Hz here).
#
# A 10 W (10 dBW) broadband jammer 1 km from the receiver produces J/S ≈ 72 dB —
# far beyond the ~35 dB a C/A loop can tolerate — so every visible satellite drops
# below the tracking threshold and the receiver is denied (availability → 0) while
# the satellites remain geometrically visible. Move the jammer out or cut its
# power and J/S falls ~40 dB per decade of range: the same jammer at 100 km only
# degrades the links (J/S ≈ 32 dB, effective C/N0 ≈ 28 dB-Hz) without losing lock.
kind = "jamming"
seed = 1
mask_deg = 5.0
tracking_threshold_dbhz = 25.0

[time]
step_s = 30.0
duration_s = 1800.0

[receiver]
lat_deg = 52.0
lon_deg = 4.0
alt_m = 0.0

# A GPS-like 24-satellite Walker shell (6 planes × 4), propagated through the
# 4.12 mm-validated SGP4 core.
[constellation]
altitude_km = 20200.0
inclination_deg = 55.0
planes = 6
sats_per_plane = 4
phasing_f = 1.0

# 10 W broadband jammer 1 km East of the receiver (ECEF; J/S depends only on
# range, so the exact direction is immaterial).
[jammer]
position_ecef_m = [3926375.101, 274488.966, 5002803.345]
power_dbw = 10.0
gain_dbi = 0.0
jammer_type = "broadband"
bandwidth_mhz = 20.0
l-band-waterfall-jamming.toml:
# L-band waterfall under jamming: the whole Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS)
# L band as one power spectral density (PSD), frequency across, time down, while a
# scripted sequence of jammers switches on.
#
# The question a spectrum monitor or a receiver designer asks: what does the band look
# like while this happens, and which signals does each jammer actually take away? The
# navigation signals sit about 20 dB below the thermal noise floor, so the picture shows
# the floor and the jammers; the per-band carrier-to-noise density (C/N0) bars show what
# despreading recovers. Each jammer is scored against each band by its spectral
# separation coefficient (SSC), the overlap of the two spectra over the receiver band
# (Betz 2001; Kaplan & Hegarty, Understanding GPS/GNSS, 3rd ed., section 9.4), so a
# jammer only hurts the bands its spectrum reaches.
#
# Timeline (60 s, one row per second):
#   10 s  a swept (chirp) jammer, 16 MHz wide around L1, a 9 microsecond sawtooth, the
#         shape of a car-cigarette-lighter privacy device: 50 mW (-13 dBW) at 100 m.
#         It takes GPS L1 coarse/acquisition (C/A) and Galileo E1 away together.
#   30 s  a continuous-wave (CW) tone exactly on the L1 carrier, 10 mW at 1 km. On C/A
#         it lands on the peak of the binary phase-shift keying (BPSK) spectrum; on
#         Galileo E1 it lands in the null of the multiplexed binary offset carrier (MBOC)
#         spectrum, so E1 recovers when the chirp stops at 40 s while C/A stays lost.
#   45 s  flat 2 MHz noise on the L2 carrier, received at -135 dBW: GPS L2 civil (L2C)
#         is degraded but keeps tracking.
# GPS L5 and Galileo E5a, at 1176.45 MHz, are outside every jammer's spectrum.
#
# The [iq] section draws the model at 35 s as complex IQ samples (20.48 MHz around L1),
# writes them as a Signal Metadata Format (SigMF) recording and reads them back, and
# compares a Welch estimate with the model: a check of the synthesis, the SigMF codec and
# the estimator, not a measurement. A real recording can be compared instead with a
# [recording] section (meta_path = "capture.sigmf-meta"), native builds only.
#
# Assumptions: signal powers are the interface-specification minimum received powers
# (IS-GPS-200, IS-GPS-705, Galileo Open Service Signal-in-Space Interface Control
# Document); a 290 K antenna and a 2 dB receiver noise figure; free-space propagation
# to the jammers, 0 dBi receive gain toward them. MODELLED: the signal spectra are
# validated closed forms, but every jammer, power and timing here is a scenario input.
kind = "spectrum"
seed = 7
duration_s = 60.0
step_s = 1.0

[receiver]
noise_figure_db = 2.0
antenna_temp_k = 290.0
tracking_threshold_dbhz = 25.0

[grid]
f_min_mhz = 1160.0
f_max_mhz = 1590.0
n_freq = 430

[[jammers]]
name = "chirp privacy device"
waveform = "chirp"
centre_mhz = 1575.42
bandwidth_mhz = 16.0
sweep_period_us = 9.0
eirp_dbw = -13.0
range_m = 100.0
on_s = 10.0
off_s = 40.0

[[jammers]]
name = "CW tone on L1"
waveform = "cw"
centre_mhz = 1575.42
eirp_dbw = -20.0
range_m = 1000.0
on_s = 30.0

[[jammers]]
name = "L2 narrowband noise"
waveform = "narrowband"
centre_mhz = 1227.60
bandwidth_mhz = 2.0
received_power_dbw = -135.0
on_s = 45.0

[iq]

# Launch-window & ascent geometry demonstrator (mission analysis, trade-study tier).

leo-band-trade.toml:
# LEO-PNT band trade, UHF to wide C band: what a low Earth orbit (LEO) positioning,
# navigation and timing (PNT) signal gains and loses in each band, independent of any
# particular system.
#
# Five REPRESENTATIVE designs from the compiled-in `generic-bands` preset, each a pilot
# and data pair with a 50/50 power split sized to its band:
#   UHF   465 MHz,      BPSK(5) in 10 MHz
#   L     1191.795 MHz, BPSK(10) in 20.46 MHz (the Galileo E5 centre)
#   S     2492.028 MHz, BPSK(5) in 16.5 MHz (the NavIC S-band carrier, in the RDSS band)
#   C     5020 MHz,     BPSK(10) in 20 MHz (the middle of the 5010-5030 MHz RNSS band)
#   wide C 5100 MHz,    BPSK(50) in 120 MHz
# (BPSK binary phase-shift keying; RDSS Radio Determination Satellite Service; RNSS Radio
# Navigation Satellite Service.)
#
# The trade table puts four things side by side:
#   * ionospheric delay: first order, 40.3 TEC / f^2, for a 50 TECU slant total electron
#     content: UHF carries (1191.795/465)^2 = 6.6 times the L-band delay, C band 0.056;
#   * free-space loss at a 1000 km slant range: +20 log10(f/f_L) dB relative to L;
#   * ranging accuracy (delay-lock-loop thermal-noise jitter, 0.5 chip coherent
#     early-late spacing, 1 Hz loop) at equal C/N0 (45 dB-Hz for all), and at equal
#     radiated power (C/N0 falls with the free-space loss: isotropic antennas at both
#     ends, so the higher band's smaller receive aperture is charged in full);
#   * the J/S a CW tone, wideband noise and matched noise may reach before the tracked
#     pilot falls below 25 dB-Hz, at the equal-power C/N0.
# MODELLED: the closed forms are validated; the designs, the TEC, the range and the
# equal-power assumption are inputs. No rain or atmospheric loss (it matters at C band).
kind = "leo-signal"
presets = ["generic-bands"]

leo-doppler-positioning.toml:
# Positioning from LEO Doppler alone, over a generic LEO navigation constellation.
#
# A receiver near Munich measures the Doppler shift of every satellite of a 258-satellite
# LEO navigation constellation (the public Xona Pulsar X1 signal table and constellation,
# arXiv:2509.19551; the split between its two inclinations is representative) for ten
# minutes and solves for its position and clock drift by batch least squares. Doppler gives
# range rate, and only the part of the satellite velocity across the line of sight carries
# position information, so the geometry is the change of the lines of sight over the pass,
# not the spread of satellites at one instant.
#
# The report gives the full-window error, the error against window length (how quickly a
# Doppler fix forms), the Doppler, Doppler-rate and jerk envelope of the system over an
# overhead pass, and a single-pass table: the formal along-track and cross-track errors of a
# fix from ONE satellite pass against the user's distance from the ground track. The
# cross-track error grows without bound as the pass goes overhead, where the Doppler curve
# stops depending on the cross-track distance (and the mirror image across the track fits
# almost as well).
#
# MODELLED. Doppler noise 1 Hz one sigma (0.19 m/s at 1593 MHz), perfect ephemeris, no
# ionosphere or troposphere rate, a height-free three-dimensional fit.
kind = "leo-pvt"
mode = "doppler"
seed = 7
duration_s = 600.0
step_s = 10.0

lat_deg = 48.14
lon_deg = 11.58

# corrupted frame that must be rejected.

leo-focus-fused-pnt-sisre.toml:
# LEO-PNT focus area: MEO + LEO fused PNT.
#
# A receiver in Madrid fuses GPS, Galileo and the Xona Pulsar X5 signal (public signal
# table, arXiv 2509.19551; the inclined 1080 km shell) in one weighted least-squares
# pseudorange solution with an inter-system bias per system. How good must the LEO orbit
# and clock be for the LEO layer to help? The campaign sweeps the LEO signal-in-space
# range error (SISRE) from 5 cm to 5 m and records the root-mean-square (RMS) 3D error of
# the GNSS-only, LEO-only and fused solutions over half an hour, and the fused median
# position dilution of precision (PDOP).
#

leo-focus-science-iono-sounding.toml:
# LEO-PNT focus area: LEO-PNT science, ionosphere sounding from the dual-band delay.
#
# The first-order ionospheric group delay is 40.3*STEC/f^2 (STEC slant total electron
# content), so the difference of two bands' pseudoranges to one satellite measures the
# slant TEC below the satellite: STEC = (P2 - P1)*f1^2*f2^2 / (40.3*(f1^2 - f2^2)). A low
# Earth orbit (LEO) positioning, navigation and timing (PNT) satellite transmitting in
# several bands is therefore also an ionosphere sounder, and one below most of the
# plasmasphere: it sees only the electron content under its own altitude.
#
# One generic LEO satellite at 550 km passes 70 deg over the Tromso ionospheric
# observatory region (69.66 N) in UHF, L, S and C bands; the ionosphere is a 25 TEC-unit
# vertical content on a 350 km shell, scaled by the fraction of a Chapman layer below the
# satellite. For every band pair the report gives the slant TEC the geometry-free
# combination recovers at the pass peak and its 1-sigma from the two bands' code noise.
# Pairs with UHF sound best (UHF with L to about 0.02 TEC units): UHF carries the largest
# delay and, here, the strongest signal. The close S and C bands sound worst (about 3 TEC
# units): their delay difference is small against their code noise.
#
# MODELLED: the recovered TEC equals the model's by construction (the combination is exact
# at first order); the precision is the thermal code noise alone, without multipath or
# inter-frequency biases, which a real sounder must calibrate.
kind = "leo-pass"
name = "LEO ionosphere sounding from multi-band delays"
epoch = "2026-09-28T11:00:00"
duration_s = 900.0
step_s = 5.0

# LEO navigation message: Kshana's binary encoding, its quantisation budget, and the
# RINEX-style and CSV exports.
#
# The binary frame is Kshana's own documented encoding (preamble, version, model, length,
# payload, CRC-24Q). It carries the published components of a LEO message (a Galileo-
# style Keplerian set with along/cross/radial corrections, a second-order clock
# polynomial, SVID, issue of data, band and health, a Klobuchar and a NeQuick-G
# ionospheric set, and UTC parameters) with steps sized so that every field's half-step
# error stays under a millimetre over the validity window. It is not the bit layout of
# any operational or demonstration system; none is public.
#
# The run fits three consecutive messages, encodes the first, decodes it, checks the
# CRC (and that a flipped bit is rejected), prints the per-field half-step budget and
# the SISRE of the exact and decoded message against the truth, then writes all three as
# a RINEX-4-style block (a documented Kshana extension: RINEX 4.02 has no LEO records;
# prior art arXiv 2401.17767) and as a CSV table, and reads both back.

leo-navmsg-fit-interval-trade.toml:
# LEO navigation message: signal-in-space range error (SISRE) versus fit interval.
#
# A low Earth orbit (LEO) positioning, navigation and timing (PNT) satellite broadcasts
# its orbit as a compact parameter set fitted to a short arc. The question: how long can
# one message cover before its representation error outgrows the target, and what does a
# set of along-track, cross-track and radial (RAC) correction polynomials buy?
#
# Truth: a 550 km, 97.6 deg orbit integrated with the EGM2008 gravity field to degree 20
# and drag. Each message is fitted over its interval and used over a period centred in
# it. Two models: the Galileo Open Service Signal-in-Space Interface Control Document
# (OS SIS ICD) 16-parameter Keplerian set, and that set plus RAC polynomials of degree
# 7 (along), 5 (cross) and 6 (radial). Why so high: the least-squares Keplerian residual
# is what the 16 parameters cannot span, so it oscillates across the window, and only a
# polynomial of higher degree than the Keplerian set already spans removes it (a
# cross-track polynomial of lower degree removes almost nothing). SISRE uses the
# global-average weights for the
# orbit altitude (Montenbruck et al. 2018 method): at 550 km the radial weight is about
# 0.47 and the transverse weight squared about 1/2.6, so along- and cross-track errors
# count far more than for medium Earth orbit.
#
# The first table sets the usage period equal to the fit interval (1 to 15 minutes);
# the second holds a 5-minute fit and shortens the update period. No preset is used: the
# numbers are Kshana's own truth and fit, the representation error only (no orbit
# determination or prediction error). MODELLED.
kind = "leo-navmsg"
name = "LEO message fit-interval trade"
seed = 11
analysis = ["fit-interval-trade"]

altitude_km = 550.0
inclination_deg = 97.6

# LEO navigation message: a message update in the middle of a pass, and whether the user

# A LEO pass lasts minutes, so a satellite may switch to a new message while a user is
