leo-navmsg-model-comparison.toml:
# LEO navigation message: four ephemeris models on one orbit, and the Liu et al. 2025
# SISRE-versus-altitude table.
#
# Models: the Galileo 16-parameter Keplerian set; that set plus along/cross/radial
# polynomials; the 22-parameter extension of Liu, Su, Xie, Zhou and Qu (2025, Remote
# Sensing 17(16):2894, doi 10.3390/rs17162894), which adds a semi-major-axis rate, a
# mean-motion rate and once- and three-per-revolution radius harmonics; and the Earth-
# centred Earth-fixed (ECEF) 6th-order polynomial with no clock terms that the ATOMIC
# payload flew ("zero-clock": the satellite clock is steered to system time, and the
# message is scored against a steered clock with a 0.24 m residual). Each at fit
# intervals of 1, 5 and 10 minutes, with its parameter count and its size in Kshana's
# binary encoding.
#
# The Liu table fits Kshana's 22-parameter model over 20-minute arcs at the five
# altitudes of the paper (320, 475, 786, 966, 1336 km) and prints the published SISRE
# beside it. The paper fitted real precise science orbits of named satellites; Kshana
# fits its own integrated orbit at the same altitude and inclination, so the comparison
# is MODELLED, not VALIDATED.
kind = "leo-navmsg"
name = "LEO message model comparison"
seed = 12
analysis = ["model-comparison"]

[orbit]
altitude_km = 550.0
inclination_deg = 97.6
gravity_degree = 20

[message]
model = "kepler-rac"
rac_degrees = [7, 5, 6]

[comparison]
models = ["kepler16", "kepler-rac", "liu22", "ecef-poly"]
fit_intervals_s = [60, 300, 600]
span_s = 1200
liu_table = true
liu_arcs = 3

leo-pass-vs-gnss-cn0.toml:
# A LEO-PNT pass against the Galileo satellites in view: C/N0 over one pass.
#
# LEO-PNT is positioning, navigation and timing from satellites in low Earth orbit (LEO). A
# ground user near Munich watches one pass of a generic LEO navigation satellite (the
# representative generic-leo preset: 550 km sun-synchronous, an L-band carrier at the Galileo
# E5 centre frequency of 1191.795 MHz, 0 dBW EIRP from a nadir-pointing 110 deg Gaussian beam)
# and the Galileo satellites above a 5 deg mask on E1, all through the same patch antenna and
# receiver noise model. The pass is designed to peak at 80 deg elevation mid-window.
#
# The result reproduces, qualitatively, what LEO-PNT demonstrations show: the LEO carrier-to-
# noise density (C/N0) rises and falls in a bell a few minutes long, peaking several dB above
# the flat MEO (medium Earth orbit) GNSS carriers, which sit in the mid-40s to about 50 dB-Hz.
# The larger LEO signal comes from a range some forty times shorter than to a MEO satellite
# (about 26 to 32 dB less free-space loss), not from a stronger transmitter. The Galileo
# carriers use the minimum received power of the Galileo OS SIS ICD Issue 2.1 Table 12, plus
# 2 dB, scaled by range.
#
# MODELLED. No Celeste or other workshop data is used: every LEO number here comes from the
# representative preset in src/leo_link/presets/generic.rs.
kind = "leo-pass"
name = "LEO pass versus MEO GNSS C/N0"
epoch = "2026-09-28T08:00:00"
duration_s = 900.0
step_s = 2.0

leo-pnt-end-to-end.toml:
# LEO-PNT end to end on a generic constellation: signal design -> pass link budget ->
# navigation message -> fused MEO + LEO fix and precise point positioning convergence.
#
# One low Earth orbit (LEO) positioning, navigation and timing (PNT) system is followed
# through every stage of the engine, with no named system's data at all:
#
# - Signal: the representative L-band design `generic-l` (binary phase-shift keying at
#   10.23 Mchip/s, pilot and data halves, 20.46 MHz transmit bandwidth) from the public
#   preset file data/leo-signals/generic-bands.toml.
# - Pass: a user in Madrid watches a designed pass of a 1080 km, 53 deg satellite peaking at
#   75 deg. The band takes the design's centre, bandwidth and chip rate and splits its
#   EIRP (equivalent isotropically radiated power) across the design's components; every
#   epoch gives the tracked (pilot) component's C/N0 (carrier-to-noise density) and its
#   band-limited code-tracking jitter.
# - Navigation message: the Galileo Keplerian set with along-track, cross-track and radial
#   correction polynomials, fitted every 300 s to a truth orbit at the pass satellite's
#   altitude and inclination; its broadcast signal-in-space range error (SISRE) is the LEO
#   orbit-and-clock error downstream.
# - Positioning: GPS and Galileo with a generic 240-satellite LEO layer (Walker 240/12/1
#   at 1080 km, 53 deg). The LEO system takes the pass's C/N0 line, the message's SISRE
#   and the design's carrier and chip rate.
# - Precise point positioning (PPP): GPS and Galileo alone and with the same LEO layer, the
#   LEO orbit-and-clock error taken from the message.
#
# MODELLED: every stage keeps its own label; the chain adds no physics.
kind = "leo-pnt-chain"
name = "LEO-PNT end to end, generic 1080 km constellation"
seed = 5
signal_design = "generic-l"
# Orbit determination and clock prediction, as a range error (m): representative of on-board
# GNSS orbit determination with a steered chip-scale clock at the decimetre level (the ATOMIC
# payload reports under 10 cm per axis in orbit and 24 cm in clock: InsideGNSS,
# https://insidegnss.com/first-steps-toward-a-fully-operational-leo-pnt-payload/).

leo-pnt-mega-shell.toml:
# A low-Earth-orbit positioning, navigation and timing (PNT) mega-constellation: 5 000
# satellites in four Walker shells, scored as a coverage and dilution-of-precision (DOP) map.
#
# The shells are an illustrative design, not any operator's filing:
#   - 1 600 satellites, Walker delta 1600/32/1 at 550 km and 53 deg;
#   - 1 600 satellites, Walker delta 1600/32/7 at 540 km and 53.2 deg;
#   - 1 000 satellites, Walker delta 1000/20/3 at 570 km and 70 deg;
#   -   800 satellites, Walker star 800/16/1 at 560 km and 97.6 deg (near-polar, planes
#       spread over 180 deg) to fill the high latitudes.
#
# At this size the visibility prefilter matters: each epoch the satellites are sorted by
# sub-satellite latitude and a grid row only tests those within one coverage half-angle of
# it. The `work` block of the result states how many satellite-point pair tests a brute-force
# scan would have made and how many were made. The secular J2 drift of the nodes is on, and
# the tracks are downsampled to 120 satellites.
#
# What the run answers: satellites in view, PDOP/HDOP/VDOP/GDOP per 10 deg cell, and the
# share of time with PDOP at or below 3 above a 20 deg mask over two hours. The weak spot the
# map shows is the polar caps: no shell reaches above about 82 deg latitude, so a user near a
# pole sees every satellite on one side of the sky and the vertical geometry degrades. MODELLED: an
# illustrative design, two-body orbits with J2, a spherical Earth, geometry only.

body = "earth"
duration_s = 7200.0
step_s = 600.0

leo-resilience-gnss-jammed-leo-carries.t:
# LEO-PNT resilience mission: GNSS jammed, LEO-PNT carries the user, integrity maintained.
#
# Three phases on one 30 s timeline, each running a `spectrum` receiver (what it can still
# track) and an `integrity` run (receiver autonomous integrity monitoring, RAIM, against a
# 40 m horizontal and 50 m vertical alert limit):
#
#   nominal   GPS L1 C/A, Galileo E5a and a generic low Earth orbit (LEO) positioning,
#             navigation and timing (PNT) layer in the S and C bands all track; integrity
#             uses the GNSS layer (24 satellites at 20 200 km) and the LEO layer (240 at
#             1080 km, 53 deg, and 72 at 1080 km, 97 deg) together.
#   jammed    two barrage jammers, one over L1 and one over L5/E5, at -95 dBW received:
#             both GNSS signals fall below the 25 dB-Hz tracking floor; the S- and C-band
#             LEO signals are untouched. Integrity runs on the LEO layer alone.
#   recovery  the jammers stop; both layers again.
#
# The alarm channel is the integrity kind's own: raised at epochs where the protection
# level cannot be formed or exceeds the alert limit. With GNSS jammed the LEO layer alone
# still forms a protection level at every epoch; it is under the 50 m alert limit at 28
# of the 30 grid times and the alarm is raised at the other two. That is integrity
# working: the user is warned whenever the bound is too large, and availability, not
# integrity, is what the jamming costs.
#
# The integrity runs use that kind's own user track (a circular track 0.4 km up, the
# convention of the other bundled integrity runs), not the spectrum receiver's site, and
# a 1 m user-equivalent range error for both layers; those are scenario choices, stated
# here. The integrity kind does not see the jammer: the jammed phase's LEO-only
# constellation is the campaign's statement of what the spectrum run says is left.
# MODELLED.
kind = "campaign"
title = "GNSS jammed, LEO-PNT carries the user, integrity maintained"
seed = 20260929

[timeline]
step_s = 30.0

[[phases]]
name = "nominal"
duration_s = 600.0

[[phases.runs]]
series = [
  { channel = "cn0_gps_l1ca_dbhz", unit = "dB-Hz", t = "timeline.t_s[]", y = "timeline.bands[0].cn0_effective_dbhz[]" },
  { channel = "cn0_galileo_e5a_dbhz", unit = "dB-Hz", t = "timeline.t_s[]", y = "timeline.bands[1].cn0_effective_dbhz[]" },
  { channel = "cn0_leo_s_dbhz", unit = "dB-Hz", t = "timeline.t_s[]", y = "timeline.bands[2].cn0_effective_dbhz[]" },
  { channel = "cn0_leo_c_dbhz", unit = "dB-Hz", t = "timeline.t_s[]", y = "timeline.bands[3].cn0_effective_dbhz[]" },
  { channel = "cn0_floor_dbhz", t = "timeline.t_s[]", y = "receiver.tracking_threshold_dbhz" },
]

kind = "spectrum"

leo-resilience-js-margin.toml:
# LEO-PNT resilience from received power: the jammer-to-signal (J/S) margin.
#
# A jammer denies a signal when the jammer power it lets through, relative to the signal's
# own received power, pushes the effective carrier-to-noise density (C/N0) below the
# tracking threshold. A low Earth orbit (LEO) satellite is about 20 to 40 times closer than
# a medium Earth orbit (MEO) GNSS satellite, so the same transmitter delivers 26 to 32 dB
# more power, and every dB of received power is a dB of J/S margin.
#
# One wideband (barrage) noise jammer, 40 MHz wide at 1185 MHz, covers GPS L5, Galileo E5a
# and two LEO signals in the same band. Its received power steps up by 5 dB every 10 s
# from -125 dBW at 10 s to -90 dBW at 80 s. The `spectrum` kind's first-loss time of
# each band is where the jammer takes it:
#   gps-l5       interface-document minimum, -157.9 dBW
#   galileo-e5a  interface-document minimum, -155.0 dBW
#   xona-x5      the published minimum received power, -144.9 dBW (arXiv 2509.19551)
#   generic-l    a representative LEO L-band signal at -135 dBW, 1191.795 MHz
# GPS L5 is lost at the -105 dBW step, Galileo E5a at -100 dBW, Xona X5 at -95 dBW; the
# generic signal still tracks at -90 dBW. Received power buys J/S margin dB for dB.
# Received powers are those at the stated minimum; a real pass varies over it (see the
# leo-pass scenarios).
#

# received powers are scenario inputs.

# LEO-PNT resilience by band diversity: one jammer, a four-band receiver.
#
# A receiver tracks a low Earth orbit (LEO) positioning, navigation and timing (PNT)
# system in four bands (UHF, L, S and C) beside GPS L5 and Galileo E5a. One wideband
# (barrage) noise jammer, 50 MHz wide and centred at 1185 MHz, covers the whole L5/E5
# band. The campaign sweeps its received power from -140 to -80 dBW and records each
# band's effective carrier-to-noise density (C/N0) from the `spectrum` kind's spectral
# separation coefficient (SSC) chain.
#
# What the sweep shows: the jammer takes every L-band signal, GNSS and LEO alike, in
# order of their received power; the UHF, S- and C-band LEO signals keep their nominal
# C/N0 at every power, because no jammer power falls in their bands. A system that
# spreads its signals over several bands is only denied by a jammer in every band.
#
# Signals (every one public or representative; no system-specific data):
#   gps-l5, galileo-e5a   interface-document minimum received power
#   generic-uhf  465 MHz, BPSK(5), 10 MHz, -150 dBW          [representative]
#   generic-l    1191.795 MHz (the Galileo E5 centre), -150 dBW  [representative]
#   generic-s    2492.028 MHz (the NavIC S carrier), -150 dBW    [representative]
#   generic-c    5020 MHz (the 5010-5030 MHz RNSS allocation), -152 dBW [representative]
# (BPSK binary phase-shift keying; RNSS radionavigation-satellite service.)
#
# MODELLED: the spectra are validated closed forms; the jammer and the received powers
# are scenario inputs. This is the "PNT resilience in L, S and C bands" focus area.

title = "LEO-PNT band diversity against an L-band barrage jammer"

leo-resilience-spoof-doppler.toml:
# LEO-PNT resilience against spoofing: Doppler and pass-geometry consistency.
#
# A timing receiver at a surveyed site (Frankfurt, position known to 1 m, velocity known
# to be zero within 2 mm/s) tracks Galileo E1 and a generic low Earth orbit (LEO)
# positioning, navigation and timing (PNT) layer (240 satellites at 1080 km, 53 deg; the
# 16 highest passes of the half hour). At 300 s a spoofer captures every channel and
# presents a position 30 m east of the true one, self-consistently in range and range
# rate: the counterfeit signals are what a receiver 30 m away would see, the ionospheric
# delay included (so the cross-band monitor has nothing to see; `leo-resilience-spoof-
# monitors` shows the spoofers it does catch).
#
# The receiver predicts each satellite's range rate from the broadcast orbit and its
# surveyed position and tests the measured range rates (chi-square, false-alarm
# probability 1e-5 per epoch, detection declared at 99.9 % probability). A 30 m error
# changes a MEO GNSS range rate by about 4 mm/s, inside the frequency-lock-loop noise;
# it changes a LEO range rate by about 10 cm/s, because a LEO satellite's transverse
# velocity over its range is about 25 times larger. The GNSS-only test never sees the
# spoofer; the test on every channel (GNSS and LEO, sharing one receiver clock drift, which
# the GNSS channels pin) detects it once enough LEO satellites are in view, 105 s after
# the onset.
#
# MODELLED: the monitor's statistics are exact for the stated Gaussian noise; the spoofer
# is an idealised position jump (its power, angle of arrival and correlation-peak
# signatures are not modelled), and the prior is independent of the spoofed fixes.
kind = "leo-pass"
name = "Spoofing detection by LEO Doppler consistency"
epoch = "2026-09-28T08:00:00"
duration_s = 1800.0
step_s = 5.0

leo-resilience-spoof-monitors.toml:
# LEO-PNT resilience against spoofing: which monitor sees which spoofer.
#
# Four spoofers attack the same receiver (Frankfurt, surveyed position known to 1 m,
# static), which tracks Galileo E1 and a generic low Earth orbit (LEO) layer in its L
# and C bands (240 satellites at 1080 km). Each spoofer moves the position the receiver
# computes 30 m east at 300 s (a shared value, so the four cannot disagree). Two monitors
# run on every member (the `leo-pass` kind's `[spoofer]` section):
#   * Doppler and pass-geometry consistency: measured range rates against those predicted
#     from the broadcast orbits and the surveyed position (chi-square, false-alarm
#     probability 1e-5 per epoch);
#   * cross-band consistency: the step of each LEO satellite's L-minus-C geometry-free
#     pseudorange combination, which should hold only the slowly changing ionospheric
#     delay.
# The members:
#   l-band-only          counterfeits GNSS and the LEO L band, not the C band (a spoofer
#                        built for the GNSS band): the L and C pseudoranges of one
#                        satellite disagree by the push, so both monitors see it;
#   all-bands-no-iono    counterfeits every band from the ground, where no ionosphere
#                        delays its signals: the geometry-free combination collapses to
#                        zero at the onset, a step of the L-minus-C ionospheric delay;
#   all-bands-with-iono  counterfeits every band and simulates the ionosphere: the
#                        cross-band monitor cannot see it, the Doppler monitor can;
#   gnss-only            counterfeits GNSS alone: a 30 m push moves GNSS range rates by
#                        millimetres per second, which neither monitor sees; a cross-check
#                        of the GNSS and LEO pseudorange positions would (not modelled).
#
# MODELLED: the monitors' statistics are exact for the stated Gaussian noise; each
# spoofer is an idealised position jump, and the receiver's ionosphere model is the
# engine's, so only the tolerated unmodelled rate (1 cm/s) stands for its error.

title = "Spoofing monitors against four spoofers"

leo-timing-utc.toml:
# Time transfer to UTC from LEO satellites, against C/N0 and the receiver oscillator.
#
# A timing receiver at a surveyed site in Boulder, Colorado recovers its clock from the
# Iridium constellation (the `iridium-stl` preset: 66 satellites at 780 km, L-band bursts,
# received power 300 to 2400 times GPS), holds time with its own oscillator when no
# satellite is in view, and converts the system time to UTC with the broadcast offset
# (IS-GPS-200 expression; the parameters below are illustrative, with a 5 ns uncertainty).
# Four oscillator classes (TCXO, OCXO, chip-scale atomic clock, rubidium) and four C/N0
# offsets are compared over six hours, every row with the same seed so the rows differ only
# in C/N0 and oscillator. The Iridium bursts arrive 25 to 34 dB above GPS, so the loop noise
# of the 25 000 symbol/s ranging signal matters only when the C/N0 is cut by 20 dB or more;
# at nominal power the 5 m representative signal-in-space range error and the UTC-offset

# LEO-PNT vertical: critical infrastructure timing, holdover with LEO time.
#
# A grid-edge time server at a substation in Boulder, Colorado must hold the 1 microsecond
# synchronisation that power-system protection and phasor measurement need (the IEC/IEEE
# 61850-9-3 power profile). Its oscillator is a temperature-compensated crystal (TCXO)
# class part, disciplined to GNSS. When GNSS is lost:
#
#   gnss-locked  (10 min) the `clock` kind's TCXO tracks GNSS: time error near zero.
#   gnss-denied  (24 h) the same TCXO coasts on its own: its random-walk frequency noise
#                makes the time error grow as t^1.5, through the 1000 ns guard a little
#                over an hour after the loss and to about 29 microseconds by the end of
#                the day. Beside it, a `leo-pvt` timing run disciplines the same TCXO class
#                to the Iridium constellation (the public `iridium-stl` preset: 66
#                satellites at 780 km, L-band bursts 25 to 34 dB above GPS), holding
#                between passes, and converts system time to UTC (Coordinated Universal
#                Time) with the broadcast offset. A `leo-pass` run of one Iridium pass over
#                the site carries the geometry the campaign exports.
#
# The alarm is raised on the LEO-disciplined time error against the 1000 ns guard; it
# stays down. The free-running error is shown for comparison and is not alarmed. Both
# runs use the same oscillator noise (the engine's TCXO class); the deterministic
# frequency offset and ageing are taken as calibrated at the loss of GNSS.
#
# NIST measured Iridium PNT timing receivers with a miniature atomic clock within 40 ns of
# UTC(NIST) over 40 days (https://www.nist.gov/publications/validating-timing-performance-improvement-ionospheric-corrections-iridium-pnt-receivers);
# the modelled figures are a consistency comparison with that, not a reproduction.
# MODELLED.

# LEO-PNT vertical: polar and Arctic users.
#
# GNSS medium Earth orbit (MEO) planes are inclined 55 to 56 deg, so from the Arctic every
# GNSS satellite sits in the southern half of the sky at low elevation, and the vertical
# geometry suffers. A polar low Earth orbit (LEO) constellation passes overhead there
# most often. A user travels north through three phases of an hour each, Tromso (69.7 N),
# Longyearbyen on Svalbard (78.2 N) and the North Pole drift ice (89.5 N); each phase runs
# a `leo-pvt` joint fix of GPS and Galileo, with and without the Iridium constellation (the
# public `iridium-stl` preset: 66 satellites at 780 km, 86.4 deg, with its representative
# 5 m signal-in-space range error), and a `leo-pass` run of the three highest Iridium
# passes of a quarter hour over the site, whose geometry the campaign exports.
#
# Channels: the GNSS-only and fused 3D errors, their position dilution of precision
# (PDOP) and the satellites in view. The alarm is raised where the fused error exceeds
# 3 m. `polar-arctic-leo-coverage` gives the same comparison as a table over latitude.
#
# MODELLED: two-body orbits with J2 from each constellation preset; no ionospheric
# scintillation, which the auroral zone would add.

#
#   strait-jammed  `maritime-strait-jamming` (a ship in the Gulf of Finland, a 17 dBW
#                  broadband L1 jammer about 30 km away): the GNSS carriers fall below
#                  the 25 dB-Hz floor. A `leo-pass` run of the same ship (maritime user,
#                  8 m/s) tracks a generic LEO satellite (1080 km, 97 deg polar orbit)
#                  in its S and C bands, which the L1 jammer does not reach.
#   rail-tunnel    `rail-tunnel-coast` (a train at 44.4 m/s coasting on a tactical inertial
#                  unit in a tunnel, no aiding): the event marks the moment its position
#                  error reaches 2 m, the kind's own crossing time.
#   rail-open      back in the open, a `leo-pass` run of the train (160 km/h east of
#                  Hamburg) tracks a generic LEO satellite (1080 km, 97 deg) in its L
#                  and S bands, the signals a re-acquiring receiver would use to end
#                  the coast.
#
# The alarm follows the jamming kind's own rule (fewer than four GNSS satellites
# tracking) in the strait. The jamming and LEO runs do not share a model: the leo-pass kind
# has no jammer, and the S and C bands are outside the L1 jammer's 20 MHz by construction.
# MODELLED.

link-budget.toml:
# One-way link budget demonstrator (comms & link budgets, trade-study tier).
#
# Applies the CCSDS 401 / DSN 810-005 link equation
#   C/N0 = EIRP - FSPL - L_other + G/T - k ;  Eb/N0 = C/N0 - 10log10(R_b)
# and reports free-space path loss, C/N0, Eb/N0, margin and whether the link closes
# against a required Eb/N0.
#
# HONEST SCOPE: a deterministic engineering calculation from the supplied inputs
# (EIRP / G/T / range / rate / losses) -- NOT a calibrated terminal datasheet.
# Run:  kshana scenarios/link-budget.toml
kind = "link-budget"

band = "x"                  # s | x | ka (sets the free-space-loss frequency)
eirp_dbw = 55.0
g_over_t_db = 53.0
range_km = 2000.0
data_rate_bps = 1.0e6
other_losses_db = 3.0
required_eb_n0_db = 4.5

# Optional: the receive system noise temperature (K). It is NOT an input to the link
# equation -- that needs only the ratio G/T -- but stating it lets the report also give
# the receive antenna gain the figure of merit implies (G = G/T + 10*log10(T_sys)).
# Left out, the gain split is absent from the report rather than assumed.
# tsys_k = 300.0
lunanet-araim.toml:
# Lunar south-pole integrity: an Artemis-region landed receiver against a
# representative LunaNet relay set, ARAIM protection levels over a 24 h pass.
#
# The lunar navigation signal is far weaker and the relay constellation far sparser
# than GPS (LunaNet LNIS: σ_URE ≈ 30 m vs GPS ≈ 0.6 m), and the protection level
# scales linearly with σ_URE — so this honestly surfaces the integrity gap: with
# 30 m ranging the HPL is finite but exceeds a 50 m surface-ops alert limit, i.e. the
# surface user is not yet "available". This is the quantitative statement that lunar
# PNT integrity is hard, not a claim that it is met.
#
# Scope: a representative selenocentric relay sky (src/lunar.rs south_pole_hpl_pass),
# not the precise differential-corrected 9:2 LANS NRHO — the CR3BP three-body core is
# in src/cr3bp.rs; wiring real NRHO relay ephemerides + DE421 libration are follow-ons.
kind = "lunar-integrity"

step_s = 3600.0        # 1 h samples
duration_s = 86400.0   # 24 h pass
alert_limit_m = 50.0   # LunaNet surface-ops alert limit
p_hmi = 1.0e-4         # lunar surface integrity-risk budget (not aviation 1e-7)
lunar-attack-surface.toml:
# Lunar surface-navigation signal-security attack surface (paper P1).
#
# Composes the open signal-security analyses into one binary-reachable run:
#   * link-budget power deficit vs a terrestrial GPS reference + the 12-18 dB
#     sensitivity band (a genuine reference x EIRP x slant-range sweep) with the
#     32x-rounded / 36x-unrounded linear-factor reconciliation,
#   * the attacker transmit power required to spoof (J/S = 3 dB) and to deny
#     (J/S = 30 dB) at each standoff (the inverse of the J/S link),
#   * the orbital capture footprint under a real uniform-aperture antenna pattern
#     (an altitude-limited sub-hemispheric cap whose limb is NOT captured),
#   * a computed tracking-loop spoof-capture pull-in outcome (does a matched-code
#     spoofer at +6 dB / 0.3-chip actually drag the DLL/PLL) rather than the
#     asserted 3 dB threshold,
#   * the airless-body geometric horizon reach of a raised surface transmitter, and
#   * the OSNMA/TESLA authentication budget (20 bit/s = ~40 % of a 50 bit/s AFS nav
#     message, key-disclosure latency, 2^-40 forgery).
#
# Every input is defaulted to the P1 baseline; the body below leaves them at their
# defaults (so this reproduces the paper's headline figures) while naming the knobs.
# Override any field to explore a different attacker / link geometry.

kind = "lunar-attack-surface"

# Link geometry (defaults shown for transparency).
afs_eirp_dbw = 26.0
user_gain_dbi = 3.0
slant_range_m = 3.0e6
carrier_hz = 2.4e9
gps_reference_dbw = -155.0       # GPS L1 C/A typical received power, dBW (was -125.0, which is dBm)
gps_reference_min_dbw = -158.5   # ICD-GPS-200 specification minimum, dBW (was -128.5, which is dBm)

# Orbital transmitter + footprint.
transmitter_altitude_m = 100_000.0
antenna_diameter_m = 1.0
footprint_grid = 400

# Attacker standoffs (m) for the required-transmit-power curve.
standoffs_m = [1_000.0, 10_000.0, 100_000.0]

# Representative spoofer for the tracking-loop pull-in.
spoof_power_advantage_db = 6.0
spoof_code_offset_chips = 0.3

# Capture-footprint sweep axes: the captured fraction above is ONE operating point
# (100 km, 1 m dish); these sweep it over transmitter altitude x beamwidth so the
# fraction is read against the two inputs that set it, and so limb capture is reported
# as a threshold (the altitude / beamwidth / transmit power at which it switches on)
# rather than a boolean at a single point. Both defaults are chosen so the baseline
# operating point above is an exact sample of the grid.
footprint_altitude_min_m = 20_000.0    # 20 km ... 500 km in 80 km steps
footprint_altitude_max_m = 500_000.0
footprint_altitude_steps = 7
footprint_altitude_scale = "linear"
footprint_diameter_min_m = 0.25        # 0.25 m ... 4 m, i.e. HPBW 29.2 deg ... 1.83 deg
footprint_diameter_max_m = 4.0
footprint_diameter_steps = 5
footprint_diameter_scale = "log"
lunar-beacon.toml:
# Surface-beacon augmentation of a lunar orbital navigation service.
#
# A south-polar lunar user sees a sparse orbital constellation inside a narrow, slowly
# moving patch of sky. Every line of sight points into roughly the same direction, so the
# ranging design matrix is ill-conditioned and the dilution of precision is large — the
# geometry problem, not a signal-power problem. A handful of SURVEYED SURFACE BEACONS fix
# it cheaply: a beacon near the local horizon contributes the low-elevation, wide-azimuth
# line-of-sight rows an all-overhead orbital set structurally cannot supply, and the
# horizontal DOP collapses.
#
# This run reports three configurations at one epoch, so the two routes to usable geometry
# can be compared directly:
#
#   * the satellites alone,
#   * the satellites plus whichever beacons clear the horizon, and
#   * a larger constellation instead — the expensive alternative to the same end.
#
# Each row carries its visible-source counts, its full DOP, and the realised 1-sigma
# accuracy in METRES. That last step is the point: a bare "PDOP 1.6" is dimensionless and
# easy to over-read, so the report multiplies it through a per-beacon user-equivalent
# ranging error (the root-sum-square of the clock-synchronisation, multipath and survey
# terms below) and states the answer as a distance.
#
# WHY THIS FILE EXISTS
# The module behind this kind has been in the engine since L08/L09 and is checked against
# an independent DOP path in tests/validate_p2_beacon_before_after_independent_dop.rs. But
# it was not reachable from a run — no scenario kind, no dispatch arm, no bundled example.
# The README advertised the capability; the verification matrix carried NO row for it at all.
# So it was claimed in prose, unclaimed in the ledger, and unreachable in the engine at the
# same time. A capability the engine cannot be ASKED to perform is not a capability of the
# engine, and one the ledger does not list is not accounted for either.
#
# DEFAULTS ARE THE GOLDEN GEOMETRY
# Every value below is the configuration that already carries a committed golden
# (tests/validate_p2_beacon_before_after_table.rs against
# tests/fixtures/lunar_service/beacon_before_after_golden.csv). Running this file therefore
# reproduces a table an oracle already covers, instead of inventing a fresh configuration
# whose numbers nothing checks. Change them freely — they are inputs, not constants.
#
# WHAT IS ANCHORED AND WHAT IS NOT
# Anchored: the DOP assembly is the kernel cross-checked against gnss_lib_py in
# tests/dop_reference.rs; beacon visibility is the airless-Moon two-height geometric horizon
# closed form (no atmosphere, so there is no refractive extension and the bound is exact);
# and sigma = DOP x sigma_URE is the standard relation (Kaplan & Hegarty, Understanding
# GPS/GNSS, section 7).
# NOT anchored — MODELLED inputs, every one: the constellation design, the beacon
# placement, the antenna heights, and all three error-budget magnitudes. They are
# representative choices, not a fielded survey or a measured link. Nothing here is a
# service-performance commitment, a TRL claim, or affiliated with any agency's programme.

kind = "lunar-beacon"

# EVERY SCALAR KEY MUST STAY ABOVE THE [[beacons]] ARRAY BELOW.
# In TOML, a bare key after an array-of-tables header belongs to that TABLE, not to the
# document root. These keys were originally written underneath [[beacons]] and were
# therefore parsed as fields of the LAST beacon, where serde silently dropped them: the
# scenario ran entirely on its defaults, and because the defaults matched what was written
# here, every printed number looked correct. `deny_unknown_fields` on BeaconSite now makes
# that mistake an error instead of silence, and
# tests/lunar_beacon_scenario_reference.rs asserts the parsed scenario really carries
# these values.

# A sparse six-satellite service, and a 24-satellite service as the contrast.
n_satellites = 6
comparison_n_satellites = 24
epoch_s = 0.0
elevation_mask_deg = 5.0

# Per-beacon ranging error budget, in metres of range. Root-sum-squared into sigma_URE.
clock_sync_m = 1.0
multipath_m = 0.5
survey_m = 0.3

# The user: a south-polar site with a 2 m antenna.
[user]
lat_deg = -80.0
lon_deg = 0.0
alt_m = 2.0

# Three surveyed beacons on 2 km relief, spread in azimuth about the user. The two flanking
# sites at +/-60 deg longitude are what supply the wide-azimuth rows.
[[beacons]]
lat_deg = -80.0
lon_deg = 0.0
alt_m = 2000.0

[[beacons]]
lat_deg = -79.0
lon_deg = 60.0
alt_m = 2000.0

[[beacons]]
lat_deg = -79.0
lon_deg = -60.0
alt_m = 2000.0
lunar-differential-pnt.toml:
# Lunar DIFFERENTIAL PNT — a lunar DGNSS / SBAS analogue.
#
# A NovaMoon-class reference station at a KNOWN selenographic location computes
# per-satellite differential corrections from an ILLUSTRATIVE Moonlight / LCNS-class
# constellation; a roving user offset from it by baseline_km applies those corrections so
# the COMMON-MODE broadcast-ephemeris errors (orbit + clock) cancel.
#
# THE IDENTITY (what src/lunar_dpnt.rs implements):
#   ref_error_i      = -e_i . u_ref_i  + c_i           (the correction the station broadcasts)
#   user_raw_i       = -e_i . u_user_i + c_i
#   corrected_user_i = user_raw_i - correction_i = -e_i . (u_user_i - u_ref_i)
# The clock term c_i CANCELS EXACTLY (it is identical in both observations); the orbit
# term collapses to the projection onto the DIFFERENCE of the two line-of-sight unit
# vectors, which -> 0 as the baseline -> 0 (the spatial-decorrelation floor) and grows
# ~linearly with baseline. Mapping the corrected per-satellite range errors through the
# user geometry (a weighted-least-squares snapshot solve) gives the user POSITION error.
#
# NovaMoon is referenced only as a system CLASS (a public description of a lunar reference
# station); the constellation reuses the illustrative public-source LCNS-class set. These
# are illustrative parameters for exercising the differential method, NOT a real ephemeris,
# and imply NO affiliation, endorsement, heritage, certification or TRL.
#
# HONESTY: MODELLED. The common-mode cancellation is an EXACT algebraic identity; the
# spatial-decorrelation residual is a FIRST-ORDER geometric model (the LOS-difference
# projection of an injected orbit error), not a fitted decorrelation model from real lunar
# tracking. The user protection level REUSES the DO-229E SBAS protection-level machinery
# (crate::sbas) with the differential residual sigma as the per-satellite error budget.
# Deterministic given the seed. No real-data validation; no TRL/heritage/agency endorsement.
kind = "lunar-differential-pnt"

# Illustrative LCNS-class constellation (public-source approximation; not affiliated).
n_sats = 8
sma_km = 9737.4        # ~8000 km perilune altitude above the mean lunar radius
eccentricity = 0.6
inc_deg = 57.7
argp_deg = 90.0        # apolune over the southern hemisphere (south-pole favouring)

# NovaMoon-class reference station at a known south-polar selenographic location.
ref_lat_deg = -89.0
ref_lon_deg = 0.0

# User offset from the reference station along the surface (the baseline).
baseline_km = 50.0

# Injected COMMON-MODE per-satellite broadcast errors (the errors the correction removes).
orbit_err_m = 100.0    # orbit-error vector magnitude (random direction per satellite)
clock_err_m = 30.0     # clock error in range units (random sign per satellite)
noise_m = 0.0          # per-receiver measurement noise (0 => exact cancellation at 0 baseline)

seed = 42
t_s = 0.0              # epoch (seconds past the MCI/MCMF-aligned epoch)

# Differential residual sigma fed to the SBAS DO-229E protection-level reuse.
residual_sigma_m = 5.0
p_hmi = 1e-4           # integrity-risk budget (interface parity; DO-229E K-factors fixed)

# ── THE CORRECTION LINK ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# The identity above assumes a PERFECT correction: computed by a station that knows
# exactly where it stands, delivered instantly, at infinite resolution. None of the three
# holds, and the three inputs below model what each costs. They feed the `correction_link`
# block of the result document ONLY -- with all three at the values written here, every
# number this scenario emitted before they existed is bit-for-bit unchanged.
#
# 1. SURVEY ERROR. The station forms its correction against the coordinate it BELIEVES.
#    An error there rides on every correction it broadcasts and reaches the user as
#    -delta . u_ref -- which contains no user geometry at all, so unlike the orbit term it
#    neither vanishes at zero baseline nor grows with baseline, and it transfers about
#    one-for-one into the user's position. Default 0.30 m is the crate's own lunar
#    reference-frame position-realisation allocation (lunar_time_budget frame_pos_error_m),
#    itself MODELLED: no lunar surface station has a published surveyed accuracy.
survey_sigma_m = 0.30      # reference-station 3-D coordinate 1-sigma (m), isotropic

# 2. CORRECTION AGEING. A correction computed at t and applied at t+tau is stale two ways.
#    Orbit: the satellite has MOVED, so the frozen orbit-error vector now projects onto a
#    rotated line of sight; the rotation comes from this crate's own propagator, so no
#    orbit-error rate is assumed anywhere. Clock: the satellite clock has drifted by
#    c*sigma_y(tau)*tau for the full-RAFS power law in crate::clock_specs, calibrated there
#    to a published one-day spec row. ILLUSTRATIVE default -- no lunar correction link has
#    a published latency -- which is why the report also emits a 0-300 s latency curve.
latency_s = 10.0           # age of the correction when the user applies it (s)

# 3. QUANTIZATION. The correction crosses a finite-rate link. The quantizer range is NOT a
#    free parameter: it is +/-(orbit_err_m + clock_err_m), an exact bound on the correction
#    magnitude for the injected error model, so the step is 2*(100+30)/2^bits = 1.0156 m at
#    8 bits and the residual variance is the uniform quantizer's step^2/12. The bit count
#    itself is an ILLUSTRATIVE input; 0 disables the term.
quantization_bits = 8      # bits per transmitted correction
lunar-frame-campaign.toml:
# Seven-parameter Helmert lunar frame datum driven by a SIMULATED OBSERVING CAMPAIGN (G9).
#
# The lunar-frame-realisation scenario injects a known similarity transform and recovers
# it — a solver unit test wearing the clothes of a result. This kind removes the planted
# answer: a network of Earth stations observes a catalogue of lunar-surface beacons over an
# explicit schedule, the lunar-VLBI delay partials are accumulated over that schedule into
# a beacon-coordinate Fisher information matrix exactly as lunar-vlbi-fim does, and that
# information is propagated through the Helmert design A = [I3 | [p]_x | p] at the
# catalogue points into the datum covariance H = A^T M_b A.
#
# Nothing is recovered from a planted transform, so the reported datum accuracy derives
# from the observing programme: halving the delay sigma halves it exactly, and lengthening
# the arc improves it because the libration the report MEASURES
# (sub_earth_direction_sweep_deg) is what separates the line-of-sight beacon coordinate
# from the plane-of-sky ones.
#
# Beacon-error correlation is MEASURED, not assumed. With the stations held fixed no
# observation touches two beacons, so the information matrix is exactly block-diagonal
# (offblock_fraction 0); with the stations estimated the Schur-marginalised block is
# coupled, the induced correlation is printed, and the whole propagation is re-run with it
# discarded so the price of an independence assumption is a number rather than a claim.
#
# The same propagation under an isotropic per-coordinate sigma, and the recovery error the
# lunar-frame-realisation scenario reports, are both run here and printed beside the
# campaign value with their ratios.
#
# MODELLED: the beacon catalogue is sourced but the CAMPAIGN is simulated — the station
# network and the delay sigma are illustrative inputs, individual delay observations are
# treated as independent, and the Moon-centre ephemeris, station clocks, troposphere and
# Earth-orientation parameters are held FIXED. Not a geodetic product.

kind = "lunar-frame-campaign"
lunar-frame-realisation.toml:
# Lunar reference-frame realisation — a 7-parameter Helmert (similarity) datum fit.
#
# Where src/lunar_frame.rs APPLIES the IAU 2015 WGCCRE lunar body orientation (a forward model),
# src/lunar_frame_realise.rs ESTIMATES (realises) a lunar reference frame from a network of point
# coordinates tied to a datum. The estimation core is a classic 7-parameter similarity transform
# mapping points p_i (estimated frame) to q_i (datum frame):
#
#     q_i = t + (1 + s) * R(theta) * p_i
#
# with translation t (m), scale s (dimensionless, ~1e-6 level) and the small rotation
# R(theta) = rz(theta_z) * ry(theta_y) * rx(theta_x). The seven parameters
# [tx, ty, tz, theta_x, theta_y, theta_z, s] are estimated from >= 3 non-collinear point pairs by
# weighted least squares via crate::batch_ls::gauss_newton (forward model flattens every q_i over
# all three components; weights = 1/sigma^2; x0 = zeros). A small orientation tie expresses the
# realised small rotation about the ICRF axes (relative to the IAU body orientation).
#
# THIS SCENARIO injects a KNOWN small Helmert transform (translation ~tens of m, rotation ~uradian,
# scale ~1e-7) into a well-spread synthetic point network (varied selenographic lat/lon mapped to
# MCMF, some points at altitude), adds seeded Gaussian noise, recovers the datum with helmert_fit,
# and reports the recovered transform, the per-parameter recovery error vs the injected truth, and
# the post-fit RMS residual.
#
# Honesty: MODELLED self-consistency. The oracle is the recovery of an injected 7-parameter
# similarity transform (noiseless to ~machine precision) plus the algebraic round-trip identity of
# apply_helmert. This is NOT a realisation of the lunar reference frame against real tracking / VLBI
# data and claims no absolute frame accuracy. Deterministic (seeded). No TRL, flight heritage or
# agency endorsement is claimed.
kind = "lunar-frame-realisation"

# Number of well-spread selenographic network points (>= 3).
n_points = 8

# Injected (truth) translation (m).
tx_m = 25.0
ty_m = -40.0
tz_m = 15.0

# Injected (truth) small rotation (micro-radians).
rot_x_urad = 3.0
rot_y_urad = -2.0
rot_z_urad = 5.0

# Injected (truth) scale (parts-per-billion; 100 ppb = 1e-7).
scale_ppb = 100.0

# Per-coordinate measurement noise standard deviation (m); weights = 1/sigma^2.
noise_sigma_m = 1.0

# Deterministic seed (measurement noise).
seed = 42

# Epoch (UTC) for the ICRF orientation tie.
epoch_year = 2024
epoch_month = 1
epoch_day = 1
lunar-interop-export.toml:
# Lunar interoperability export — LunaNet / IOAG-aligned, CCSDS-based interchange.
#
# Exports the lunar reference frame, the lunar time scale and a lunar ephemeris in
# CCSDS-based interchange forms, with round-trip / field conformance as the oracle.
#
# WHAT src/lunar_interop.rs does:
#   * export_lunar_oem  — REUSES the crate's CCSDS OEM 2.0 emitter (crate::oem),
#     re-tagged for the lunar context: REF_FRAME = the IAU 2015 WGCCRE lunar body
#     frame (MOON_ME / MOON_PA), TIME_SYSTEM = the lunar time scale (LTC / TCL / UTC),
#     CENTER_NAME = MOON, over a sample ILLUSTRATIVE LCNS-class ephemeris (positions
#     from crate::lunar_service, velocity by central finite difference).
#   * export_lunar_time_metadata — a LunaNet/IOAG-aligned lunar-time descriptor (scale
#     id, secular rate µs/day from crate::lunar_time, the published 56-59 µs/day band,
#     reference surface) that round-trips via serde_json.
#   * export_kif_lunar — wraps the OEM + time descriptor + frame label in the existing
#     KIF envelope (crate::interchange) with the MODELLED honesty label.
#   * oem_conformance — checks the required CCSDS/LunaNet header fields are present, the
#     REF_FRAME/TIME_SYSTEM carry the expected lunar tokens, the META_START..META_STOP
#     framing and the position+velocity data lines are well-formed.
#
# HONESTY: MODELLED. The field NAMES and units are aligned with PUBLIC standards
# (CCSDS 502.0-B OEM, IAU WGCCRE 2015 lunar frames, LunaNet Interoperability
# Specification / IOAG lunar architecture). The deterministic round-trip and the
# field-name conformance are the oracle. This is NOT a certified interoperability
# conformance test. The ephemeris is illustrative, public-source, NOT affiliated with
# ESA, and implies no TRL / heritage / agency endorsement.
kind = "lunar-interop-export"

# Lunar body frame: MOON_ME (mean-Earth / polar-axis) or MOON_PA (principal-axis).
frame = "MOON_ME"

# Lunar time scale tag: LTC (Lunar Coordinate Time), TCL or UTC (the Earth tie).
time_system = "LTC"

# Sample ephemeris grid.
n_states = 9
step_min = 30.0

# Informational epoch label (the OEM grid hangs off a fixed deterministic epoch).
epoch = "2030-01-01T00:00:00"

# Object name written to the OEM OBJECT_NAME / OBJECT_ID.
object = "LCNS-ILLUSTRATIVE-1"
lunar-jamming.toml:
# Lunar-native RF jamming: per-satellite J/S for a lunar surface user.
#
# The `jamming` kind is Earth-shaped — it takes a Walker/SGP4 shell and a WGS-84
# geodetic receiver, so a lunar case could only be assembled outside the engine by
# running `link-budget` twice (once for the jammer leg, once for the satellite leg)
# and subtracting the two received powers by hand. This kind runs that subtraction
# inside the engine, per satellite, per epoch.
#
# It composes, and re-derives nothing:
#   * jamming::j_over_s_db, effective_cn0_dbhz, rx_antenna_gain_db, lock_status,
#     q_factor, nominal_cn0_dbhz, free_space_path_loss_db  (the interference chain),
#   * lunar_service::LunarConstellation + topocentric, lunar::selenographic_to_mcmf
#     (the lunar sky geometry: MCI -> MCMF, then az / el / slant range from a
#     selenographic surface user).
#
# Unlike the Earth kind, the signal leg is not a fixed received power: each
# satellite's isotropic received power is its own link budget,
# `sat_eirp_dbw - FSPL(slant range, carrier)`, so the J/S moves satellite by
# satellite with lunar range and elevation. The result is a TABLE — one row per
# visible (epoch, satellite) link — published as JSON and as `*.table.csv`. The
# aggregate figures of merit sit beside that table, never in place of it.
#
# Every field below is optional; the values shown are the defaults except for the
# jammer block. Run it with:  kshana scenarios/lunar-jamming.toml
#
# MODELLED. The constellation is the illustrative, public-source Moonlight/LCNS-class
# geometry (not the real ephemeris; no affiliation or endorsement implied), and the
# interference model is a link budget: no terrain shadowing of the jammer (a
# first-order effect in south-polar terrain), no multipath, no AGC near/far dynamics,
# no adaptive nulling, no acquisition-vs-tracking hysteresis.

kind = "lunar-jamming"

# --- constellation (illustrative LCNS-class; apolune over the south) ------------
n_sats = 4
sma_km = 9737.4          # R_moon + 8000 km
eccentricity = 0.6
inc_deg = 57.7
argp_deg = 90.0

# --- surface user (selenographic) ----------------------------------------------
site_lat_deg = -89.67    # Shackleton crater rim
site_lon_deg = 129.78
site_alt_m = 0.0

# --- epoch grid ------------------------------------------------------------------
horizon_hours = 12.0
step_min = 60.0
elev_mask_deg = 5.0

# --- signal leg (link-budget leg 2, evaluated per satellite) ---------------------
sat_eirp_dbw = 26.0            # representative lunar AFS EIRP
carrier_hz = 2.4e9             # S-band AFS carrier
chip_rate_hz = 1.023e6         # despreading processing gain
user_boresight_gain_dbi = 3.0  # J/S is invariant to this; it moves C/N0 only

# --- receiver ---------------------------------------------------------------------
temp_k = 290.0
tracking_threshold_dbhz = 25.0
degraded_margin_db = 6.0

# --- jammer (link-budget leg 1). Omit this whole block for a clean-sky baseline. --
# Placed directly by standoff here. Give `lat_deg` and `lon_deg` instead to place it
# selenographically, and its range and elevation come from the same lunar geometry
# the satellites use (on an airless body a distant surface jammer then lands below
# the local horizon, and the antenna pattern hands it the horizon gain).
#
# 25 km is chosen because it splits the table: part of the visible set holds on and
# part does not. A single median J/S over these rows classifies the whole set as
# lost, which is exactly the collapse this kind exists to avoid.
[jammer]
power_dbw = 10.0        # 10 W
gain_dbi = 0.0
range_m = 25000.0
el_deg = 0.0            # a surface jammer on the user's local horizon
jammer_type = "broadband"
bandwidth_mhz = 20.0
lunar-joint-od-clock.toml:
# Lunar joint multi-technique OD + clock determination (a SIMULATED network).
#
# A single-epoch (snapshot) batch least-squares fit (src/lunar_combination.rs, on top of
# crate::batch_ls::gauss_newton) that FUSES three observation techniques to recover, together:
#   * a lunar surface station's 3-D position (NovaMoon-class, MCI metres),
#   * a small lunar constellation's per-satellite positions (MCI metres), and
#   * every asset's clock offset (station + each satellite, seconds).
#
# The three techniques:
#   1. Earth-baseline geodetic VLBI delays to the lunar station treated as the VLBI beacon
#      (reusing src/lunar_vlbi.rs, in geocentric inertial) — these make the station's FULL
#      3-D position observable;
#   2. lunar-local station<->satellite ranges (MCI Euclidean distance + the differenced clock
#      term scaled by c) — these tie the satellite positions and clock differences;
#   3. inter-satellite ranges (same form) — these tie the constellation's relative geometry.
#
# THE HEADLINE HONEST RESULT: lunar-local ranging alone leaves the station's position weakly
# observed along one direction (the range-only solve is ill-conditioned and the recovered
# station 3-D error is large). Adding the Earth-baseline VLBI delays makes the station's full
# 3-D position observable, and the recovered station error collapses to the metre level. The
# report runs the solve WITH and WITHOUT the VLBI legs on the same seed/truth and reports the
# station-observability improvement factor.
#
# Honesty: MODELLED simulated closed-loop recovery. An injected truth is mapped to synthetic
# observables through the SAME geometry model the solver inverts, seeded Gaussian noise is added,
# and the estimator recovers the injected truth within the noise. The oracle is internal
# consistency (truth recovery + NEES covariance realism), NOT real-data validation. There is no
# force-model propagation inside the solver — the satellites are fixed, distinct, illustrative
# points on a representative lunar orbit. No TRL, flight heritage or agency endorsement claimed.
kind = "lunar-joint-od-clock"

# Network size.
n_sat = 3     # constellation satellites
n_earth = 6   # Earth ground stations (more stations -> more independent VLBI baselines and
              # better Earth->sat radiometric multilateration geometry)

# Deterministic seed (measurement noise + truth jitter).
seed = 42

# Per-observable measurement noise standard deviations (weights = 1/sigma^2). Illustrative,
# representative of the modelled class (geodetic VLBI, coherent two-way + optical ISL ranging).
sigma_vlbi_s = 1.0e-11   # VLBI delay sigma (s) ~ 3 mm path length
sigma_range_m = 0.1      # radiometric / lunar-local range sigma (m)
sigma_isl_m = 0.1        # inter-satellite (optical) range sigma (m)

# Lunar surface station (south-polar NovaMoon-class site), selenographic.
station_lat_deg = -88.0
station_lon_deg = 23.0
station_alt_m = 0.0

# Representative constellation orbit radius (km, MCI) the illustrative fixed satellites sit on.
orbit_radius_km = 6000.0

# Snapshot epoch (UTC).
epoch_year = 2024
epoch_month = 1
epoch_day = 1
lunar-llr-datum.toml:
# Seven-parameter Helmert lunar frame datum from a REAL, ARCHIVED observing campaign (V3).
#
# Where lunar-frame-campaign removed the injected transform but still stated its station
# network, its schedule and its per-observation sigma as ILLUSTRATIVE inputs, this kind
# takes all three from measurement:
#
#   * the epochs are the ground-transmit times of archived ILRS Consolidated Laser Ranging
#     Data normal points;
#   * the observations are the laser ranges really fired at the five retroreflector arrays
#     on the Moon;
#   * every observation weight is that normal point's OWN archived precision,
#     bin_rms/sqrt(n_raw), read out of the file rather than assumed.
#
# Station coordinates come from the IERS ITRF2020 SLR solution propagated to epoch by their
# published velocities; reflector coordinates from JPL DE430 Table 7 in the
# mean-Earth/mean-rotation frame the IAU 2015 WGCCRE model realises.
#
# WHICH LINKS ARE MEASURED AND WHICH ARE MODELLED IS THE REPORT, NOT A FOOTNOTE. The
# Moon-centre ephemeris and the IAU body orientation stay modelled, and their combined size
# is emitted as the observed-minus-computed one-way range residual over every point used;
# troposphere, solid-body tides, station eccentricity, polar motion, UT1-UTC, relativistic
# delay and station clocks are absent and sit inside that residual. Because an ephemeris
# error reaches a covariance only through the DIRECTION of each line of sight, every run
# also re-solves the whole datum with all partials tilted by sensitivity_tilt_deg (sign
# alternating) and emits the ratio — so the covariance's insensitivity to the modelled
# ephemeris is a number, not an argument.
#
# Inter-array correlation is MEASURED at exactly zero rather than assumed, because a laser
# range touches one array. A record the catalogues cannot place — a station with no
# published ITRF position — is SKIPPED AND COUNTED, never given a substituted coordinate.
# The simulated campaign's own figures are RUN and printed beside the measured ones.
#
# MODELLED: the seven-parameter figures are a Cramer-Rao bound for a reduced parameter set
# on a real schedule. Not a solved datum, not an LLR analysis, not a geodetic product.
#
# DATA: the committed real-data slice ships with the repository but NOT with the published
# crate. From a repository checkout this file runs as written; from the crate, set
# data_dir to a copy of that slice.

kind = "lunar-llr-datum"
lunar-relay-constellation.toml:
# A lunar relay and navigation constellation: satellites in elliptical lunar frozen orbits
# (ELFO) plus a circular low-lunar-orbit shell, scored as a coverage and dilution-of-precision
# (DOP) map over the whole Moon for one day.
#
# The central body is the Moon: gravitational parameter, 1 737.4 km radius and spin rate come
# from the body module (the DE and IAU values cited there). The design is illustrative, not
# any agency's:
#   - an ELFO shell: 8 satellites as a Walker 8/4/1 with perilune about 720 km and apolune
#     about 7 500 km (semi-major axis 5 847.4 km, eccentricity 0.58), 57.8 deg inclination
#     and argument of perilune 90 deg, so every satellite lingers at apolune over the south
#     polar region;
#   - a circular shell: 6 satellites as a Walker 6/3/1 at 1 500 km and 85 deg.
#
# One receiver clock is shared (clock = "common"): the relay set is one system on one time
# scale. Latitude is lunar body-fixed; the map is an equirectangular projection with no land
# outline.
#
# What the run answers: where on the Moon four or more of these satellites are in view above
# a 10 deg mask, the PDOP/HDOP/VDOP/GDOP per 10 deg cell, and the share of the day with PDOP
# at or below 6. MODELLED: two-body orbits around a spherical Moon (no Earth third-body
# perturbation, which a real frozen-orbit design depends on), geometry only.

kind = "constellation-design"
body = "moon"
duration_s = 86400.0
step_s = 1800.0
mask_deg = 10.0
