lunar-time-budget.toml:
# Coordinated Lunar Time (LTC) end-to-end time-error budget over a tau grid.
#
# A single averaging-time (tau) error table invites the objection "you picked the tau that
# flatters your clock." This scenario answers it: the seven LTC error terms are assembled as
# time-error curves x_i(tau) (seconds) across a whole grid of averaging times, root-summed into
# x_Sigma(tau), and the clock-vs-frame CROSSOVER tau is located — the tau at which the growing
# clock term overtakes the constant real-time frame-realisation term. Below the crossover the
# budget is frame-limited (the reference-frame realisation dominates, not the clock); above it the
# clock dominates. Where the crossover falls depends entirely on the clock class — for the default
# passive H-maser it is far out in tau, for a coarse mini-RAFS it is seconds — which is exactly why
# a single-tau number is misleading. (src/lunar_time_budget.rs)
#
# Honesty: MODELLED. The tau-slopes are closed-form and analytically checkable (clock tau^{+1/2}
# or tau^{+1}, floors tau^0, measurement tau^{-1/2}) and the clock rows reproduce the published
# one-day clock specs; but the RF/optical-link, frame-realisation, relativistic-residual and
# ephemeris floor MAGNITUDES are Modelled budget allocations (documented defaults, caller-
# overridable), not measurements. The contribution is the reproducible crossover tau, not a
# certified per-term number. Nothing here is certified for operational timekeeping.
kind = "lunar-time-budget"

# On-board clock class driving the (growing) clock term. One of:
#   optical-master | passive-h-maser | rafs | mini-rafs
clock = "passive-h-maser"

# The averaging-time (tau) grid is the default 1 s ... 1e7 s log-spaced grid (8 points/decade).
# Uncomment to override:
# tau_min_s = 1.0
# tau_max_s = 1.0e7
# points_per_decade = 8
lunar-time-offset.toml:
# Lunar coordinate time (LTC/TCL): the relativistic Earth-Moon clock rate.
#
# A clock on the lunar surface ticks faster than an Earth-geoid (TT) clock. A
# first-principles post-Newtonian identity (src/lunar_time.rs) sums two named terms:
#   - self-potential difference: the IAU L_G geoid potential (W0 = L_G*c^2) minus the
#     Moon's surface self-potential GM_moon/R_moon -> the dominant ~ +57.5 us/day; and
#   - kinetic (second-order Doppler): -<v^2>/2c^2 from the geocentric Moon velocity
#     (finite-differenced from the Montenbruck-Gill lunar series) -> ~ -0.5 us/day.
# The total secular rate ~ 57 us/day is reported with the published 56-59 us/day band.
#
# Honesty: MODELLED, not certified. The headline us/day figure is reference-dependent
# (Earth geoid W0 vs a lunar selenoid, the time-averaging window, neglected sub-us/day
# centrifugal/J2 corrections) -> a band, not a single number, is the honest output.
# Nothing here is validated to sub-nanosecond absolute accuracy or certified for
# operational timekeeping. The report also gives the accumulated LTC-TT offset over the
# horizon and supports an inverse-variance ensemble (a minimal lunar paper-clock).
kind = "lunar-time-offset"

epoch_year = 2000    # LTC origin epoch (UTC); rate varies < 1e-3 us/day over the J2000 era
epoch_month = 1
epoch_day = 1
horizon_days = 1.0   # accumulate the LTC-TT offset over one day (~57 us)
lunar-vlbi-fim.toml:
# Lunar-VLBI station-coordinate covariance from an explicit observing schedule (G8, paper D3).
#
# D3's published chain goes from a per-observation delay precision to a station coordinate
# uncertainty through an assumed ISOTROPIC equipartition factor g = 3. That step is the one
# the paper's own abstract calls modelled rather than measured. This scenario removes it:
# the lunar-VLBI delay partials are accumulated over a real schedule of (baseline x epoch)
# pairs into a Fisher information matrix, inverted, and reported as the station coordinate
# covariance — so the station sigma is an engine output.
#
# The state carries Earth-FIXED (ITRS) coordinates, so the Jacobian is the inertial partial
# rotated by each epoch's GCRS->ITRS matrix: Earth rotation is what makes those coordinates
# observable at all, and the report MEASURES the Earth-fixed line-of-sight sweep and the
# beacon declination rather than assuming them. One observation is one (baseline, epoch)
# pair with BOTH stations above the elevation mask, weighted 1/delay_sigma_s^2.
#
# What to read in the report
#   * per-station per-axis and 3-D sigmas — the computed answer;
#   * the equipartition value c*delay_sigma_s*sqrt(g/N) for the SAME schedule, printed
#     beside it with the ratio. That ratio IS the anisotropy the assumption discarded, and
#     the isotropic trace bound sqrt(p/trace(M)) makes AM-HM a hard floor, so the
#     assumption can only ever understate;
#   * rank, datum defect, condition number, the full spectrum and the free-network null
#     space, on every run. Under a rank deficiency the headline sigma is published NULL
#     with a status, never read out of a near-singular inverse;
#   * both baseline counts: delay closure tau_ik = tau_ij + tau_jk leaves only n-1 of the
#     n(n-1)/2 baselines geometrically independent.
#
# MODELLED: the Moon-centre ephemeris, station clocks, troposphere and Earth-orientation
# parameters are held FIXED and observations are treated as independent, so this is a
# Cramer-Rao bound for a reduced parameter set, not a predicted session result. The
# omitted differenced-Shapiro partial is measured by finite difference and emitted.
# Not a geodetic product.
#
# Every field below is the module default, written out so the run is reproducible from
# this file alone. Delete any line to fall back to the same value.

kind = "lunar-vlbi-fim"
lunar-vlbi.toml:
# Lunar geodetic VLBI: an Earth baseline observing a lunar-surface beacon.
#
# Two ground stations (a VLBI baseline, here a Goldstone-like and a Canberra-like site)
# observe a one-way signal from a NovaMoon-class transmitter on the lunar near side. The
# geodetic observable (src/lunar_vlbi.rs) is the NEAR-FIELD two-range difference
#   tau_geom = (|r2 - r_B| - |r1 - r_B|) / c
# (the Moon is near-field, not a plane wave), plus the station clock-offset difference and a
# differenced Earth-potential Shapiro term. The report gives the delay, its finite-difference
# rate, and the wavefront-curvature near-field correction over the pass, with partials
# available for OD/frame work.
#
# Oracle: in the far-field limit the geometric delay collapses to the same-codebase plane-wave
# delta-DOR observable (src/radiometric.rs), matched to machine precision; the partials are
# finite-difference checked. At true lunar distance the near-field correction is a non-zero
# tens-to-hundreds-of-microseconds term.
#
# Honesty: MODELLED, NOT validated against real VLBI data. Polar motion is dropped
# (xp = yp = 0) so station inertial positions carry a few-metre frame error; the beacon mixes
# a mean-equator-of-date Moon series with an ICRF body-fixed offset (jd_tdb ~ jd_tt), a
# frame-consistency mismatch below model fidelity; no light-time iteration, media or aberration
# beyond the differenced Shapiro. No TRL, flight heritage or agency endorsement is claimed.
kind = "lunar-vlbi"

# Station 1 (DSN Goldstone-like, California).
station1_lat_deg = 40.4256
station1_lon_deg = -116.8893
station1_alt_m = 1000.0

# Station 2 (DSN Canberra-like, Australia) — a long intercontinental baseline.
station2_lat_deg = -35.4014
station2_lon_deg = 148.9819
station2_alt_m = 688.0

# Beacon on the lunar near side (equatorial, sub-Earth point).
beacon_lat_deg = 0.0
beacon_lon_deg = 0.0
beacon_alt_m = 0.0

# Epoch (UTC) and pass sampling.
epoch_year = 2024
epoch_month = 1
epoch_day = 1
horizon_hours = 6.0
step_min = 30.0
maritime-port-approach-coast.toml:
# Maritime port approach with GNSS jammed: how long an inertial navigation system
# (INS) keeps a ship inside the harbour-approach accuracy budget once the Global
# Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) is lost.
#
# The mission question: a vessel fitted with an INS enters a harbour approach at
# 12 knots (6.17 m/s) when GNSS is jammed (see `maritime-strait-jamming.toml` for why).
# How many seconds of free-inertial coast does it have before its position error passes
# 10 m, and before it passes 100 m? Those are the two accuracy figures that
# International Maritime Organization (IMO) Resolution A.1046(27), on the World-Wide
# Radionavigation System, gives for harbour entrances and approaches (10 m, 95 %) and
# for ocean waters (100 m, 95 %). They are used here as budgets, not as a claim of
# compliance.
#
# The model is `ins-trn-coast`: five growth terms (accelerometer bias, gyro-bias tilt
# through gravity, velocity random walk, angle random walk and scale factor times the
# distance run), combined root-sum-square and searched for the crossing times. The IMU
# (inertial measurement unit) is the representative navigation-grade class from the
# engine's grade table (Groves 2013, Table 4.1 band), the class of INS fitted to naval
# and high-end offshore vessels. It is NOT a datasheet for any product. Change
# `imu_grade` to "tactical" or "industrial" to see how a cheaper unit shortens the coast.
#
# Honest scope: most merchant ships carry no INS; they dead-reckon on a gyrocompass and
# a speed log, which this engine does not model. No terrain or radar aiding is applied
# (`trn_fix_mode = "none"`), so this is the unaided coast. MODELLED: every figure is
# modelled from class coefficients, not measured on a vessel.
kind = "ins-trn-coast"

imu_grade = "navigation"

# 12 knots, a typical harbour-approach speed. The scale-factor term grows with the
# distance run, so speed is part of the error model.
speed_m_s = 6.17
ref_accel_m_s2 = 0.0

combination = "rss"

# IMO A.1046(27) harbour-approach and ocean-waters figures, used as budgets (m).
crossing_thresholds_m = [10.0, 100.0]

drift_band_lo_m_per_s = 0.001
drift_band_hi_m_per_s = 0.050

# No aiding: the free-inertial coast over the whole approach.
trn_fix_mode = "none"

# A one-hour approach and berthing window.
mission_duration_s = 3600.0
maritime-spoof-position-push.toml:
# Maritime GNSS spoofing: detecting a transmitter that drags a ship's reported position.
#
# The mission question: a spoofer near a shipping lane broadcasts counterfeit Global
# Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) signals slightly stronger than the real ones and
# pulls the ship's position fix several hundred metres off its true track. Position
# spoofing affecting ships has been publicly reported, for example vessels whose
# reported positions appeared on land; this file describes that pattern generically and
# models no particular incident. Would the receiver's own monitors catch it?
#
# The pack runs the combined spoof detector (`spoof-detect`): receiver autonomous
# integrity monitoring (RAIM) parity across satellites, automatic gain control (AGC)
# power monitoring and signal quality monitoring (SQM) of correlation distortion, fused
# into one decision. The attack is described in the parameters of the public TEXBAT test
# battery (Humphreys et al., ION GNSS 2012): the spoofer's power advantage, whether it
# is carrier-phase aligned, and whether it pushes position (a subset of satellites,
# visible to RAIM) or time.
#
# Here: a +2 dB power advantage (under the 3 dB AGC margin, so power alone misses it),
# not carrier aligned, pushing four satellites to drag the fix by 500 m. Try
# `carrier_aligned = true`, `push = "time"` and a smaller `power_advantage_db` to see
# the hard case that defeats these receiver-level layers.
#
# Honest scope: parameterised receiver observables, not raw signal samples; Kshana is a
# simulator, not a receiver. MODELLED: every figure is modelled, not validated against
# recorded maritime spoofing.

kind = "spoof-detect"

[attack]
power_advantage_db = 2.0
carrier_aligned = false
push = "position"
push_magnitude_m = 500.0
num_biased = 4
el_imbalance = 0.12

[detector]
sat_power_dbm = -130.0
agc_margin_db = 3.0
sqm_tolerance = 0.10
raim_p_fa = 1.0e-3
sigma_m = 5.0
fusion_threshold = 0.5
maritime-strait-jamming.toml:
# Maritime GNSS jamming: a shore- or vessel-borne broadband jammer denying the Global
# Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) to a ship crossing open water.
#
# The mission question a ship's navigator or a coastal authority asks: how far across
# the water does a modest jammer take GNSS away? Over the sea there is no terrain or
# clutter between the jammer and the ship's antenna, so free-space path loss is the
# only thing that weakens the jammer, and a low-power device reaches a long way.
# Widespread GNSS interference affecting shipping has been publicly reported in several
# sea areas; this file does not model any particular incident.
#
# The chain is the one in `jamming-demo.toml` (Kaplan & Hegarty, Understanding GPS/GNSS,
# 3rd ed., §9.4): jammer received power sets the jammer-to-signal ratio J/S, despreading
# and the spectral-separation factor turn it into an effective carrier-to-noise density
# C/N0 per satellite, and a satellite is lost below the 25 dB-Hz tracking threshold.
# Here a 50 W (17 dBW) broadband jammer on a 30 m mast sits 30 km from a ship at sea
# level. Free-space loss over 30 km at the L1 frequency (1575.42 MHz) is about 126 dB,
# which leaves a mean J/S of about 48 dB, well past the roughly 35 dB a coarse/acquisition (C/A)
# code tracking loop tolerates, so the receiver loses every satellite. Move the jammer
# out or cut its power to find the range at which tracking returns (J/S falls about
# 20 dB per decade of range).
#
# Assumptions: 0 dBi jammer and ship antennas toward each other (a ship's GNSS antenna
# is not a controlled-reception pattern antenna (CRPA)), free-space propagation with no
# sea-surface multipath, a GPS-like 24-satellite Walker shell. The receiver position is
# a generic point in the northern Baltic Sea. MODELLED: every figure is modelled, not
# validated against measured maritime interference.
kind = "jamming"
seed = 1
mask_deg = 5.0
tracking_threshold_dbhz = 25.0

[time]
step_s = 30.0
duration_s = 1800.0

[receiver]
lat_deg = 59.80
lon_deg = 24.90
alt_m = 0.0

# A GPS-like 24-satellite Walker shell (6 planes x 4), propagated through the SGP4 core.
[constellation]
altitude_km = 20200.0
inclination_deg = 55.0
planes = 6
sats_per_plane = 4
phasing_f = 1.0

# 50 W broadband jammer on a 30 m mast, 30 km due east of the ship (ECEF, metres).
[jammer]
position_ecef_m = [2904623.523, 1381438.498, 5489328.347]
power_dbw = 17.0
gain_dbi = 0.0
jammer_type = "broadband"
bandwidth_mhz = 20.0
mars-orbit-pnt.toml:
# Positioning a low Mars orbiter with a Mars navigation constellation and a deep-space link.
#
# A 300 km near-polar orbiter navigates around Mars for one sol (88 775 s) from the
# 2027-02-19 opposition, when the Earth is closest and far from a solar conjunction. Two
# kinds of measurement:
#
#   1. ONE-WAY PSEUDORANGES from twelve navigation satellites at 10 000 km in three planes
#      inclined 60 deg (a Walker delta, phasing 1), flown as two-body orbits with the secular
#      drift from Mars' J2 (the second zonal harmonic, its oblateness). The user clock is
#      unknown, so these rows carry a clock column.
#   2. A TWO-WAY RANGE FROM EARTH, clock-free, whenever the Earth is above the Mars limb
#      for the orbiter. The Earth's direction and distance come from the analytic
#      solar-system ephemeris at every epoch.
#
# The report gives, per epoch, the relays in view, the constellation-only dilution of
# precision, the formal position uncertainty with and without the Earth row, and the
# error of a seeded least-squares fix each way; over the sol, the availability and the
# root-mean-square errors, and the Earth-Mars light time and round trip.
#
# MODELLED. The relay orbits, the 1 m range noise and the instantaneous measurement model
# are modelling choices; nothing here is validated against a mission's navigation data.
# The Mars constants are the published values cited in src/body.rs.
kind = "body-pnt"
body = "Mars"
epoch = "2027-02-19T00:00:00"
duration_s = 88775.0
step_s = 300.0
seed = 7

[user]
kind = "orbiter"
altitude_km = 300.0
inclination_deg = 93.0

[constellation]
planes = 3
sats_per_plane = 4
altitude_km = 10000.0
inclination_deg = 60.0
sigma_range_m = 1.0

[earth_link]
enabled = true
sigma_range_m = 1.0
mars-pnt-lmo.toml:
# Mars PNT — Low-Mars-Orbit user navigated against the simulated MARCONI relay
# constellation (areostationary relays broadcasting one-way + relaying two-way to a
# deep-space station) through the joint one-way/two-way radiometric fusion estimator.
#
# Figures of merit are the estimator's FORMAL COVARIANCE bounds (1σ / 3σ position) and
# the achieved RMS vs a synthetic closed-loop truth — a simulated navigation FoM, NOT an
# aviation-certified protection level (no certified fault model or integrity monitor here).
kind = "mars-pnt"

user = "lmo"                 # ~400 km circular Low-Mars-Orbit, inclined 60°
clock_class = "uso"          # onboard ultra-stable oscillator
step_s = 60.0                # observation cadence
duration_s = 7200.0          # ~one LMO orbit (period ≈ 7100 s)
nmax = 4                     # Mars gravity field degree/order (mars_gmm3, shipped to 4)
range_sigma_m = 1.0          # DSN-class range noise
doppler_sigma_mps = 1.0e-4   # 0.1 mm/s Doppler noise
dynamic_tightness = 0.1      # reduced-dynamic knob (dynamic → kinematic), 0..1
two_way_period_s = 1800.0    # a coherent two-way (clock-free, orbit-pinning) pass every 30 min
seed = 331514052             # deterministic noise seed
mars-pnt-surface.toml:
# Mars PNT — a fixed surface user (a lander / rover on the rotating Mars surface)
# navigated against the simulated MARCONI relay constellation through the joint
# one-way/two-way radiometric fusion estimator.
#
# A surface point is NOT in free-fall — it co-rotates rigidly with Mars (held up by the
# ground), so its dynamics are pure centripetal co-rotation, not orbital free-flight. The
# relays sweeping overhead give the geometric diversity that makes the near-static point
# observable.
#
# Figures of merit are the estimator's FORMAL COVARIANCE bounds (1σ / 3σ position) and
# the achieved RMS vs a synthetic closed-loop truth — a simulated navigation FoM, NOT an
# aviation-certified protection level.
kind = "mars-pnt"

user = "surface"             # fixed point on the equator at the prime meridian (co-rotating)
clock_class = "uso"
step_s = 30.0                # tighter cadence (the relays sweep overhead quickly)
duration_s = 7200.0          # 2 h (several relay passes)
nmax = 4
range_sigma_m = 1.0
doppler_sigma_mps = 1.0e-4
dynamic_tightness = 0.1
two_way_period_s = 1800.0
seed = 331514052
mars-pnt-transfer.toml:
# Mars PNT — a Mars transfer / capture user (a high, eccentric areocentric arc — the
# long arc a vehicle flies on approach / in a capture orbit) navigated against the
# simulated MARCONI relay constellation through the joint one-way/two-way radiometric
# fusion estimator.
#
# Figures of merit are the estimator's FORMAL COVARIANCE bounds (1σ / 3σ position) and
# the achieved RMS vs a synthetic closed-loop truth — a simulated navigation FoM, NOT an
# aviation-certified protection level.
kind = "mars-pnt"

user = "transfer"            # high eccentric capture-class arc (perigee ~500 km, apogee ~6 Rm)
clock_class = "dsac"         # a deep-space atomic clock (the most stable class)
step_s = 120.0               # coarser cadence over the long arc
duration_s = 28800.0         # 8 h
nmax = 4
range_sigma_m = 1.0
doppler_sigma_mps = 1.0e-4
dynamic_tightness = 0.1
two_way_period_s = 3600.0    # a two-way pass every hour
seed = 331514052
meo-leo-fused-pvt.toml:
# Fused MEO and LEO pseudorange positioning: GPS and Galileo with a LEO navigation layer.
#
# A receiver in Madrid tracks the GPS baseline constellation (GPS SPS Performance Standard,
# 5th edition), Galileo (Walker 24/3/1, Galileo OS SDD) and a LEO navigation constellation
# (the public Xona Pulsar X5 signal: 10.23 Mchip/s in the L5 band, received power -144.9 to
# -136.2 dBW, arXiv:2509.19551). Each system carries its own receiver clock, so the
# inter-system bias of Galileo and of the LEO layer is estimated with the position; the LEO
# pseudoranges are simulated with a 40 ns bias to show it recovered. Every pseudorange's
# sigma is the delay-lock-loop thermal noise at the C/N0 of its elevation combined with the
# system's signal-in-space range error.
#
# The report compares GNSS-only, LEO-only and fused fixes epoch by epoch and gives the PDOP,
# HDOP and VDOP against the number of LEO satellites added to the GNSS geometry (highest
# elevation first). MODELLED.
kind = "leo-pvt"
mode = "joint"
seed = 3
duration_s = 1800.0
step_s = 30.0

[user]
lat_deg = 40.42
lon_deg = -3.70
height_m = 650.0

[joint]
max_leo_sweep = 12

[[system]]
name = "GPS"
preset = "gps-baseline"
cn0_dbhz = [38.0, 48.0]
sisre_m = 0.6

[[system]]
name = "Galileo"
preset = "galileo"
cn0_dbhz = [38.0, 48.0]
sisre_m = 0.3
isb_ns = 12.0

[[system]]
name = "Pulsar X5"
leo_preset = "xona-pulsar"
signal = "X5"
isb_ns = 40.0
moonlight-service-volume.toml:
# Lunar navigation SERVICE-VOLUME analysis — Moonlight / LCNS-class constellation.
#
# Where src/lunar.rs runs a single south-pole protection-level PASS, src/lunar_service.rs
# analyses a whole SERVICE VOLUME: it sweeps a selenographic latitude/longitude grid over a
# time horizon and reports, for an ILLUSTRATIVE Moonlight / LCNS-class lunar-orbit
# constellation:
#
#   * DOP / coverage / availability — the fraction of (grid point, epoch) samples with
#     >= 4 visible satellites AND PDOP < threshold, plus the PDOP and visible-count
#     envelopes. The DOP geometry REUSES the gnss_lib_py-VALIDATED kernel
#     (crate::orbit::dop) exactly — service_dop is a thin filter + that kernel.
#
#   * Generalised lunar ARAIM protection levels (HPL/VPL) over the volume — the SAME
#     LunaNet LNIS lunar ARAIM machinery the south-pole pass uses (crate::lunar::lunar_araim,
#     sigma_URE ~ 30 m, P_sat ~ 1e-4), generalised from the south pole to an arbitrary
#     surface point. At the south pole with the same geometry/budget it reduces to the
#     existing south-pole protection level.
#
# CONSTELLATION (ILLUSTRATIVE; PUBLIC-SOURCE; NOT AFFILIATED WITH ESA): public ESA material
# describes LCNS / Moonlight as a small constellation (~4 satellites, first phase) on
# elliptical lunar frozen orbits favouring south-pole coverage (apolune over the south).
# The defaults below APPROXIMATE that public description (4 sats, eccentric inclined orbit,
# argument of perilune 90 deg so apolune sits over the southern hemisphere). These are
# illustrative parameters for exercising the method, NOT the real Moonlight/LCNS ephemeris,
# and imply no affiliation, endorsement, heritage, certification or TRL.
#
# HONESTY: MODELLED composition. The DOP geometry is validated BY REUSE of the validated
# kernel; the coverage / availability / integrity composition is MODELLED — a circular-/
# elliptical-Keplerian relay set (not a differential-corrected LCNS / 9:2 NRHO ephemeris),
# a mean-rotation Moon (no physical libration / precessing pole), and published LunaNet LNIS
# integrity parameters. This demonstrates the lunar service-volume METHOD, not an
# operational Moonlight availability number. Deterministic (pure geometry; no randomness).
kind = "moonlight-service-volume"

# Illustrative LCNS-class constellation (public-source approximation; not affiliated).
# The public first-phase description is ~4 satellites; the generalised lunar ARAIM
# protection level needs >= 6 satellites IN VIEW (the single-fault hypothesis set needs
# n-1 >= 5 redundancy), so this default uses a fuller (illustrative, expanded) set so the
# PL envelope is exercised alongside the DOP / coverage headline. Set n_sats = 4 to model
# the first-phase constellation (DOP/coverage only; the PL envelope is then empty).
n_sats = 8
sma_km = 9737.4        # ~8000 km perilune altitude above the mean lunar radius
eccentricity = 0.6
inc_deg = 57.7
argp_deg = 90.0        # apolune over the southern hemisphere (south-pole favouring)

# Service-volume grid (south-polar region by default — the Artemis target).
lat_min_deg = -90.0
lat_max_deg = -60.0
lat_step_deg = 10.0
lon_min_deg = -180.0
lon_max_deg = 180.0
lon_step_deg = 60.0

# Time horizon and sampling.
horizon_hours = 12.0
step_min = 60.0

# Geometry / availability thresholds.
elev_mask_deg = 5.0
pdop_threshold = 6.0

# Integrity (LunaNet LNIS): surface-ops alert limit and integrity-risk budget.
alert_limit_m = 50.0
p_hmi = 1e-4

# OPTIONAL per-satellite geometry export for ONE named selenographic site. Off unless
# BOTH coordinates are given; the aggregate coverage / DOP summary above collapses
# per-satellite geometry, but slant range and look angles are what a link budget consumes.
#   export_site_lat_deg = -89.9
#   export_site_lon_deg = 0.0
#
# OPTIONAL transmit antenna for that export. Read only when the export site is also set.
# Each exported row then also carries the off-boresight angle AT THE SATELLITE and the
# transmit gain toward the site from the REAL Airy aperture pattern
# (antenna::pattern_gain_dbi), and the report gains an `antenna_pattern` block reporting
# the in-beam count under that pattern BESIDE the in-beam count under the symmetric
# gain-to-beamwidth approximation (theta_3dB[deg] = sqrt(31000/G_lin)), plus the
# correction between them. Both are emitted; neither replaces the other. The defaults
# below are the engine's own representative lunar transmit aperture, the same 1 m dish at
# 2.4 GHz that scenarios/lunar-attack-surface.toml runs.
#   [export_antenna]
#   diameter_m = 1.0       # required: the pattern is a statement about one aperture
#   carrier_hz = 2.4e9     # default 2.4e9 (S-band lunar AFS)
#   efficiency = 0.60      # default 0.60 (antenna::DEFAULT_APERTURE_EFFICIENCY)
#
# With an export site set, a plain run ALSO emits <scenario>.table.csv: the per-satellite
# geometry in long form, one row per (epoch, satellite), with the row count on the header
# line. This is the largest array the crate publishes — 2304 rows in the released joint
# communications-and-navigation table — and inside JSON it is the shape a naive consumer
# truncates without anything objecting. The four antenna columns are present only when
# export_antenna is configured, and the header says which case the file is. No export
# site, no array, no file.
#
# OPTIONAL real, retrieved geometry in place of the illustrative constellation above.
# UNSET BY DEFAULT, and unset changes nothing: the report is byte-identical to what it is
# without this line. Point it at a file and that file's geometry drives the headline
# coverage / DOP / protection-level figures, the report gains an `ephemeris` provenance
# block (path, SHA-256 of the exact bytes, upstream document, URL, retrieval date), and an
# `ephemeris_comparison` block carries the sigma_URE RANGING REQUIREMENT under that
# geometry BESIDE the unchanged Keplerian and perturbed results, with the difference and
# the ratio emitted as their own named quantities. Nothing is replaced; nothing is tuned to
# bring the geometries together.
#
# Two file formats, two distinct provenance classes (see src/lunar_ephemeris.rs and
# tests/fixtures/lunar_ephemeris/NOTICE.md):
#   * `# format: elements` -> a PUBLISHED CONSTELLATION DEFINITION, propagated by the same
#     Kepler solver the illustrative set uses, so the only difference between the two runs
#     is the constellation design. Provenance class `published-elements`.
#   * `# format: states`   -> a TABULATED MOON-CENTRED STATE EPHEMERIS (what an SPK/BSP
#     kernel evaluates to), Lagrange-interpolated and reduced to MCMF by the IAU 2015 /
#     WGCCRE lunar orientation. Provenance class `published-ephemeris`. A horizon past the
#     end of the table is REFUSED rather than extrapolated.
#
# An `elements` file states its own frame (`# elements_frame: icrf` or `mci`, default
# `mci`) and may give the phase as either a mean or a TRUE anomaly, so a fixture can carry
# exactly the numbers its source printed. An ICRF-stated set is propagated in ICRF and
# reduced by the IAU 2015 / WGCCRE lunar orientation, with no frame approximation; an
# OP-frame set (the Ely / Ely and Lieb convention) is read as MCI, and the report emits the
# COMPUTED tilt that introduces as `ephemeris.published_frame_tie_angle_deg`.
#
# The committed candidates (all regenerable from their recorded sources):
#   ephemeris_path = "tests/fixtures/lunar_ephemeris/lans_demo_ntrs20250009447.csv"
#     the 5-satellite joint ESA/NASA/JAXA LANS interoperability-demonstration reference
#     constellation, Table 3 of Melman et al., ION GNSS+ 2025 / NASA NTRS 20250009447.
#     Elements in ICRF at a stated epoch; the source calls the orbits NOTIONAL and that
#     caveat is emitted with them. Five satellites can never put the six in view ARAIM
#     needs, so this yields coverage and DOP but NO protection level and NO sigma
#     requirement - reported absent, not manufactured.
#   ephemeris_path = "tests/fixtures/lunar_ephemeris/lncss_case_a_navi613.csv"
#     8-satellite LNCSS case study A, Table 1 of Bhamidipati, Mina, Sanchez and Gao,
#     NAVIGATION 70(4) navi.613, 2023 (open access, CC BY). Cases B (12 sats) and C (16)
#     are committed beside it.
#   ephemeris_path = "tests/fixtures/lunar_ephemeris/horizons_lunar_orbiters_2023001_12h.csv"
#     the four spacecraft really in lunar orbit on 2023-01-01, from JPL Horizons. NOT a
#     navigation constellation: 1-2 in view over the south pole, no protection level, so
#     the sigma requirement comes back ABSENT rather than invented.
multi-band-jamming-waterfall.toml:
# Multi-band jamming waterfall: low Earth orbit (LEO) positioning, navigation and timing
# (PNT) signals in four bands (UHF, L, S and C) beside GPS and Galileo, each band with
# its own jammer, drawn as one waterfall per band on one timeline.
#
# A LEO-PNT system that spreads its signals over several bands is harder to deny than a
# single L-band system: a jammer built for one band leaves the others alone. This
# scenario shows that with the `spectrum` kind's spectral separation coefficient (SSC)
# chain, band by band. Every signal is public or representative; none depends on a
# particular LEO system:
#   UHF  generic-uhf (465 MHz, BPSK(5) pilot and data, 10 MHz), -150 dBW   [representative]
#   L    xona-x5 (1190.51625 MHz, published), at its -144.9 dBW minimum; GPS L1 C/A and
#        Galileo E5a at their specification minimums
#   S    generic-s (2492.028 MHz, BPSK(5), 16.5 MHz), -150 dBW              [representative]
#   C    generic-c-band-leo (5020 MHz, BPSK(10), 20 MHz), -152 dBW          [representative]
# (BPSK binary phase-shift keying.) The LEO designs are drawn with every component,
# band-limited to their transmit bandwidth.
#
# Timeline (60 s, one row per second):
#   10 s  a continuous-wave (CW) tone at the UHF carrier, -120 dBW received.
#   20 s  a chirp (swept) jammer 16 MHz wide around L1, 9 microsecond sweeps, 50 mW at
#         100 m: it takes GPS L1 C/A and leaves the L5-band signals alone.
#   30 s  wideband (barrage) noise, 40 MHz around 1185 MHz, -118 dBW: it hits Galileo E5a
#         and Xona X5 together.
#   40 s  narrowband noise, 2 MHz at the S carrier, -128 dBW.
#   50 s  noise matched to the C-band signal's own spectrum, -124 dBW.
# The [grid] waterfall is the L band; three [[panels]] add UHF, S and C.
# MODELLED: the signal spectra are validated closed forms; every jammer, power and
# timing here is a scenario input.
kind = "spectrum"
seed = 11
duration_s = 60.0
step_s = 1.0

[receiver]
noise_figure_db = 2.0
antenna_temp_k = 290.0
tracking_threshold_dbhz = 25.0

f_max_mhz = 1600.0
n_freq = 440

[[panels]]

f_max_mhz = 2502.0
n_freq = 200

[[panels]]

f_max_mhz = 5035.0
n_freq = 200

ntn-5g-positioning.toml:
# Positioning from a 5G non-terrestrial network (NTN) downlink in the mobile-satellite S band.
#
# 3GPP band n256 (downlink 2170 to 2200 MHz, 3GPP TS 38.101-5) serves handsets from
# satellites. A positioning reference signal in a 5 MHz New Radio channel (4.5 MHz occupied)
# or a 200 kHz narrowband channel (180 kHz occupied) bounds the time-of-arrival accuracy
# through its root-mean-square bandwidth: the Cramér-Rao bound is c / (2 pi beta
# sqrt(2 (C/N0) T)), with beta = B / sqrt(12) for a flat spectrum. The scenario compares the
# two channels over a representative NTN shell (324 satellites at 600 km, 55 deg, 10 deg mask), adds a
# 1 m network synchronisation and ephemeris error, and runs downlink time-of-arrival fixes and
# a single-satellite Doppler fix over the longest pass (height held to 10 m).
#
# The bandwidth-to-bound step is a textbook closed form; the positioning accuracy is MODELLED
# (a bound on a multipath-free channel, not an achieved result).
kind = "ntn-positioning"
seed = 5
carrier_hz = 2172.5e6
integration_s = 0.1
doppler_integration_s = 1.0
cn0_dbhz = [38.0, 50.0]
sync_error_m = 1.0
duration_s = 600.0
step_s = 10.0

[user]
lat_deg = 52.5
lon_deg = 13.4
height_m = 40.0

[[signal]]
name = "NR 5 MHz"
bandwidth_hz = 4.5e6

[[signal]]
name = "NB 200 kHz"
bandwidth_hz = 180e3

[[system]]
name = "NTN shell"
role = "leo"
mask_deg = 10.0
[[system.shell]]
total = 324
planes = 18
phasing = 1
altitude_km = 600.0
inclination_deg = 55.0
oem-interop.toml:
# CCSDS OEM interoperability-bridge demonstrator (GMAT / Orekit / STK interop).
#
# GMAT, Orekit and STK all EXPORT CCSDS Orbit Ephemeris Messages; this is the
# IMPORT side of the bridge that lets Kshana ingest them. With no `oem_text` the
# scenario round-trips a generated reference constellation (a MEO + a LEO orbit)
# through export -> import and reports the round-trip fidelity, proving the importer
# is the exact inverse of the writer. Set `oem_text` to an inline OEM string to
# ingest a real external file instead (segments, frames, epoch span + a
# velocity-consistency check are reported).
#
# HONEST SCOPE: MODELLED structural + physical ingest check, NOT an orbit-accuracy
# validation of the source ephemeris.
# Run:  kshana scenarios/oem-interop.toml
kind = "oem-interop"
orbit-gnss-challenged.toml:
# GNSS availability derived from orbital geometry (not hand-authored windows).
#
# A spacecraft well inside the GNSS shell (here ~8,000 km altitude) does not have
# continuous coverage: as the constellation moves, the count of satellites that
# clear the elevation mask and are not occulted by Earth rises and falls. The
# visible count is computed from line-of-sight geometry at each step and mapped to
# a GNSS state (>=4 visible = nominal fix, 1-3 = degraded, 0 = denied). When the
# fix drops, the onboard clock must hold time across the gap; the quantum clock
# coasts far longer within a tight timing bound than the chip-scale reference.
# Vendor-neutral; constellation and clock parameters are public/cited.

kind = "orbit"
seed = 7
threshold_ns = 5.0
# Elevation mask (deg) above the user's local horizontal.
mask_deg = 10.0
# 1-sigma user-equivalent range error (m) for the position-accuracy summary;
# position sigma = position-DOP * this. ~1 m is a representative modern
# dual-frequency UERE (Kaplan & Hegarty, Understanding GPS/GNSS).
sigma_uere_m = 1.0

[time]
step_s = 60.0
duration_s = 86400.0   # one day

# User spacecraft at ~8,000 km altitude, inside the GNSS shell.
[user]
altitude_km = 8000.0
inclination_deg = 0.0
raan_deg = 0.0
u0_deg = 0.0

# GPS-like Walker-delta constellation: 24 satellites, 6 planes, 55 deg inclination,
# ~20,180 km altitude (GPS public constellation parameters; IS-GPS-200 / USCG NAVCEN).
[constellation]
altitude_km = 20180.0
inclination_deg = 55.0
planes = 6
sats_per_plane = 4
phasing_f = 1.0

# Quantum: strontium optical lattice clock (space-oriented goal on ground hardware).
[clock_quantum]
id = "optical-sr-lattice"
provenance = "Strontium optical lattice clock, space-oriented stability goal sigma_y(1s)=1e-15 (arXiv:1503.08457); lab Sr reaches 4.8e-17 (Oelker et al., Nature Photonics 2019). Not flown."
y0 = 1.0e-15
q_wf = 1.0e-30
q_rw = 1.0e-40
flicker_floor = 1.0e-16

# Classical: chip-scale atomic clock (deployed commercial part).
[clock_classical]
id = "csac-sa45s"
provenance = "Microchip SA.45s / SA65 chip-scale atomic clock, sigma_y(1s)=3.0e-10 (datasheet); deployed commercial part."
y0 = 1.0e-11
q_wf = 9.0e-20
q_rw = 1.0e-28
flicker_floor = 2.0e-11
orbit-molniya.toml:
# GNSS availability for a highly-eccentric (Molniya) user, from orbital geometry.
#
# A Molniya orbit is a 12-hour, highly-eccentric, critically-inclined orbit
# (a ~ 26,600 km, e ~ 0.74, i = 63.4 deg, argument of perigee 270 deg) that
# loiters near apogee over the northern hemisphere. The user spends most of the
# revolution far above the GNSS shell (looking "down" at the constellation, with
# Earth often occulting the far side) and races through perigee below it. The
# visible-satellite count therefore swings widely over the orbit, and during the
# long high-apogee dwell the onboard clock must hold time across the gaps.
#
# The critical inclination (63.4 deg) freezes the argument of perigee under J2;
# `j2 = true` additionally applies the secular nodal regression. Vendor-neutral;
# orbit and clock parameters are public/cited.

kind = "orbit"
seed = 11
threshold_ns = 5.0
mask_deg = 5.0
sigma_uere_m = 1.0

[time]
step_s = 120.0
duration_s = 43200.0   # one ~12 h Molniya revolution

# User on a Molniya orbit. altitude_km sets the semi-major-axis altitude
# (a = 6371 km + 20229 km = 26,600 km); with e = 0.74 the perigee is ~540 km and
# the apogee ~38,900 km. u0_deg = 0 starts the revolution at perigee.
[user]
altitude_km = 20229.0
inclination_deg = 63.4
argp_deg = 270.0
eccentricity = 0.74
u0_deg = 0.0
j2 = true

# GPS-like Walker-delta constellation: 24 satellites, 6 planes, 55 deg inclination,
# ~20,180 km altitude (GPS public constellation parameters; IS-GPS-200 / USCG NAVCEN).
[constellation]
altitude_km = 20180.0
inclination_deg = 55.0
planes = 6
sats_per_plane = 4
phasing_f = 1.0

# Quantum: strontium optical lattice clock (space-oriented goal on ground hardware).
[clock_quantum]
id = "optical-sr-lattice"
provenance = "Strontium optical lattice clock, space-oriented stability goal sigma_y(1s)=1e-15 (arXiv:1503.08457); lab Sr reaches 4.8e-17 (Oelker et al., Nature Photonics 2019). Not flown."
y0 = 1.0e-15
q_wf = 1.0e-30
q_rw = 1.0e-40

# Classical: chip-scale atomic clock (deployed commercial part).
[clock_classical]
id = "csac-sa45s"
provenance = "Microchip SA.45s / SA65 chip-scale atomic clock, sigma_y(1s)=3.0e-10 (datasheet); deployed commercial part."
y0 = 1.0e-11
q_wf = 9.0e-20
q_rw = 1.0e-28

orbit-real-tle.toml:
# GNSS availability from REAL satellite geometry, via two-line element sets.
#
# Instead of a synthetic Walker pattern, the constellation is parsed from a block
# of TLEs (the standard NORAD/Celestrak format) given inline below. Drop in the

# Ground-station pass prediction demonstrator (ground segment & operations).
#
# Predicts the visibility passes (AOS / TCA / LOS, maximum elevation, duration) of

polar-arctic-leo-coverage.toml:
# Satellites in view and dilution of precision from the equator to the pole: MEO GNSS alone,
# a near-polar LEO constellation alone, and both.
#
# GPS and Galileo orbit at 55 and 56 deg inclination, so north of about 70 deg every MEO

# thirteen epochs over two hours at each latitude and reports the mean satellites in view,
# the median PDOP, HDOP and VDOP and the availability (PDOP at or below 6) for each group.
#
# MODELLED: geometry only; ionospheric scintillation, strong at high latitude, is not modelled.

duration_s = 7200.0
