attack_delay_s = 5.0e-9
clock_fault_sigma = 4.0
quantum-trade.toml:
# Quantum-vs-classical PNT trade with measured-ADEV ingestion (ESA AO/1-13503 demonstrator).
#
# Computes the timing-holdover and inertial-holdover benefit of a CANDIDATE clock
# over a CLASSICAL baseline, plus a GNSS-denied resilience-vs-time envelope. The
# candidate floor is driven by a partner clock's MEASURED overlapping-ADEV curve
# (the defensibility hinge) fitted by non-negative least squares — so the holdover
# budget rests on real data, not an assumed long-tau floor.
#
# HONEST SCOPE: MODELLED — it QUANTIFIES a partner's quantum-clock benefit; it does
# NOT validate the device, and never borrows the SGP4/Allan/IGS validation islands.
# When any row's floor is an assumed class default, a floor caveat renders on the
# artifact. Run:  kshana scenarios/quantum-trade.toml
kind = "quantum-trade"

timing_threshold_s = 20.0e-9     # 20 ns phase-error threshold
position_threshold_m = 100.0     # 100 m position-error threshold

# Classical baseline clock class: csac | uso | dsac
baseline_clock_class = "csac"

# Candidate = a partner optical clock's MEASURED overlapping-ADEV curve
# (tau seconds; sigma_y). The slight long-tau upturn is a realistic red-noise floor,
# so the recovered holdover is defensible rather than a white-noise artefact.
candidate_adev_taus   = [1.0, 10.0, 100.0, 1000.0, 10000.0, 100000.0]
candidate_adev_values = [5.0e-16, 1.6e-16, 6.0e-17, 4.0e-17, 6.0e-17, 2.0e-16]

# Resilience envelope sample times (s).
resilience_times_s = [1.0, 60.0, 600.0, 1800.0, 3600.0, 7200.0, 14400.0, 28800.0]
rail-tunnel-coast.toml:
# Rail tunnel coast: how long a train's inertial navigation system (INS) keeps it
# inside a track-discrimination budget with no Global Navigation Satellite System
# (GNSS) in a tunnel.
#
# The mission question: GNSS-based train positioning loses the sky in every tunnel,
# cutting and covered station. On a line with parallel tracks, telling which track the
# train is on needs a cross-track error well under half the track spacing (track
# centres on European main lines are typically around 4 m apart). How many seconds
# into a tunnel does the position error pass 2 m, and 20 m? At 160 km/h (44.4 m/s) the
# answer converts directly into how long a tunnel the INS alone can bridge.
#
# The model is `ins-trn-coast` (five growth terms combined root-sum-square). The IMU
# (inertial measurement unit) is the representative tactical-grade class from the
# engine's grade table (Groves 2013, Table 4.1 band), NOT a datasheet for any product.
#
# Honest scope: real train positioning also uses wheel odometry and trackside balises.
# This engine has no odometer model, so this file is INS only, which is the
# pessimistic bound; an odometer would hold along-track error far lower. No aiding is
# applied (`trn_fix_mode = "none"`). MODELLED: every figure is modelled from class
# coefficients, not measured on a train.
kind = "ins-trn-coast"

imu_grade = "tactical"

# 160 km/h. The scale-factor term grows with the distance run.
speed_m_s = 44.4
ref_accel_m_s2 = 0.0

combination = "rss"

# Track discrimination (2 m) and a coarse along-line budget (20 m).
crossing_thresholds_m = [2.0, 20.0]

drift_band_lo_m_per_s = 0.001
drift_band_hi_m_per_s = 0.050

trn_fix_mode = "none"

# A 10-minute GNSS-denied section: at 160 km/h, about 27 km of tunnel.
mission_duration_s = 600.0
realtime-frame-eop.toml:
# Real-time lunar frame / Earth-orientation (EOP) prediction budget.
#
# A lunar navigation frame realised from an Earth-based UT1/polar-motion product is only as good
# as the PREDICTED Earth orientation available in real time: the final IERS values for a given day
# are published weeks later, so an operational service runs on the Bulletin A prediction. This
# scenario emits the two P4 tables (src/frame_eop.rs):
#
#   Table 1 (frame-error consistency): the post-processed (definitive, zero-latency) ~0.27 m frame
#     position and the real-time (predicted, one-hour latency) ~14.4 m frame position, each
#     expressed as its equivalent UT1 error via the L19 lever arm Dr = D_EM * omega_earth * dUT1 —
#     0.27 m <-> ~0.010 ms and 14.4 m <-> ~0.51 ms. The ~14.4 m is the GENUINE propagation of a
#     round representative OD covariance (0.27 m / 4 mm/s) through the one-hour latency — NOT
#     back-solved to hit 15 m; the order-15-m scale is independently bracketed by the real EOP-
#     prediction curve (Table 2: ~9.9 m at 1 day, ~18.8 m at 2 days).
#   Table 2 (UT1 prediction error vs horizon): the L18 curve read directly off the real IERS
#     finals2000A series — the Bulletin A minus Bulletin B final floor and the multi-day
#     persistence-predictor error — each mapped to a Moon-frame position by L19.
#
# It also reports the L21 root-sum-square real-time frame-error budget (EOP + ephemeris + frame-
# realisation floor). The frame-realisation floor is DERIVED from an actual 7-parameter Helmert
# datum realisation (its post-fit RMS residual), and the polar-motion term is sourced from the
# measured Bulletin-A-minus-Bulletin-B pole residual when a real EOP series is supplied.
#
# A plain run emits <scenario>.table.csv — the P4 Table 1 + Table 2 reproducibility artifact
# (byte-stable, golden-pinned in tests/golden/realtime-frame-eop.csv).
#
# Honesty: VALIDATED closed form (the L19 lever arm, omega_earth cross-checked against the CIO
# Earth-rotation angle) and VALIDATED real data (the L18 UT1 and polar-motion curves off the real
# finals2000A rows). DERIVED frame-realisation floor (the Helmert post-fit residual). MODELLED are
# the lunar-relay OD covariance magnitudes (0.27 m post-processed, ~14.4 m real-time at one-hour
# latency — a round, not back-solved, allocation), and the multi-day predictor is persistence, not
# IERS's operational Bulletin A algorithm. Not a certified real-time frame product.
kind = "realtime-frame-eop"

# THE EOP INPUT. Always a REAL IERS finals2000A product, used verbatim. With no path the
# library's own embedded copy of the 2026 extract (tools/finals2000A_2026.txt, MJD 61173-61204)
# is in force: 20 rows carry a Bulletin B final block and 12 are Bulletin A PREDICTION-ONLY rows
# (MJD 61193-61204), so a bare run reports `predicted_rows.n` = 12 and a populated
# `table2_error_vs_horizon` with no file argument and no network (G12).
#
# Other verbatim extracts committed with the repository, for `eop_finals2000a`:
#
#   eop_finals2000a = "tests/fixtures/agency/eop/finals2000A_2022001_longspan.txt"   # 45 final rows
#   eop_finals2000a = "tests/fixtures/agency/eop/finals2000A_2022001.txt"            # 5 final rows
#                                                                                    # (the pre-G12 default)
#
# Both of those are FINAL-ONLY: every row carries a Bulletin B block, so they publish no Bulletin A
# prediction row and `predicted_rows.n` is 0 on them. That zero is the FILE's property, not a
# parser failure, and it stays exercised by test. Moving the default onto the 2026 extract moved
# ten cells of the released p4_frame_eop.csv; they are enumerated old-to-new in
# docs/revisions/G12-default-eop-cell-changes.md under programme rule R4. The emitted `eop_input`
# block names whichever input is actually in force and carries its row census.
#
# `eop_finals2000a_later` takes an ARCHIVED LATER VINTAGE of the same product — the file as it
# stood once the dates the first file predicts had become Bulletin B final. Supplying it turns on
# the true predicted-vs-final vintage differencing. Without it, `table4_predicted_vs_final_horizon`
# is emitted with no rows and says so explicitly: a single instantaneous fetch predicts only dates
# that have no final yet, so the residual does not exist and none is synthesised.
#
# The defaults below reproduce the representative lunar-relay OD covariance (0.27 m / ~14.4 m) and
# the P4 markers; uncomment to override.
epoch = "2022-01-01"
horizons_days = [1, 2, 3]
# ephemeris_pos_sigma_m = 0.27
# ephemeris_vel_sigma_mps = 4.0e-3
# latency_s = 3600.0
# frame_realization_floor_m = 0.2  # explicit override; default is DERIVED from the Helmert residual
# frame_realization_tie_noise_m = 0.2
# delta_ut1_ms = 0.5
# delta_xp_mas = 0.0
# delta_yp_mas = 0.0
# eop_finals2000a = "tests/fixtures/agency/eop/finals2000A_2022001_longspan.txt"
# eop_finals2000a_later = "<archived later vintage of the SAME product>"

# THE OPERATIONAL-STYLE PREDICTOR (Table 5 + Table 6).
#
# Table 2's multi-day curve is PERSISTENCE ("tomorrow's UT1 is today's"), which is not what an
# operational user runs on: they consume the IERS Bulletin A prediction. Table 5 adds the class of
# model Bulletin A uses — a least-squares bias + rate fit over a trailing window plus the principal
# periodic terms (annual, semi-annual and the two principal zonal tides for UT1; the Chandler
# wobble, annual and semi-annual for the pole), extrapolated, with the last in-window residual
# carried forward — and scores it PREDICTED-VERSUS-FINAL: a forecast for T+h built only from rapid
# Bulletin A rows at or before T, measured against the LATER-PUBLISHED Bulletin B final at T+h.
# Persistence is scored over the identical epochs against the identical finals beside it, so the
# two columns differ in the predictor and in nothing else. Both are reported; neither replaces the
# other, and Table 2 is unchanged.
#
# IERS fits 365 days. No series committed with this repository is close to that, so the default
# window is 15 days: at most 19 so BOTH committed real extracts can populate it (the 2026 extract
# spans 19 days of finals), and at least ~13.8 so the monthly zonal tide clears the half-cycle
# admission threshold. A term the window cannot constrain is REPORTED as rejected, with the cycles
# the window spans, rather than silently dropped. The bundled 2026 default spans 19 days of
# finals, so a bare run populates Table 5. The 5-row finals2000A_2022001 excerpt supports no
# complete window at all, and on that input Table 5 reports `insufficient-data` and says why.
#
# operational_window_days = 15.0          # 365.0 against a real year-long product
# operational_min_cycle_fraction = 0.5    # cycles of a period the window must span to admit it
# operational_anchor_residual = true      # false gives the bare least-squares extrapolation
reentry.toml:
# Ballistic re-entry corridor demonstrator (Allen-Eggers, mission analysis).
#
# Closed-form analytic entry of a non-lifting body through an exponential
# atmosphere at constant flight-path angle: peak deceleration (independent of the
# ballistic coefficient), the velocity and altitude at peak-g, and the
# peak-heating velocity.
#
# HONEST SCOPE: MODELLED ballistic (no-lift), exponential isothermal atmosphere,
# constant flight-path angle. No aerothermal/TPS model -- the heating output is the
# peak-heating VELOCITY, not a heat-flux. Not a 3-/6-DoF trajectory.
# Run:  kshana scenarios/reentry.toml
kind = "reentry"

entry_velocity_m_s = 7800.0      # near-circular LEO entry interface speed
flight_path_angle_deg = 6.0      # below local horizontal
ballistic_coeff_kg_m2 = 100.0    # m / (C_D * A)
slot-timing-ocxo-leo.toml:
# Slot timing: how long an oven-controlled crystal oscillator (OCXO) on a low-Earth-orbit
# smallsat stays inside the guard of a time-indexed routing slot after its last Global
# Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) fix, and how often it needs a fix.
#
# The oscillator figures are the Allan-deviation maxima, ageing and temperature bound of
# the Microchip OX-208 datasheet (Rev 12-1-2021), the telecom-timing `ocxo` preset. The
# noise model is fitted to lie at or above every datasheet point, so it is an envelope of
# maxima, not a measurement of any unit. The slot figures below are illustrative choices,
# not a requirement from any operator:
#   - a 100 ns guard at k = 3 (about 99.7 % of a Gaussian error inside the guard);
#   - a 10 ns one-sigma fix, taken 10 minutes ago, applied 5 s after it is taken;
#   - a 2 K temperature change since the fix, read through the datasheet bound.
#
# The optional [spoofing] section adds the timing protection level for the same clock
# in a 550 km orbit, with a ground-station two-way time transfer every 45 minutes as the
# only independent timing cross-check.
#
# What the run answers: seconds until the guard breaks, the term that breaks it, the fix
# cadence that keeps the clock inside, and how far a single ground spoofer can pull the
# clock before the satellite leaves its reach. MODELLED throughout.
kind = "slot-timing"

[oscillator]
preset = "ocxo"

[slot]
guard_ns = 100.0
k_sigma = 3.0
fix_sigma_ns = 10.0
elapsed_since_sync_s = 600.0
fix_latency_s = 5.0
temperature_excursion_k = 2.0

[spoofing]
altitude_km = 550.0
spoofer_min_elevation_deg = 0.0
receiver_time_sigma_ns = 10.0
max_ramp_rate_ns_per_s = 10.0

[[spoofing.checks]]
kind = "ground-contact"
revisit_s = 2700.0
sigma_ns = 2.0
small-uas-jammed-nav.toml:
# Small uncrewed aircraft under GNSS jamming: how far a flight-controller-class
# MEMS inertial unit drifts once the receiver loses lock, against a tactical-grade
# unit, on the same closed-loop GNSS/INS filter as `gnss-ins.toml`.
#
# The question a small-UAS (uncrewed aircraft system) builder asks: after a jammer
# takes the Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) away, how many seconds does the
# inertial solution stay inside a position budget? `jamming-demo.toml` shows why the
# outage happens (a 10 W broadband jammer 1 km away puts the jammer-to-signal ratio
# near 72 dB, far past what a C/A tracking loop tolerates); this scenario takes that
# denial as given (GNSS nominal for 100 s, then denied for 60 s) and asks what the
# inertial navigation system (INS) does next.
#
# The flight-controller unit is a Bosch BMI088, a common 6-axis MEMS (micro-electro-
# mechanical system) inertial unit on small-UAS flight controllers. Its biases are the
# RESIDUALS left after the usual start-up calibration, not the raw datasheet offsets:
#   - gyro: the zero-rate offset (±1 °/s, raw) is estimated at rest before take-off,
#     so the residual is its temperature drift, ±0.015 °/s per K (Bosch BST-BMI088-
#     DS000-19, rev 1.9, gyroscope table), over an assumed 10 K warm-up after
#     calibration: 0.15 °/s = 2.618e-3 rad/s per axis;
#   - accelerometer: the zero-g offset (20 mg typical, raw) is removed by a one-off
#     calibration, so the residual is its temperature drift, < 0.2 mg per K (same
#     datasheet, accelerometer table), over the same 10 K: 2 mg = 0.0196 m/s² per axis.
# In flight the unit keeps warming (motor and speed-controller heat, sun, altitude), so
# the bias keeps moving after the filter has learned it. That drift is what the
# filter cannot learn in advance, and it is what ends the coast: the same two
# temperature coefficients times an ASSUMED in-flight warming rate of 1 K per minute,
# entered as linear rate-ramps in `[imu_classical.error_model]` below:
#   - gyro: 0.015 °/s per K x 1 K/min = 4.363e-6 rad/s per s;
#   - accelerometer: 0.2 mg per K x 1 K/min = 3.269e-5 m/s² per s.
# The signs are chosen, not measured. The 10 K warm-up and the 1 K/min rate are
# assumptions, and they are the numbers to change first: a slower warming rate
# lengthens the in-spec coast and a faster one shortens it (scale both rate_ramp
# lines together and rerun, rather than trusting a figure typed here). White noise,
# scale-factor and misalignment are not layered on. The tactical-grade comparator is taken as
# temperature-compensated and carries no ramp.
#
# The pack has two fixed slots named `imu_quantum` and `imu_classical`. Here the
# `imu_quantum` slot carries the BETTER unit, the tactical-grade comparator with the
# same biases as `gnss-ins.toml`, and `imu_classical` carries the flight-controller
# MEMS unit. Nothing quantum is modelled in this file.
#
# Honest scope (inherited from the `gnss-ins` pack): loosely coupled, a single
# deterministic manoeuvring profile (a forward-acceleration and yaw square wave), not a
# recorded drone flight; flat-Earth tangent-plane comparison. Every figure this file
# produces is MODELLED. Validating it needs flight logs from a jammed environment.
kind = "gnss-ins"
seed = 7
threshold_m = 50.0
fix_interval_s = 1.0
sigma_pos_m = 1.0
sigma_vel_mps = 0.05
lat_deg = 59.437
lon_deg = 24.745
alt_m = 120.0

[time]
step_s = 0.1
duration_s = 160.0

[gnss]
windows = [
  { t0 = 0.0,   t1 = 100.0, state = "nominal" },
  { t0 = 100.0, t1 = 160.0, state = "denied" },
]

[imu_quantum]
id = "tactical-imu"
provenance = "Tactical-grade MEMS/quartz inertial unit, the comparator: the same residual biases as scenarios/gnss-ins.toml"
accel_bias = [0.03, -0.02, 0.0]
gyro_bias = [0.0, 0.0, 1.0e-4]

[imu_classical]
id = "bmi088-flight-controller"
provenance = "Bosch BMI088 MEMS IMU (BST-BMI088-DS000-19 rev 1.9): residual bias after start-up calibration = temperature drift over an assumed 10 K warm-up; gyro 0.015 deg/s/K x 10 K = 2.618e-3 rad/s, accel 0.2 mg/K x 10 K = 0.0196 m/s^2 per axis; signs chosen"
accel_bias = [0.0196, -0.0196, 0.0196]
gyro_bias = [2.618e-3, -2.618e-3, 2.618e-3]

# The filter's prior on this unit's biases: the same datasheet-derived residual bounds
# as above, taken as 1-sigma. Without it the filter keeps the pack default prior (a
# gyro bias of 1e-4 rad/s, 1-sigma), which puts this unit's 2.618e-3 rad/s residual
# 26 sigma out: the filter then never learns the bias, and the coast measures that
# mis-tuning rather than the sensor.
[imu_classical.filter_prior]
sigma_accel_bias = 0.0196
sigma_gyro_bias = 2.618e-3

# Continued in-flight warming, 1 K/min (assumed), through the datasheet temperature
# coefficients above: the bias drift the filter has not seen when GNSS is lost.
[imu_classical.error_model]
rate_ramp_gyro = [4.363e-6, -4.363e-6, 4.363e-6]
rate_ramp_accel = [3.269e-5, -3.269e-5, 3.269e-5]
solar-system-tour.toml:
# The whole solar system at one epoch.
#
# Every body the engine knows — the Sun, the eight planets, Pluto, the Moon, Phobos,
# Deimos, Io, Europa, Ganymede, Callisto and Titan — at 2026-09-28 00:00 UTC: its
# heliocentric position and velocity in the ICRF (International Celestial Reference
# Frame, equatorial J2000), its physical constants (gravitational parameter, radii, J2 — the
# second zonal harmonic — where published, sidereal rotation, International Astronomical
# Union (IAU) pole, its J2000 mean value, and prime meridian at the epoch), the light time and one-way and
# two-way range from the Earth, and an orbit track sampled over one revolution.
# result.json carries enough to draw an interactive solar system.
#
# WHERE THE NUMBERS COME FROM
#   planets  Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) Keplerian elements (Standish and Williams),
#            Table 1 for 1800 AD to 2050 AD
#   Moon     the Montenbruck & Gill lunar series, splitting the Earth-Moon barycentre
#   moons    JPL mean elements with the IAU synchronous rotation rate; Titan from the IAU
#            rotation model
#   light    the radiometric light-time solve, transmitter at its retarded position
#
# WHAT IS VALIDATED, AND WHAT IS NOT
# Each body carries its own label. Mercury to Saturn and the Earth are VALIDATED against
# JPL Horizons (Development Ephemeris DE441) within twice the Standish page's nominal
# error. Uranus and Neptune from Table 1 exceed the page's figures against DE441 (by 2.0
# and 5.2 times) and are MODELLED; so are Pluto, the Moon and the seven moons, which
# were measured against Horizons but have no published bound. See tests/solar_system_horizons_reference.rs.
#
# The three links below add the Mars-to-Jupiter, Saturn-to-Earth and Europa-to-Jupiter
# light times: interplanetary relay geometry, a ringed-planet downlink and a moon-to-planet
# hop.
kind = "solar-system"
epoch = "2026-09-28T00:00:00"
observer = "Earth"
track_points = 180

[[links]]
from = "Mars"
to = "Jupiter"

[[links]]
from = "Saturn"
to = "Earth"

[[links]]
from = "Europa"
to = "Jupiter"
space-packet.toml:
# CCSDS 133.0-B Space Packet framing demonstrator (TM/TC interop).
#
# Frames a synthetic telemetry/telecommand packet stream (6-octet primary header +
# data field) and reports the per-packet primary-header decode, total stream bytes,
# and that the encode<->decode round trip is exact -- the agency packet-format
# bridge that lets any Kshana scenario output be wrapped as a conformant stream.
#
# HONEST SCOPE: exact, deterministic CCSDS-133.0 *framing* (primary-header bit
# layout + round-trip). NOT a conformance certification; no secondary header / CRC /
# segmentation logic beyond the sequence flags.
# Run:  kshana scenarios/space-packet.toml
kind = "space-packet"

apid = 100              # Application Process Identifier (0..=2047)
telecommand = false     # false = TM (telemetry), true = TC (telecommand)
packet_count = 4        # frame a short sequence (first/continuation/last flags)
data_len = 32           # user-data-field octets per packet
space-weather.toml:
# Space-weather environment model demonstrator.
#
# Solar (F10.7 / F10.7a) and geomagnetic (Kp) activity drive the Jacchia-1971
# exospheric temperature, which in turn scales thermospheric neutral density above
# the static US-Standard-Atmosphere-1976 model — the solar-cycle density dependence
# (a ~5–10x swing at LEO) the static atmosphere omits. Reports the indices, the
# exospheric temperature, and the activity-corrected vs static density at a set of
# altitudes.
#
# HONEST SCOPE: MODELLED. The Kp<->ap conversion is the definitional IAGA table and
# the exospheric temperature is validated against published solar-min/mean/max
# magnitudes, but the density correction is a CALIBRATED FIRST-ORDER scale-height
# coupling — it captures the right sign, monotonicity and order of magnitude, NOT
# the absolute accuracy of a data-validated (NRLMSISE-00) atmosphere.
# Run:  kshana scenarios/space-weather.toml
kind = "space-weather"

f107 = 180.0       # daily 10.7 cm solar radio flux (sfu) — an active sun
f107a = 165.0      # 81-day average (sfu)
kp = 4.0           # planetary geomagnetic index (0-9); 4 = unsettled
altitudes_km = [300.0, 400.0, 500.0, 600.0, 800.0]
spoof-attack.toml:
# Active time-spoofing attack: can each clock's integrity monitor catch the spoof
# before it does harm?
#
# An attacker injects a slowly-ramping false GNSS time (0.1 ns/s from t = 60 s).
# The receiver cross-checks the asserted time against its own clock's coasted
# prediction and flags the spoof when the discrepancy exceeds the detection bound
# (5 sigma of the clock-aided monitor). The optical clock's bound is a fraction of
# a nanosecond, so it detects the spoof almost immediately — far below the 20 ns
# operational spec. The chip-scale clock's own coast noise over the monitoring
# window already exceeds 20 ns, so it cannot distinguish the spoof from its own
# drift and the attack reaches the spec undetected. Vendor-neutral.

kind = "spoof"
threshold_ns = 20.0

[time]
step_s = 10.0
duration_s = 660.0

[attack]
start_s = 60.0
rate_ns_per_s = 0.1

[clock_quantum]
id = "optical-sr-lattice"
provenance = "Strontium optical lattice clock, space-oriented goal sigma_y(1s)=1e-15 (arXiv:1503.08457); not flown."
y0 = 5.0e-17
q_wf = 1.0e-30
q_rw = 0.0

[clock_classical]
id = "csac-sa45s"
provenance = "Microchip SA65 / SA.45s CSAC datasheet sigma_y(1s)=3e-10; q_wf=sigma_y(1s)^2."
y0 = 5.0e-10
q_wf = 9.0e-20
q_rw = 0.0
spoof-detect.toml:
# Combined RF/measurement spoof detector: multi-SV RAIM-consistency + AGC + SQM, fused.
#
# This pack runs `kshana::spoof_detect` — the integrated CombinedSpoofDetector — against a
# parameterised spoofing attack. Where the `spoof` pack catches a *time* spoof via the clock,
# this catches the spoof *transmitter* via three independent receiver observables and fuses
# them into one weighted decision (which layer fired, and the overall verdict).
#
# The attack is described in the parameters the TEXBAT public test battery (Humphreys et al.,
# ION GNSS 2012) uses to classify a record: the spoofer power advantage over the authentic
# floor (dB), whether it is carrier-phase aligned (an aligned spoofer leaves no SQM
# correlation-distortion signature), and whether it pushes time (common-mode, RAIM-invisible)
# or position (a satellite subset, RAIM-detectable).
#
# This example is a static matched-power POSITION push (~ds4): a +1.5 dB advantage (under the
# 3 dB AGC margin, so power alone misses it) that biases three satellites — caught by the RAIM
# parity layer and corroborated by SQM. Try `carrier_aligned = true`, `push = "time"`, and a
# small `power_advantage_db` to reproduce the documented hard case (ds7) that defeats the RF
# layers and is left to the clock-aided `spoof` pack.
#
# Honest scope: this drives the detector with parameterised observables, not raw IQ — kshana is
# a simulator, not an SDR receiver; raw-vector (TEXBAT IQ / licensed Spirent) validation is a
# documented follow-on.

kind = "spoof-detect"

[attack]
power_advantage_db = 1.5
carrier_aligned = false
push = "position"
push_magnitude_m = 75.0
num_biased = 3
el_imbalance = 0.12

[detector]
sat_power_dbm = -130.0
agc_margin_db = 3.0
sqm_tolerance = 0.10
raim_p_fa = 1.0e-3
sigma_m = 5.0
fusion_threshold = 0.5

# `satellites` is optional; omitting it uses a well-spread 8-satellite geometry. To specify your
# own sky, list azimuth/elevation rows, e.g.:
# [[satellites]]
# az_deg = 0.0
# el_deg = 80.0
spoof-meaconing.toml:
# Time-spoof detection with an explicit attack shape and a stochastic detector.
#
# The clock-aided monitor forms the GNSS-vs-clock time discrepancy y over a 600 s
# window with 1σ uncertainty σ set by the clock's noise PSD. A spoof shifts y's
# mean to the spoof offset μ. The detector is a two-sided χ²₁ energy test
# (y/σ)² > λ, with λ read off the inverse χ²₁ CDF at the target false-alarm
# probability. The Security figure of merit is 1 − P_md, the probability of
# correctly detecting a spec-sized spoof; both the closed-form P_md and a
# Monte-Carlo estimate (mc_runs trials per hypothesis) are reported.
#
# Here the attack is a meaconing (delayed re-broadcast) shape rather than the
# default linear ramp: a constant delay with a sinusoidal component from the relay
# geometry. Switch `kind` to `linear_ramp`, `step_jump`, or `replay` for the other
# shapes.
# The timing spec is deliberately tight (0.5 ns) so the chip-scale clock sits at a
# stressed operating point (its ~0.24 ns monitor noise puts a spec-sized spoof at
# only ~2σ → it is missed most of the time), while the optical clock — ~50× quieter
# — still catches it with near-certainty. A looser spec is caught by both.
kind = "spoof"
threshold_ns = 0.5

[time]
step_s = 1.0
duration_s = 1200.0

[attack]
start_s = 100.0
target_pfa = 0.001
mc_runs = 20000

[attack.shape]
kind = "meaconing"
delay_ns = 8.0
oscillation_hz = 0.01

# An optical clock (quiet) vs a chip-scale atomic clock (noisier short-term).
[clock_quantum]
id = "optical-lattice"
provenance = "Optical lattice clock: ADEV ~1e-16/sqrt(tau); laboratory maturity"
y0 = 0.0
q_wf = 1.0e-26
q_rw = 1.0e-34
drift = 0.0
flicker_floor = 0.0

[clock_classical]
id = "csac"
provenance = "Chip-scale atomic clock (Microsemi SA.45s class): ADEV ~3e-10/sqrt(tau)"
y0 = 0.0
q_wf = 1.0e-22
q_rw = 1.0e-30
drift = 0.0
flicker_floor = 0.0
starlink-sop-doppler-positioning.toml:
# Doppler-only positioning from a broadband constellation used as a signal of opportunity.
#
# The Starlink downlink carries no navigation message and its code and carrier phase are not
# usable for ranging, but its Doppler is: Kozhaya, Saroufim and Kassas ("Unveiling Starlink
# for PNT", NAVIGATION 72(1), 2025, https://navi.ion.org/content/72/1/navi.685) track the
# 240 MHz OFDM beacon at 11.325 GHz with a Doppler error of about 30 Hz (one sigma) and report
# about 2 m three-dimensional error in 20 s with three satellites. This scenario uses the
# `starlink-sop` preset: the first shell of 1584 satellites at 550 km and 53 deg (FCC 21-48;
# the Walker phasing is representative) with that Doppler error, a stationary receiver in
# Columbus, Ohio, a window of one minute, and one Doppler measurement per satellite every
# 0.1 s (the beacon repeats every 4/3 ms, so a receiver can form Doppler far faster; whether
# faster estimates are independent is not known, so the rate is a modelling input).
#
# The error-against-window table is the comparison with the published figure. It is a
# MODELLED consistency check, not a reproduction: the paper's receiver estimated the
# satellite states and oscillator offsets from real captures, while this model has a perfect
# ephemeris and puts every error into the 30 Hz Doppler sigma.
kind = "leo-pvt"
mode = "doppler"
seed = 11
duration_s = 60.0
step_s = 0.1

[user]
lat_deg = 40.0
lon_deg = -83.0
height_m = 220.0

[doppler]
# The receiver knows its height to 5 m (a barometer or a terrain model): Doppler from one
# shell at 53 deg constrains the vertical weakly over a short window.
height_sigma_m = 5.0
windows_s = [5.0, 10.0, 20.0, 40.0, 60.0]

[[system]]
name = "Starlink SoP"
leo_preset = "starlink-sop"
mask_deg = 25.0
sweep-clock-stability.toml:
# Trade study: how does holdover scale with clock stability?
#
# Sweep the classical clock's white-FM noise PSD (q_wf = sigma_y(1s)^2) across
# five decades and record the holdover time — the seconds the clock keeps the
# timing solution inside the spec after GNSS is lost. The quantum clock is held
# fixed, so its curve is flat and the gap to the classical curve is the stability
# advantage as a function of clock grade. Vendor-neutral; the base scenario is the
# 2 h clock-holdover reference.

kind = "sweep"
parameter = "classical_q_wf"   # vary the classical white-FM PSD
metric = "holdover_s"          # record the holdover time
start = 1.0e-24                # ~ optical-class sigma_y(1s)=1e-12
stop = 1.0e-18                 # ~ poor oscillator sigma_y(1s)=1e-9
steps = 25
scale = "log"

[base]
seed = 42
threshold_ns = 20.0

[base.time]
step_s = 10.0
duration_s = 7200.0

[base.gnss]
windows = [
  { t0 = 0.0,    t1 = 600.0,  state = "nominal" },
  { t0 = 600.0,  t1 = 7200.0, state = "denied" },
]

[base.clock_quantum]
id = "optical-sr-lattice"
provenance = "Strontium optical lattice clock, space-oriented goal sigma_y(1s)=1e-15 (arXiv:1503.08457); q_wf=sigma_y(1s)^2; flicker floor modeled at sigma_y=1e-16; not flown."
y0   = 5.0e-17
q_wf = 1.0e-30
q_rw = 0.0
flicker_floor = 1.0e-16

[base.clock_classical]
id = "csac-sa45s"
provenance = "Microchip SA.45s CSAC datasheet sigma_y(1s)=3e-10; q_wf is swept by this study; flicker floor modeled at sigma_y=2e-11."
y0   = 5.0e-10
q_wf = 9.0e-20
q_rw = 0.0
flicker_floor = 2.0e-11
sweep-nd-inertial.toml:
# Generic N-D parameter sweep over ANY scenario kind. Unlike the clock-only
# `sweep` kind, `sweep-nd` varies dotted TOML keys of the `[base]` scenario over
# the Cartesian product of the axes, re-runs each grid node, and reads the chosen
# metrics out of the result by dotted JSON path. It works for every pack
# (inertial, gnss-ins, integrity, spoof, …) because it operates at the
# TOML/result boundary, not on a per-pack Rust type. Native runs evaluate the
# grid in parallel (no extra dependency); wasm falls back to sequential. The
# output grid is deterministic and row-major (the last axis varies fastest).
#
# This example sweeps the inertial dead-reckoning pack over the GNSS-outage alert
# threshold and the classical accelerometer bias, recording the holdover and the
# drift RMS for the classical sensor at every node.
kind = "sweep-nd"
metrics = ["classical.fom.holdover_s", "classical.fom.pos_rms_m"]

[[axes]]
key = "threshold_m"
start = 100.0
stop = 500.0
steps = 5

[[axes]]
key = "accel_classical.bias"
start = 1.0e-3
stop = 3.0e-3
steps = 3
scale = "log"

[base]
kind = "inertial"
seed = 42
threshold_m = 100.0

[base.time]
step_s = 10.0
duration_s = 7200.0

[base.gnss]
windows = [
  { t0 = 0.0,   t1 = 600.0,  state = "nominal" },
  { t0 = 600.0, t1 = 7200.0, state = "denied" },
]

[base.accel_quantum]
id = "cold-atom-quat"
provenance = "Cold-atom quantum accelerometer: low residual bias"
bias = 5.88e-7
q_va = 4.6656e-8

[base.accel_classical]
id = "nav-grade-quartz"
provenance = "Navigation-grade quartz accelerometer: larger residual bias"
bias = 1.57e-3
q_va = 3.8416e-8
bias_instability = 1.0e-5
q_aa = 1.0e-13
telecom-prtc-holdover-24h.toml:
# Telecom timing reference: a rubidium clock that loses its Global Navigation Satellite
# System (GNSS) reference and holds over for 24 hours, checked against the masks of the
# International Telecommunication Union Telecommunication Standardization Sector (ITU-T).
#
# The record is 25 hours at one sample per second. For the first hour the clock is
# disciplined, and its time error is 1 ns of white phase noise. At 3 600 s the GNSS
# reference is lost and the clock free-runs for 24 hours with:
#   - white, flicker and (where the fit needs it) random-walk frequency noise, fitted to
#     the datasheet's Allan-deviation maxima and scaled to lie at or above every one;
#   - linear frequency aging at the datasheet's monthly figure;
#   - a daily temperature cycle of +/-2 K (an illustrative indoor swing) through the
#     datasheet's temperature bound, read linearly as a worst case.
# The oscillator figures come from the Microchip 8040C Rubidium Frequency Standard
# datasheet (DS00003047A). How they become a noise model is MODELLED: see the report's
# `oscillator` block and docs/TELECOM-TIMING.md.
#
# What the run answers: how long this clock stays inside each time-error budget, and
# whether the record meets the ePRTC-A holdover requirement of ITU-T G.8272.1 (a time
# error that may rise from 30 ns to 100 ns over the holdover period). A rubidium clock is
# not the caesium-class reference that requirement assumes, so a FAIL there is the
# expected, informative answer. PRTC-A (ITU-T G.8272) is a LOCKED-mode requirement; it is
# applied here as a comparison only, and the report states that condition beside it.
#
# Not a conformance test and not a measurement of any unit.
kind = "telecom-timing"
seed = 20260925
masks = ["eprtc-a-holdover", "prtc-a"]

[holdover]
oscillator = "rubidium"
gnss_loss_s = 3600.0
duration_s = 90000.0
sample_interval_s = 1.0
locked_te_sigma_ns = 1.0
initial_frequency_offset = 0.0
temperature_amplitude_k = 2.0
temperature_period_s = 86400.0
# ITU-T G.8272.1 Table 3: under 6 days locked, the holdover period H is 70 000 s.
locked_duration_days = 5.0

# Budgets: each is a figure an ITU-T Recommendation states.
[[budgets]]
name = "ePRTC default max|TE_HO|"
max_abs_te_ns = 100.0
source = "ITU-T G.8272.1 (2024) Amd. 1 (07/2025) clause 8.3.1"

[[budgets]]
name = "network holdover allocation, short GNSS interruption"
max_abs_te_ns = 400.0
source = "ITU-T G.8271.1 (2022) Amd. 3 (05/2025) Table V.1, failure scenario (b) (an example allocation)"

[[budgets]]
name = "network limit at reference point C"
max_abs_te_ns = 1100.0
source = "ITU-T G.8271.1 (2022) Amd. 3 (05/2025) clause 7.3.1 (max|TE_L|, compared unfiltered)"

[[budgets]]
name = "end application, accuracy class 4"
max_abs_te_ns = 1500.0
source = "ITU-T G.8271 (03/2020) Amd. 1 (08/2024) Table 1, class 4"
terrain-nav.toml:
# Terrain-referenced navigation (TERCOM/SITAN) — GPS-denied alt-PNT.
#
# A vehicle flies a known-shape track with no GNSS, its inertial solution drifting to ≈ 70 km
# of position error. A radar/baro altimeter measures the ground elevation under each waypoint
# (with its real, seeded white-noise floor injected), and a hierarchical coarse-to-fine
# particle/grid matcher recovers the constant INS drift to a few hundred metres against a
# stored digital elevation model — the classic terrain-contour-matching (TERCOM) / Sandia
# inertial terrain-aided navigation (SITAN) technique, whose published CEP is "as low as tens
# of metres" (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TERCOM).
#
# Consumed by `kshana::altpnt::terrain::run_terrain_nav` (and its unit tests), and dispatched
# by the scenario engine as `kind = "terrain-nav"`. The DEM is the self-contained synthetic
# fixture (`DemGrid::synthetic_fixture`) — a deterministic multi-Gaussian + tilted-ridge relief
# field, the terrain analogue of the gravity mascons. A real SRTM tile and a real crustal map
# are documented follow-ons (see docs/CAPABILITY.md); the recovery is validated against the
# INDEPENDENTLY injected drift, never the DEM's own value (non-circular).
kind = "terrain-nav"

# Synthetic-DEM seed (jitters the feature placement deterministically).
dem_seed = 1

# Track flown GPS-denied: 60 waypoints over an oblique leg so the scalar altimeter sequence
# is observable in both north and east.
start_lat_deg = 12.05
start_lon_deg = 20.05
step_lat_deg = 0.004
step_lon_deg = 0.003
waypoints = 60

# True constant INS position drift over the outage (≈ 70 km at ~12° lat — far past the 10 km
# the matched solution must beat).
drift_lat_deg = 0.5
drift_lon_deg = -0.4

# Radar/baro altimeter 1σ noise (m) and the DEM representation error (m); combined into the
# matching σ = hypot(altimeter_sigma_m, map_sigma_m).
altimeter_sigma_m = 8.0
map_sigma_m = 15.0

# Hierarchical offset search: ±0.8° at 0.08° to start, then three coarse-to-fine stages each
# shrinking the window and step 8× ⇒ final offset resolution 0.08° / 8² ≈ 140 m.
search_half_deg = 0.8
search_step_deg = 0.08
refine_stages = 3
refine_factor = 8.0
noise_seed = 1
terrain-slam.toml:
# Sequential (recursive) terrain-referenced navigation — GPS-denied alt-PNT.
#
# The recursive counterpart to `terrain-nav`. There, a batch coarse-to-fine matcher recovers
# a single CONSTANT inertial drift offset over the whole pass. That model breaks when the INS
# error is not constant but GROWS with time (the realistic case for an unaided strapdown unit
# during a GNSS outage). Here a particle filter runs the same altimeter-vs-DEM measurement
# model EPOCH BY EPOCH: at each waypoint the cloud is propagated by the INS-reported increment
# (itself corrupted by the per-step drift growth), reweighted by the terrain match, and
# resampled when it degenerates — Sandia inertial terrain-aided navigation (SITAN) as a
# running estimator, i.e. Monte-Carlo localization against a digital elevation model.
#
# Consumed by `kshana::altpnt::sequential::run_sequential_trn` (and its unit tests), and
# dispatched by the scenario engine as `kind = "terrain-slam"`. The DEM is the self-contained
# synthetic fixture (`DemGrid::synthetic_fixture`) — a 0.5°×0.5° multi-Gaussian + tilted-ridge
# relief patch over [12.0–12.5, 20.0–20.5]; the track and the particle cloud stay inside it.
#
# Scope (honest): the map is KNOWN and FIXED — this is recursive localization against a stored
# DEM, not joint map estimation (full SLAM). The injected drift ramp is the independent ground
# truth and every reported error is measured against it, never the DEM's own value
# (non-circular). A real SRTM tile and a real crustal map remain documented follow-ons
# (docs/CAPABILITY.md).
kind = "terrain-slam"

# Synthetic-DEM seed (jitters the feature placement deterministically).
dem_seed = 1

# Track flown GPS-denied: 60 waypoints over an oblique leg (observable north and east),
# entirely inside the DEM patch (12.08→12.316 lat, 20.08→20.257 lon).
start_lat_deg = 12.08
start_lon_deg = 20.08
step_lat_deg = 0.004
step_lon_deg = 0.003
waypoints = 60

# True INS drift RATE (deg/waypoint): a linear ramp, zero at the first fix, reaching ≈ 5 km of
# free-inertial error by the last waypoint — the moving error the recursive filter tracks.
drift_rate_lat_deg = 0.0006
drift_rate_lon_deg = -0.0005

# Radar/baro altimeter 1σ noise (m) and the DEM representation error (m); combined into the
# matching σ = hypot(altimeter_sigma_m, map_sigma_m).
altimeter_sigma_m = 8.0
map_sigma_m = 15.0

# Particle filter: cloud size, initial spread around the first INS fix, per-step process noise
# (must span the per-step drift growth), and the resample-on-degeneracy threshold (fraction of
# n_particles). Seed drives the deterministic filter / measurement-noise stream.
n_particles = 4000
init_pos_sigma_deg = 0.006
process_sigma_deg = 0.0025
resample_ess_frac = 0.5
seed = 1
timetransfer.toml:
# Optical inter-satellite time transfer vs classical RF (TWSTFT).
#
# Each link is a two-way exchange: the reciprocal (common-mode) path delay
# cancels in the (m_AB - m_BA)/2 estimate, so the error is the white measurement
# jitter (`sigma_j_s`) plus the NON-reciprocal differential delay, modelled as a
# random-walk-FM floor (`q_rw_s`, sigma_y^2(tau) = q_rw*tau/3) — equipment-delay
# asymmetry and up/down-path variation. The reported `adev_tau0` is the link's
# Allan deviation at the 1 s base step.
kind = "timetransfer"
seed = 42
samples = 600
step_s = 1.0
range_spec_mm = 10.0

[link_quantum]
id = "optical-isl"
provenance = "Optical inter-satellite link, picosecond-level synchronization target; free-space optical two-way time-frequency transfer lab floor ~1 fs (Giorgetta 2013, Nature Photonics; Deschenes 2016, PRX). Using a 1 ps target as the on-orbit-credible figure."
sigma_j_s = 1.0e-12
# NON-reciprocity budget (NOT zero): the differential-delay floor — equipment-delay
# asymmetry + up/down-path variation that does NOT cancel in the two-way estimate.
# q_rw=1e-32 => sigma_x ~ 0.6 ps over the session, so the reported sub-mm figure is
# jitter PLUS a conservative on-orbit non-reciprocity floor, not a jitter-only limit.
q_rw_s = 1.0e-32

[link_classical]
id = "twstft-rf"
provenance = "Two-way satellite time and frequency transfer (TWSTFT, Ku-band), single-session ~0.5 ns (BIPM/PTB/NIST)."
sigma_j_s = 5.0e-10
q_rw_s = 1.0e-26   # diurnal/differential-delay random-walk floor of an RF link
tracking-loop.toml:
# Tracking-loop loss of lock: C/N0 -> lock/unlock with hysteresis, the time it takes to
# lose lock, and the spoof pull-in limits set by code and carrier offset RATE.
#
# The engine's existing denial and capture criteria are ratios on received power: a jammer
# denies at J/S = 30 dB and a spoofer captures at J/S = 3 dB. Real loss of lock is not a
# power ratio. A channel gives up when its loops can no longer hold the signal, and that
# depends on the loop noise bandwidth, the predetection integration time, the correlator
# spacing and the dynamics the loop is being asked to follow.
#
# This scenario computes that, and reports the denial radius it implies ALONGSIDE the
# power-ratio radius, with the difference named (denial.denial_radius_delta_km). Neither
# number replaces the other.
#
# Rules applied, both stated in the report rather than buried:
#   carrier: 3*sigma_PLL + theta_e <= 45 deg  (the 15-degree Costas rule, three-sigma form)
#   code:    3*sigma_DLL + ramp lag <= d/2 chips (the discriminator's linear half-range)
#
# Hysteresis is DERIVED, not asserted: re-lock is the same rule evaluated with the wider
# bandwidth a receiver re-pulls-in at, so the width must fall between 5*log10(ratio) and
# 10*log10(ratio) dB. The ratio itself is a modelled design choice.
#
# Every loop parameter below is a MODELLED representative band figure, not a datasheet.
kind = "tracking-loop"

# --- loop geometry -----------------------------------------------------------------
# A 10 Hz Costas carrier loop and a 1 Hz carrier-aided code loop, 1 ms coherent
# integration (one C/A code period, so no data-bit synchronisation is assumed), narrow
# 0.5 chip correlator.
pll_bandwidth_hz = 10.0
dll_bandwidth_hz = 1.0
predetection_integration_s = 0.001
correlator_spacing_chips = 0.5
carrier_allowance_deg = 45.0
# code_allowance_chips defaults to half the correlator spacing.

# Re-pull-in runs at twice the tracking bandwidth. This is the design choice that sets the
# hysteresis width; no physics fixes it, so it is an explicit input.
pullin_bandwidth_ratio = 2.0

# Lock-detector confirmation dwells, in epochs (1 ms each here): 50 ms to declare loss,
# 200 ms of clean signal to declare recovery.
drop_confirm_epochs = 50
relock_confirm_epochs = 200

# Dynamics the loop must follow while tracking. Zero here: a static user, so the whole
# carrier budget is available to thermal jitter and the spoofer.
doppler_rate_hz_per_s = 0.0
code_slew_chips_per_s = 0.0

# --- the C/N0 profile the lock detector is driven over ------------------------------
# A linear ramp from 45 dB-Hz down to 15 dB-Hz over 60 s, then back up over 60 s. The
# down leg gives the time to lose lock; the up leg shows the hysteresis as a recovery
# that happens later and at a higher C/N0 than the drop.
cn0_high_dbhz = 45.0
cn0_low_dbhz = 15.0
ramp_duration_s = 60.0

# C/N0 values the jitter / cycle-slip table is tabulated at.
jitter_table_cn0_dbhz = [45.0, 40.0, 35.0, 30.0, 27.5, 25.0, 22.5, 20.0]

# --- the jammer link both denial radii are evaluated on -----------------------------
# A 10 W broadband jammer against a zenith GPS L1 C/A signal at the IS-GPS-200 minimum
# received power, 290 K system noise temperature, 0 dBi everywhere. The same radiometry
# the `jamming` kind uses; this scenario only inverts it for a radius.
jammer_power_dbw = 10.0
jammer_gain_dbi = 0.0
rx_gain_toward_jammer_db = 0.0
rx_gain_toward_sat_db = 0.0
signal_power_dbw = -158.5
temp_k = 290.0
freq_hz = 1575420000.0
chip_rate_hz = 1023000.0
jammer_type = "broadband"

# The EXISTING power-ratio criteria, reported unchanged next to the loop-dynamics answer.
denial_js_threshold_db = 30.0
capture_js_threshold_db = 3.0

# --- the spoof pull-in map ------------------------------------------------------------
# A spoofer captures by slewing the victim's code and carrier away from truth. Too slow
# and it never moves the victim anywhere useful; too fast and it outruns the victim's
# loops, which is what makes this a RATE condition and not a power ratio.
spoof_code_slew_chips_per_s = [0.1, 0.5, 1.0, 2.0, 5.0]
spoof_doppler_rate_hz_per_s = [1.0, 10.0, 40.0, 100.0, 500.0]
xona-pulsar-end-to-end.toml:
# Xona Pulsar end to end: the public X5 signal -> a Pulsar pass -> a LEO navigation message
# -> GPS + Galileo + Pulsar fused fix and precise point positioning convergence.
#
# Every Pulsar number is public: Leclere, Marathe and Reid, "Insights into Xona Pulsar LEO
# PNT", ION GNSS+ 2025, https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.19551 (X5 at 1190.51625 MHz, 10.23 Mchip/s,
# data and pilot in quadrature with a 50/50 split, received power -144.9 to -136.2 dBW;
# 258 satellites in 18 planes at about 1080 km, inclined 53 deg and polar 97 deg shells).
#
# - Signal: the `xona-x5` design from data/leo-signals/xona-pulsar.toml.
# - Pass: a maritime user in the Bay of Biscay watches a Pulsar satellite of the inclined
#   shell peak at 70 deg. The band is the link preset's X5 (flat pattern, the EIRP that
#   delivers the published minimum power at 10 deg), carrying the X5 design.
# - Navigation message: the Pulsar broadcast-ephemeris model is not public (the brief marks
#   it UNCONFIRMED), so the message is Kshana's Galileo Keplerian set with along-track,
#   cross-track and radial corrections, fitted every 300 s; 0.25 m of orbit-determination and
#   clock error is added as a representative decimetre-level figure (not a Xona figure).
# - Positioning: GPS and Galileo with the Pulsar inclined shell (192 satellites, 12 planes).
# - Precise point positioning (PPP): GPS and Galileo alone and with both Pulsar shells.
#

[fusion]

[fusion.user]

xona-pulsar-signals.toml:
# Xona Pulsar signals: the X1 (L1 band) and X5 (L5 band) signals of a commercial low
# Earth orbit (LEO) positioning, navigation and timing (PNT) constellation, from their
# published signal table (Leclère, Marathe and Reid, ION GNSS+ 2025,
# https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.19551), as the compiled-in `xona-pulsar` preset.
#
# The questions: how precisely can a receiver range on each signal at its minimum
# received power; how large is the acquisition search from 1080 km, where the Doppler
# reaches the 32 to 34 kHz the paper reports; and how much does each signal overlap the
# GNSS signals near it? X5 sits at 1190.51625 MHz, inside the Galileo E5 band, so its
# spectral separation coefficient (SSC) into Galileo E5a, E5b and AltBOC and into GPS L5
# is the compatibility figure that matters; X1 sits 17.9 MHz above the GPS L1 carrier.
#
# Received power: the published minimum (X1 -148.2 dBW, X5 -144.9 dBW) against a 290 K
# antenna and a 2 dB noise figure (floor -201.98 dBW/Hz), so the reference
# carrier-to-noise density (C/N0) is about 53.8 and 57.1 dB-Hz. The enhanced Feher QPSK
# spectrum is drawn with the rectangular-chip BPSK envelope, as the preset states.
# MODELLED: the closed forms underneath are validated; the design approximations are not.
kind = "leo-signal"
presets = ["xona-pulsar"]

[receiver]
noise_figure_db = 2.0
antenna_temp_k = 290.0
cn0_dbhz = [35.0, 40.0, 45.0, 50.0, 55.0, 60.0]
reference_cn0_dbhz = 45.0
loop_bandwidth_hz = 1.0
integration_time_s = 0.02
correlator_spacings_chips = [1.0, 0.5, 0.2, 0.1]
reference_spacing_chips = 0.5

[acquisition]
elevation_mask_deg = 0.0
oscillator_ppm = 0.5
coherent_ms = 1.0
noncoherent = 1
pfa_cell = 1e-4

[compatibility]
gnss_aggregate_satellites = 1.0

[trade]
reference_signal = "xona-x5"
slant_tec_tecu = 50.0
slant_range_km = 1500.0
